Credo is an open source TypeScript framework for verifiable credentials. You use it to build issuers, verifiers, wallets and mediators that exchange SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C and AnonCreds credentials over OpenID4VC and DIDComm, on Node.js and React Native.

This page describes what you pass to new Agent(), the modules every agent has, and how to start and stop an agent. The other pages in this section cover the choices you make when you set up an agent.

Choice Mobile wallet Server Details Storage Askar on SQLite Drizzle on PostgreSQL, or on SQLite for a single instance or development Storage Key management Askar, plus the secure environment for keys that must stay in hardware Askar, with its storage turned off Key management Cache The default The default for one agent, InMemoryLruCache with tenants, Redis with several instances Caching Multi-tenancy Not needed Only when one service hosts many isolated issuers, verifiers or wallets Multi-tenancy For tests, use Drizzle on an in-memory SQLite database and keep the keys in memory with the Node.js backend.

Option Description dependencies Required. The platform implementations of the file system, fetch, WebSocket and events: agentDependencies from @credo-ts/node or @credo-ts/react-native. modules The modules of the agent, keyed by the name of their API. Include a storage module, Drizzle or Askar: without one, new Agent() throws Missing required dependency: 'StorageService'. config Agent-wide settings, described below.

Field Default Description logger ConsoleLogger at LogLevel.Off The logger of the agent and its modules. See Logging. autoUpdateStorageOnStartup false Update the storage during initialize() when it was written by an older version of Credo. See Storage updates. allowInsecureHttpUrls false Accept http:// URLs where HTTPS is otherwise required, such as OpenID4VC endpoints. For local development only. The OpenID4VC module applies it to the whole process, so it also affects other agents in it. validitySkewSeconds 30 The clock skew, in seconds, allowed when checking the validity period of credentials, status lists and other signed objects. Phones often run a little behind. getTrustedIssuersForVerification none A callback that returns the DIDs and X.509 certificates to trust for a verification. See Trusted issuers.

Credo registers these modules on every agent: Key Module API dids DidsModule agent.dids kms KeyManagementModule agent.kms sdJwtVc SdJwtVcModule agent.sdJwtVc mdoc MdocModule agent.mdoc w3cCredentials W3cCredentialsModule agent.w3cCredentials w3cV2Credentials W3cV2CredentialsModule agent.w3cV2Credentials w3cDataIntegrity W3cDataIntegrityModule agent.w3cDataIntegrity x509 X509Module agent.x509 tokenStatusList TokenStatusListModule agent.tokenStatusList genericRecords GenericRecordsModule agent.genericRecords cache CacheModule with a SingleContextStorageLruCache of 500 entries none dcql DcqlModule none pex DifPresentationExchangeModule none The kms module starts without a backend. AskarModule adds one, also when Drizzle stores the records. Without Askar, configure a backend yourself (see Key management). The default cache doesn't work with multi-tenancy, so replace it when you use tenants (see Caching).

To configure a default module, pass your own instance under the same key: agent.ts import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, DidsModule, JwkDidRegistrar, JwkDidResolver, KeyDidRegistrar, KeyDidResolver, LogLevel, WebDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' function getAgentModules() { return { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // Same key as the default module, so it replaces it dids: new DidsModule({ registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [new KeyDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver()], }), } } const agent = new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Warn), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: getAgentModules(), }) The API stays where it was, at agent.dids. When you pass resolvers or registrars to the DidsModule, your list replaces the defaults, except for did:key and did:peer, which are always added.

Default modules are at the top level, for example agent.dids, also when you replace them. Other modules are under agent.modules, for example agent.modules.askar or agent.modules.tenants. The exceptions are didcomm and openid4vc: registered under exactly those keys, they're also at agent.didcomm and agent.openid4vc. Modules without an API, such as cache, have no property on the agent. The Agent class infers these types from the modules you pass to the constructor. To type an agent you pass to other functions, derive the type from a function that returns the modules: export type MyAgent = Agent<ReturnType<typeof getAgentModules>> export async function createDid(agent: MyAgent) { const { didState } = await agent.dids.create({ method: 'jwk', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } } }, }) return didState.did } Agent without a type argument accepts any agent, but loses the types of agent.modules.

await agent.initialize() console.log(`Created ${await createDid(agent)}`) await agent.shutdown() console.log(`Agent initialized: ${agent.isInitialized}`) initialize() initializes the modules: it opens the storage (Askar creates the store on the first run), starts DIDComm transports and adds OpenID4VC routes to the Express app. Then it checks the storage version. Calling initialize() on an agent that is already initialized throws. shutdown() stops the modules and their transports and closes the storage. Afterwards agent.isInitialized is false, and you can initialize the agent again.

Credo stores the version of its storage format. When you start a newer version of Credo on storage that needs an update, initialize() throws Current agent storage is not up to date. Set autoUpdateStorageOnStartup: true to run the update during initialize(), or run it yourself. Credo doesn't back up the storage first, so make a backup before you upgrade. See Updating. With Drizzle, the database schema has its own SQL migrations, which you run separately. See Drizzle.

Credo caches data that is slow to fetch: resolved DID documents, AnonCreds objects from ledgers and revocation lists of X.509 certificates. A cache is always registered, and you only replace it in two cases: when you use multi-tenancy, and when several instances of the agent run side by side.

Keep the default for a single agent without tenants, such as a mobile wallet: nothing to configure, and entries survive a restart. Use InMemoryLruCache when the agent has tenants, because the default throws as soon as a tenant uses it. Use RedisCache when several instances of the agent run behind a load balancer, so they share one cache. With the default, instances overwrite each other's cache record in the shared storage, and with InMemoryLruCache each instance fetches and caches everything on its own. Cache Package Tenants Several processes share it Survives a restart SingleContextStorageLruCache (default) @credo-ts/core No No Yes InMemoryLruCache @credo-ts/core Yes No No RedisCache @credo-ts/redis-cache Yes Yes Yes The default keeps up to 500 entries in memory and saves them as a record in the agent's storage. When a tenant uses it, it throws SingleContextStorageLruCache can not be used with multiple agent context instances.

Register a CacheModule under the key cache to replace the default: agent.ts import { Agent, CacheModule, InMemoryLruCache } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new InMemoryLruCache({ limit: 500 }), }), }, }) InMemoryLruCache removes the least recently used entries when it reaches limit. The limit applies to all agent contexts together. CacheModule option Description cache The cache to use. Required. defaultExpiryInSeconds Expiry for entries set without one. RedisCache uses it. Default 60. useCachedStorageService Also caches DIDComm connection, mediation and mediator routing records, to save storage reads on busy DIDComm agents such as mediators. Default false. With several instances, only turn it on with a cache they share, such as Redis.

npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 ioredis pnpm add @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 ioredis yarn add @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 ioredis bun add @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 ioredis agent.ts import { Agent, CacheModule } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache' import { Redis } from 'ioredis' const redis = new Redis('redis://localhost:6379') const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup cache: new CacheModule({ // Also accepts ioredis options, e.g. new RedisCache({ host: 'localhost', port: 6379 }) cache: new RedisCache(redis), defaultExpiryInSeconds: 300, }), }, }) RedisCache takes an ioredis client or ioredis options. Keys are prefixed with the agent context, or with global: for shared entries, so tenants and instances can share one Redis database. When you create the client yourself, close it after the agent shuts down: agent.ts await agent.shutdown() // The agent doesn't close the Redis connection for you await redis.quit() cache.destroy(agentContext) removes all entries of one agent context, for example after you delete a tenant.

Data Cached for Scope Resolved DID documents, for methods whose resolver allows caching (did:web, did:webvh, did:cheqd, did:indy, did:sov, did:hedera). did:key, did:jwk and did:peer aren't cached. 5 minutes, change it with cacheDurationInSeconds when resolving Global for methods in DidsModule({ publicDidMethods }), otherwise per agent context AnonCreds schemas, credential definitions, revocation registry definitions and status lists 5 minutes Global Summaries of X.509 certificate revocation lists Until the list's next update Global Indy VDR: which ledger a DID is on Until evicted Global DIDComm connection, mediation and mediator routing records, with useCachedStorageService: true Until evicted Per agent context Global entries are public data that all tenants share. publicDidMethods defaults to web, indy, sov, cheqd, hedera and webvh.

Implement the Cache interface: get, set and remove. Each method receives the agent context and an optional scope. Keep entries of different agent contexts apart, and only share entries when scope is 'global': map-cache.ts import type { AgentContext, Cache, CacheOptions } from '@credo-ts/core' export class MapCache implements Cache { private entries = new Map<string, { value: unknown; expiresAt?: number }>() // Isolate entries per agent context unless the caller asks for the global scope private key(agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, options?: CacheOptions) { return options?.scope === 'global' ? `global:${key}` : `${agentContext.contextCorrelationId}:${key}` } public async get<CacheValue>(agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, options?: CacheOptions) { const namespacedKey = this.key(agentContext, key, options) const entry = this.entries.get(namespacedKey) if (!entry) return null if (entry.expiresAt && entry.expiresAt < Date.now()) { this.entries.delete(namespacedKey) return null } return entry.value as CacheValue } public async set<CacheValue>( agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, value: CacheValue, expiresInSeconds?: number, options?: CacheOptions ) { this.entries.set(this.key(agentContext, key, options), { value, expiresAt: expiresInSeconds ? Date.now() + expiresInSeconds * 1000 : undefined, }) } public async remove(agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, options?: CacheOptions) { this.entries.delete(this.key(agentContext, key, options)) } }

The key management service (KMS) creates and stores keys and does the cryptography with them: signing, verifying, encrypting and key agreement. Credo modules use it for DIDs, credentials, DIDComm and OpenID4VC, and you can call it directly through agent.kms. The KMS hands the work to one or more backends.

You're building Use Why A server Askar Keys are stored encrypted and survive restarts. With Drizzle storing the records, Askar keeps only the keys. A mobile wallet Askar, plus the secure environment for keys that must stay in hardware Askar handles everything the secure environment can't, such as verifying, encryption and Ed25519. Tests and other short-lived agents Node.js, with in-memory key storage Lighter than Askar: it only uses node:crypto, and the keys are gone when the process stops. Keys in a cloud KMS or an HSM Your own backend Credo doesn't ship one, but a backend is a single interface. See Build your own backend. Add the Node.js backend next to Askar to verify RSA signatures and other algorithms Askar lacks, for example of an X.509 certificate authority. Verifying with a public key stores nothing. Don't make the Node.js backend a server's only backend for keys it creates: it keeps them in memory, unless you give it a key storage of your own.

Keys in the secure environment are created in the phone's secure hardware and never leave it, so a copy of the wallet's data can't sign with them. Use it for the keys that credentials are bound to when issuers ask for it. Under HAIP, an issuer can require a key attestation that says how the keys are protected, and the EUDI Wallet requires hardware-protected keys for credentials such as the PID. When no issuer asks for it, keep the keys in Askar, because hardware keys come with trade-offs: Every signature shows a biometric prompt, so a presentation or a batch issuance asks the user to authenticate for each key it signs with. Only P-256 keys and ES256 signatures. DIDs and credentials that need Ed25519 stay in Askar. The keys can't be backed up or moved, so on a new phone the user needs new credentials. Changing the enrolled biometrics also invalidates the keys.

KeyManagementModule is a default module under the key kms, registered without backends. AskarModule adds the askar backend, unless you set enableKms: false. For other backends, register new KeyManagementModule({ backends, defaultBackend }) yourself under the key kms, as in the examples below. Import KeyManagementModule and the other KMS classes from @credo-ts/core/kms. Credo doesn't check for a backend at startup. Without one, the agent initializes, and every key operation throws No key management service backend found that supports ....
AskarKeyManagementService (backend askar) keeps keys in the Askar store, encrypted with the store key, on Node.js and React Native. See Askar.

NodeKeyManagementService from @credo-ts/node (backend node) uses node:crypto, so it needs no native library. It supports more algorithms than Askar, such as RSA, P-521 and HMAC. It has two common uses: the only backend of a test or other short-lived agent, and a second backend that verifies what Askar can't (see Verify RSA signatures). It needs a key storage. For a test agent, keep the keys in memory: agent.ts import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { kms: new KeyManagementModule({ // Keys only live in memory: they are lost when the process stops backends: [new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())], }), storage, // Storage, see Agent setup }, }) Keys are kept in memory NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage is the only key storage that Credo ships. Keys are lost when the process stops, while DIDs and credentials in storage still refer to them. To keep keys, implement the NodeKeyManagementStorage interface (get, has, set, delete). It receives private keys as JWKs, so encrypt them at rest.

SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService from @credo-ts/react-native (backend secureEnvironment) creates keys in the Secure Enclave on iOS and the Android Keystore, protected with biometrics. It needs @animo-id/expo-secure-environment 0.1 (version 0.2 doesn't match the peer dependency range). The package's README lists its platform requirements, such as Android API 30 or higher. npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 pnpm add @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 yarn add @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 bun add @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 It only creates P-256 keys, signs with ES256 and deletes keys. It can't verify, encrypt, import keys or generate random bytes, so you always use it next to Askar. See Askar and the secure environment.

Askar Node.js Secure environment Platforms Node.js, React Native Node.js React Native Keys are stored In the Askar store In memory, or your own storage In secure hardware EC curves P-256, P-384, secp256k1 P-256, P-384, P-521, secp256k1 P-256 OKP curves Ed25519, X25519 Ed25519, X25519 No RSA No Yes No Symmetric keys AES-128, AES-256, ChaCha20-Poly1305 AES, HMAC No Sign and verify EdDSA, ES256, ES384, ES256K EdDSA, ES256, ES384, ES512, ES256K, RS*, PS*, HS* ES256, sign only Encrypt and decrypt AES-GCM, AES-CBC-HMAC, (X)ChaCha20, XSalsa20, AES key wrap, ECDH-ES, HPKE AES-GCM, AES-CBC, AES-CBC-HMAC, ChaCha20, ECDH-ES, HPKE No Import keys EC and OKP keys EC, OKP, RSA and symmetric keys No

Every backend has a name (askar, node, secureEnvironment). Credo decides which one handles an operation like this: If you pass backend, that backend handles it, or the call throws if it can't. sign and getPublicKey use the backend that holds the key, which they look up by its key id. Otherwise, the default backend handles it if it supports the operation, and else the first other backend that does. This applies to createKey, importKey, randomBytes, deleteKey, verify, encrypt and decrypt. So pass backend to verify, encrypt, decrypt and deleteKey when the key isn't in the default backend. The default backend is defaultBackend, or else the first backend in the list. The list starts with the backends you pass to KeyManagementModule, and AskarModule adds askar after them. defaultBackend must name a backend in your own backends list. So to make Askar the default, add AskarKeyManagementService to backends yourself and set enableKms: false on AskarModule: agent.ts import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, TypedArrayEncoder } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage, // Storage, see Agent setup kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [new AskarKeyManagementService(), new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())], defaultBackend: 'askar', }), askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, // Askar only keeps the keys, and its backend is already in the backends list above enableStorage: false, enableKms: false, store: { id: 'kms-backends-example', key: 'kms-backends-example-store-key' }, }), }, }) Then each key goes to a backend that supports it: agent.ts // Askar supports Ed25519, so the default backend creates this key const ed25519Key = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } }) // Askar doesn't support P-521, so this falls back to the node backend const p521Key = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-521' } }) // Pass a backend to choose it explicitly const rsaKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ backend: 'node', type: { kty: 'RSA', modulusLength: 2048 } }) // sign finds the backend that holds the key const data = TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String('Hello, Credo') await agent.kms.sign({ keyId: p521Key.keyId, algorithm: 'ES512', data })

On a phone, make Askar the default and use the secure environment only for the keys that need hardware protection: agent.ts import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, TypedArrayEncoder } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies, SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' export async function initializeAgent(walletKey: string) { const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [new AskarKeyManagementService(), new SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService()], defaultBackend: 'askar', }), askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, // The Askar backend is already in the backends list above enableKms: false, store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw' }, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() return agent } Don't only list the secure environment in backends and let AskarModule add its backend: the secure environment then comes first and becomes the default, and every P-256 key Credo creates ends up in hardware behind biometrics. Create a hardware key by passing backend. Signing finds the key by its key id: hardware-key.ts export async function signWithHardwareKey(agent: Agent, message: string) { // Only P-256 keys and ES256 signatures are supported in the secure environment const { keyId, publicJwk } = await agent.kms.createKey({ backend: 'secureEnvironment', type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' }, }) const { signature } = await agent.kms.sign({ keyId, algorithm: 'ES256', data: TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String(message), }) return { publicJwk, signature } } To verify a signature from a hardware key, pass the publicJwk instead of the key id, so the default backend does it.
documents.s: Askar and the secure environment on React Native

documents.t: Neither Askar nor the secure environment supports RSA. You still meet RSA signatures from others, for example X.509 certificate authorities that sign with RSA, or JWTs signed by an external RSA key. Credo can't check those without a backend that verifies RSA, and the error doesn't always say so: an mdoc issued under an RSA certificate authority fails with an error about the certificate chain. On Node.js, add the Node.js backend next to Askar. A verification with a public key needs no stored key, so the in-memory key storage is enough: agent.ts import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage, // Storage, see Agent setup kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [ new AskarKeyManagementService(), // Only verifies with public keys passed in the call, so nothing is stored in it new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage()), ], defaultBackend: 'askar', }), askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, enableKms: false, store: { id: 'kms-node-verify-example', key: 'kms-node-verify-example-store-key' }, }), }, }) Credo then sends RSA verifications to it: verify.ts // Askar can't verify RS256, so Credo falls back to the node backend const { verified } = await agent.kms.verify({ key: { publicJwk: { kty: 'RSA', n, e } }, algorithm: 'RS256', data, signature, }) On React Native, the Node.js backend isn't available. Add your own backend that only verifies RSA signatures, as described in Build your own backend. Paradym Wallet has one, built on react-native-quick-crypto: RsaVerificationKeyManagementService. Register it next to the other backends: agent.ts new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [ new AskarKeyManagementService(), new SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService(), new RsaVerificationKeyManagementService(), ], defaultBackend: 'askar', })

A backend is a class that implements KeyManagementService from @credo-ts/core/kms. Write one to keep keys in a cloud KMS such as Google Cloud KMS or AWS KMS, in an HSM, or on a platform Credo has no backend for. Implement only what your key store can do, and leave the rest to Askar or the Node.js backend in the same agent. Credo uses these parts of the interface to route operations: Member What Credo expects backend A unique name. Users pass it as backend to choose this backend. isOperationSupported(agentContext, operation) true for each operation and algorithm the backend handles, such as createKey for P-256 keys or sign with ES256. Credo never sends this backend an operation it returns false for. A call that names this backend for such an operation throws. getPublicKey(agentContext, keyId) The public JWK, with kid, or null when the backend doesn't hold the key. For sign and getPublicKey, Credo asks each backend in turn to find the one that holds a key. createKey, importKey, deleteKey Manage keys. Return the key id that Credo stores in DIDs and credential records, so keep it stable. Respect options.keyId when it's set. sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt, randomBytes The cryptography. Throw KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError or KeyManagementError for what you don't support. This backend creates P-256 keys in a cloud KMS and signs with them. The CloudKmsClient interface stands in for your KMS SDK: CloudKeyManagementService.ts import { createHash, createPublicKey } from 'node:crypto' import { type AgentContext, utils } from '@credo-ts/core' import { derEcSignatureToRaw, KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError, KeyManagementError, type KeyManagementService, type KmsCreateKeyOptions, type KmsCreateKeyReturn, type KmsCreateKeyType, type KmsJwkPublic, type KmsOperation, type KmsSignOptions, type KmsSignReturn, PublicJwk, } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' // The calls the backend needs from your cloud KMS SDK. With Google Cloud KMS these are // `createCryptoKey`, `getPublicKey` and `asymmetricSign` of its `KeyManagementServiceClient`. export interface CloudKmsClient { createP256SigningKey(keyId: string): Promise<void> // PEM encoded public key, or null when the key doesn't exist getPublicKeyPem(keyId: string): Promise<string | null> // Signs a SHA-256 digest and returns a DER encoded ECDSA signature signDigest(keyId: string, digest: Uint8Array): Promise<Uint8Array> } export class CloudKeyManagementService implements KeyManagementService { public readonly backend = 'cloud' public constructor(private client: CloudKmsClient) {} // Credo only routes the operations this returns true for to this backend public isOperationSupported(_agentContext: AgentContext, operation: KmsOperation): boolean { if (operation.operation === 'createKey') { return operation.type.kty === 'EC' && operation.type.crv === 'P-256' } return operation.operation === 'sign' && operation.algorithm === 'ES256' } // Credo asks each backend for a key id, so return null for keys this backend doesn't hold public async getPublicKey(_agentContext: AgentContext, keyId: string): Promise<KmsJwkPublic | null> { const pem = await this.client.getPublicKeyPem(keyId) if (!pem) return null const publicJwk = PublicJwk.fromUnknown(createPublicKey(pem).export({ format: 'jwk' })) publicJwk.keyId = keyId return publicJwk.toJson() } public async createKey<Type extends KmsCreateKeyType>( agentContext: AgentContext, options: KmsCreateKeyOptions<Type> ): Promise<KmsCreateKeyReturn<Type>> { if (options.type.kty !== 'EC' || options.type.crv !== 'P-256') { throw new KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError(`kty '${options.type.kty}'`, this.backend) } // Credo stores the key id in DIDs and credential records, so keep it stable const keyId = options.keyId ?? utils.uuid() await this.client.createP256SigningKey(keyId) const publicJwk = await this.getPublicKey(agentContext, keyId) if (!publicJwk) throw new KeyManagementError(`Key '${keyId}' was not found after creating it`) // The generic return type follows from the requested key type, which is checked above return { keyId, publicJwk } as KmsCreateKeyReturn<Type> } public async sign(_agentContext: AgentContext, options: KmsSignOptions): Promise<KmsSignReturn> { if (options.algorithm !== 'ES256') { throw new KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError(`algorithm '${options.algorithm}'`, this.backend) } const digest = createHash('sha256').update(options.data).digest() const derSignature = await this.client.signDigest(options.keyId, digest) // JWA signatures are the raw r || s values, cloud KMSs return them DER encoded return { signature: derEcSignatureToRaw(derSignature, 'P-256') } } // isOperationSupported returns false for these, so Credo uses another backend for them public async verify(): Promise<never> { throw new KeyManagementError(`Verifying is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`) } public async importKey(): Promise<never> { throw new KeyManagementError(`Importing keys is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`) } public async deleteKey(): Promise<never> { throw new KeyManagementError(`Deleting keys is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`) } public async encrypt(): Promise<never> { throw new KeyManagementError(`Encrypting is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`) } public async decrypt(): Promise<never> { throw new KeyManagementError(`Decrypting is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`) } public randomBytes(): never { throw new KeyManagementError(`Generating random bytes is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`) } } Signing has two traps with most cloud KMSs. They sign a digest, so hash the data yourself with the hash of the JWA algorithm (SHA-256 for ES256). And they return ECDSA signatures DER encoded, while JWA uses the raw r || s form: convert them with derEcSignatureToRaw. Register the backend in KeyManagementModule. Here it's the default, so Credo creates P-256 keys in the cloud KMS, and Askar creates the other keys, verifies and encrypts: agent.ts import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' export function createAgent(cloudKmsClient: CloudKmsClient) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage, // Storage, see Agent setup kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [new CloudKeyManagementService(cloudKmsClient), new AskarKeyManagementService()], // P-256 keys are created in the cloud KMS. Askar creates the other keys, such as Ed25519, // and verifies and encrypts. defaultBackend: 'cloud', }), askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, enableKms: false, store: { id: 'cloud-kms-example', key: 'cloud-kms-example-store-key' }, }), }, }) } Import from @credo-ts/core before @credo-ts/core/kms in the file your app loads first, as the kms entry point doesn't load the reflect-metadata polyfill that Credo needs.

kms.ts const { keyId, publicJwk } = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' }, }) const data = TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String('Hello, Credo') const { signature } = await agent.kms.sign({ keyId, algorithm: 'EdDSA', data }) const result = await agent.kms.verify({ key: { publicJwk }, algorithm: 'EdDSA', data, signature, }) console.log(result.verified) // true Method What it does createKey({ type, keyId?, backend? }) Creates a key and returns { keyId, publicJwk }. type is for example { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } or { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' }. createKeyForSignatureAlgorithm({ algorithm }) Creates a key that fits a JWA signature algorithm, such as ES256. importKey({ privateJwk }) Imports a private JWK. Set privateJwk.kid to choose the key id. getPublicKey({ keyId }) Returns the public JWK of a key. sign({ keyId, algorithm, data }) Signs data (a Uint8Array). verify({ key, algorithm, data, signature }) Verifies with key: { keyId } or key: { publicJwk }. Returns { verified }. encrypt(...), decrypt(...) Encrypts and decrypts with a key, a JWK or key agreement. deleteKey({ keyId }) Deletes a key. randomBytes({ length }) Returns random bytes. supportedBackendsForOperation(operation) The backends that support an operation. To use a key in a DID, pass its keyId when you create the DID. See DIDs.
A Credo agent logs nothing until you give it a logger. The agent and all its modules, including tenant agents, use that one logger.

Pass a logger as config.logger: agent.ts import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' const agent = new Agent({ config: { // Logs Info, Warn, Error and Fatal messages logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup }, }) ConsoleLogger prints each message with its level as a prefix, such as INFO: Creating agent with config, using the console method that matches the level. Data passed with a message is printed as JSON. Errors in the data keep their message and stack.

A logger prints messages at its own level and above: Level What Credo logs at this level LogLevel.Test Nothing. Set it to print every message. LogLevel.Trace The most detailed steps, such as key imports, and requests to ledgers and their results. LogLevel.Debug Processing steps of protocols, including the content of DIDComm messages the agent sends. LogLevel.Info Lifecycle events, such as the agent's config when it's created, storage updates, received DIDComm messages and created tenants. LogLevel.Warn Problems the agent recovers from, such as a credential that breaks a recommendation of its specification. LogLevel.Error Failed operations, such as a DIDComm message that can't be delivered. LogLevel.Fatal A storage update that failed. LogLevel.Off Nothing. The default. Use Info or higher in production. At Debug and Trace, logs can contain message contents, credential data and other personal data.

To send logs to your own logging library, implement the Logger interface from @credo-ts/core: a logLevel property and the methods test, trace, debug, info, warn, error and fatal, each taking a message and optional data. Extending BaseLogger saves some work: it stores the level and has isEnabled(level). This logger writes one JSON object per line: JsonLogger.ts import { BaseLogger, LogLevel, replaceError } from '@credo-ts/core' type LogData = Record<string, unknown> export class JsonLogger extends BaseLogger { private log(level: LogLevel, message: string, data?: LogData) { if (!this.isEnabled(level)) return // replaceError keeps the message and stack of errors, which JSON.stringify would drop console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: LogLevel[level], time: new Date().toISOString(), message, data }, replaceError)) } public test(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Test, message, data) } public trace(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Trace, message, data) } public debug(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Debug, message, data) } public info(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Info, message, data) } public warn(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Warn, message, data) } public error(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Error, message, data) } public fatal(message: string, data?: LogData) { this.log(LogLevel.Fatal, message, data) } } Pass it as config.logger, for example new JsonLogger(LogLevel.Info).
With @credo-ts/tenants, one agent hosts many tenants. Each tenant has its own storage, keys, DIDs and credentials, while all tenants share the agent's modules, configuration and endpoints.

Use tenants for a service that issues, verifies or holds credentials on behalf of many organizations or users, such as an issuance platform or a cloud wallet. The alternative, an agent per customer, needs a process, a database and endpoints for each of them. You don't need tenants for a mobile wallet, which has one user. You don't need them either to run several issuers or verifiers for one organization: one agent can host many OpenID4VC issuers and verifiers. Use tenants when each of them needs keys, DIDs and data of its own.
npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2

agent.ts import { AskarModule, AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, CacheModule, InMemoryLruCache } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { tenantsBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/tenants' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { TenantsModule } from '@credo-ts/tenants' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' // Run the migrations of the core and tenants bundles first const database = drizzle('file:agent.db') const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { // The records of all tenants in one database storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [tenantsBundle] }), askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { id: 'credo-keys', key: 'my-agent-store-key' }, // The keys of all tenants in one Askar store, with a profile per tenant multiWalletDatabaseScheme: AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet, }), tenants: new TenantsModule({ sessionLimit: 100, sessionAcquireTimeout: 5000 }), // The default cache throws as soon as a second agent context (a tenant) uses it cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new InMemoryLruCache({ limit: 5000 }) }), }, }) The example stores the records of all tenants in one Drizzle database and their keys in one Askar store. Add tenantsBundle to bundles, pass --bundle tenants when you run the migrations, and use PostgreSQL in production. Replace the default cache: it throws as soon as a tenant uses it. Use InMemoryLruCache, or RedisCache when several instances run the agent. See Caching. TenantsModule option Description sessionLimit Maximum number of tenant sessions open at the same time. Default 100, which is low on purpose: set it based on your hardware and load. Infinity removes the limit. sessionAcquireTimeout How long, in milliseconds, opening a session waits for a free slot when the limit is reached, before it throws Failed to acquire an agent context session. Default 1000. Tenant agents get the modules you register on the root agent. To type them, pass the modules to the generic, for example new TenantsModule<{ openid4vc: OpenId4VcModule }>().

With Drizzle, all tenants share the one database, and each row is tagged with its tenant. Tenant keys are in Askar, where multiWalletDatabaseScheme decides where they go. Set it to AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet, as in the example: all tenants in one Askar store, with a profile each.

When Askar also stores the records, multiWalletDatabaseScheme decides where all tenant data goes: multiWalletDatabaseScheme Tenant records and keys ProfilePerWallet A profile per tenant in the root store DatabasePerWallet (default) A store per tenant, a SQLite file or a PostgreSQL database each, with a generated key that Credo saves in the tenant record Use ProfilePerWallet. It keeps all tenants in one database, performs better with many tenants, and doesn't create a PostgreSQL database per tenant. Store-level tasks, such as rotating the store key or exporting the store, then cover all tenants at once. DatabasePerWallet is the default for backwards compatibility: use it only to back up or delete tenants one by one. No SQLite path with DatabasePerWallet Tenant stores reuse the root store's database config. With an explicit SQLite path, all tenants resolve to the root store's file, and createTenant fails. Leave path unset so each tenant gets its own file in the data directory.

agent.ts const tenantRecord = await agent.modules.tenants.createTenant({ config: { label: 'Tenant 1' }, }) createTenant saves a TenantRecord in the root agent's storage and creates the tenant's storage. The label is for your own use. Use the tenant record's id to open the tenant later.

Work in a tenant through a tenant agent, which has the same API as the root agent, scoped to the tenant. withTenantAgent opens a session, runs your callback and ends the session, also when the callback throws: agent.ts // Opens a session, runs the callback and always ends the session const did = await agent.modules.tenants.withTenantAgent({ tenantId: tenantRecord.id }, async (tenantAgent) => { const { didState } = await tenantAgent.dids.create({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } }, }) return didState.did }) getTenantAgent returns the tenant agent without a callback. End the session yourself with endSession(): agent.ts const tenantAgent = await agent.modules.tenants.getTenantAgent({ tenantId: tenantRecord.id }) try { const createdDids = await tenantAgent.dids.getCreatedDids() console.log(`Tenant has ${createdDids.length} DID(s)`) } finally { // Every session counts against the session limit until you end it await tenantAgent.endSession() } Each open session takes a slot of sessionLimit until it ends, so a missing endSession() eventually blocks new sessions. Inbound DIDComm messages and OpenID4VC requests for a tenant open their own session.

agent.modules.tenants has methods to look up and change tenants: Method What it does getTenantById(tenantId), findTenantsByLabel(label), findTenantsByQuery(query), getAllTenants() Find tenant records. updateTenant(tenantRecord) Saves changes to a tenant record. deleteTenantById(tenantId) Deletes the tenant record and the tenant's storage. getTenantsWithOutdatedStorage(), updateTenantStorage({ tenantId }) Update tenant storage after a Credo upgrade. With autoUpdateStorageOnStartup, Credo updates a tenant when it opens a session. agent.ts await agent.modules.tenants.deleteTenantById(tenantRecord.id)

Tenants share the root agent's endpoints, and Credo finds the tenant for each incoming message or request: DIDComm: when a tenant creates routing keys, for example for a connection, Credo saves which tenant they belong to, and it routes each encrypted message by its recipient key. See DIDComm. OpenID4VC: create issuers and verifiers with a tenant agent. Credo routes requests to their URLs to that tenant. See Issuing credentials and Verifying credentials.
documents.s: Route messages and requests to tenants

documents.t: Every Credo agent needs a storage module to keep its state between restarts: DIDs, credentials, OpenID4VC issuers and sessions, DIDComm connections, tenants and generic records. Credo ships two, Drizzle and Askar, and one of them stores the records. Without one, new Agent() throws Missing required dependency: 'StorageService'.

You're building Records Keys A server Drizzle on PostgreSQL Askar, with storage turned off A server with one instance, or local development Drizzle on SQLite Askar, with storage turned off A mobile wallet Askar on SQLite Askar Tests Drizzle on in-memory SQLite Node.js backend, in memory. Askar in memory for DIDComm, which needs algorithms only Askar has Drizzle scales better on servers: records are SQL tables with indexes that the database can query, and many tenants and instances share one database. On phones, Askar encrypts the wallet with a key you keep in the device keychain, includes key management, and has no schema migrations to ship with app updates. Drizzle on expo-sqlite is an option there too. Drizzle doesn't encrypt records, so rely on encryption of the database or disk. It also adds SQL migrations, also in non-breaking Credo releases, and Credo doesn't work until you apply them. If you can't run migrations on every deploy, use Askar on PostgreSQL for the records as well: it has no schema and encrypts everything with the store key. For many tenants on Askar, use a profile per tenant.

Askar Drizzle Package @credo-ts/askar @credo-ts/drizzle-storage Encryption at rest Record values and tags are encrypted with the store key None. Use encryption of the database or disk Key management included Yes No, add a backend such as Askar Databases SQLite, PostgreSQL PostgreSQL (pg driver), SQLite (libsql or expo-sqlite driver) Platforms Node.js, React Native Node.js, React Native (with expo-sqlite) Schema and migrations No schema, nothing to migrate SQL tables. Run migrations on every Credo upgrade Multi-tenancy A database or a profile per tenant One database, rows scoped per tenant Read records outside Credo No, the data is encrypted Yes, a table per record type Cursor pagination in queries No, only limit and offset Yes Keys aren't records: the key management backend stores them. With Drizzle, Askar usually keeps the keys in a store of its own.

A server that already stores its records in Askar can copy them to Drizzle. The keys stay in Askar. See Migrate from Askar. To use a storage backend Credo doesn't ship, implement the StorageService interface from @credo-ts/core. Askar Configure Askar for encrypted storage and key management in a Credo agent, on SQLite or PostgreSQL, in Node.js and React Native. Drizzle Store Credo records in PostgreSQL or SQLite tables with Drizzle ORM, run the migrations, and move an existing Askar agent to Drizzle.
Configure Askar for encrypted storage and key management in a Credo agent, on SQLite or PostgreSQL, in Node.js and React Native.
Store Credo records in PostgreSQL or SQLite tables with Drizzle ORM, run the migrations, and move an existing Askar agent to Drizzle.

Askar is an encrypted store for records and keys. AskarModule registers it as the agent's storage and as a key management backend. It runs on SQLite or PostgreSQL, in Node.js and React Native. Askar is the default for mobile wallets: it encrypts the wallet, includes key management, and has no migrations to ship with app updates. On a server, Drizzle stores the records and Askar keeps the keys, with storage turned off. Use SQLite, the default, on phones and for a server with one instance, and PostgreSQL when several instances share the keys. To choose between Askar and Drizzle, see Storage.

Node.js React Native npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 pnpm add @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 yarn add @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 bun add @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 pnpm add @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 yarn add @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 bun add @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 Askar is a native module, so it doesn't run in Expo Go. Use a development build. The platform package pins @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared to its own version, so use a single Askar version across your project. With mixed versions, npm installs a second copy of askar-shared for @credo-ts/askar, and initialize() fails with Native askar has not been registered yet. The Askar to Drizzle migration package needs exactly 0.6.0; see Migrate from Askar.

Node.js React Native agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'my-agent', // Load the key from a secret store in production key: 'my-agent-store-key', }, }), }, }) // Creates the store on the first run, opens it on later runs await agent.initialize() agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' // walletKey: created once with Store.generateRawKey() and kept in the device keychain export async function initializeAgent(walletKey: string) { const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw', }, }), }, }) // Creates the store on the first run, opens it on later runs await agent.initialize() return agent } Pass the NativeAskar class as askar. The askar instance export of the platform package is deprecated: it's only set once the platform package has run, which depends on import order. store.id names the store. It's also the root agent's profile, the SQLite directory and the PostgreSQL database name. agent.initialize() opens the store, and creates it if it doesn't exist yet. agent.shutdown() closes it. With the wrong key, initialize() throws a CredoError caused by AskarStoreInvalidKeyError. A different id or SQLite path doesn't fail: it creates a new, empty store. To open an existing wallet, check that the database exists before you initialize.

Askar encrypts the store with store.key. keyDerivationMethod decides how it turns the key into the encryption key: keyDerivationMethod Use it for raw Random keys that you keep somewhere safe, such as the device keychain or a secret manager. Skips key derivation, so opening the store is fast. kdf:argon2i:mod (default) Passwords and PINs. Argon2i makes guessing the key slow. kdf:argon2i:int The same, faster and less secure. Use raw when you can keep a random key in a keychain or secret manager, and Argon2i when the key is something a person types. Generate a raw key once with Store.generateRawKey() from the platform package: any other string fails when Askar creates the store. To change the key of an existing store, call agent.modules.askar.rotateStoreKey({ newKey, newKeyDerivationMethod }) and then update the key in your configuration.

The store is a file at <data path>/wallet/<store id>/sqlite.db. The data path is ~/.afj/data on Node.js, and .afj in the app's document directory on React Native. To use another file, set the full path of the database file: database: { type: 'sqlite', config: { path: '/var/lib/my-agent/agent.db' } }

For tests that need Askar, such as DIDComm tests, keep the store in memory. The data is gone when the agent shuts down. Other tests can use the lighter Drizzle and Node.js setup. test-agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar, Store } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'test-agent', // A random raw key skips the slow key derivation, which keeps tests fast key: Store.generateRawKey(), keyDerivationMethod: 'raw', database: { type: 'sqlite', config: { inMemory: true } }, }, }), }, })

agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { // Also the name of the Postgres database id: 'my-agent', key: 'my-agent-store-key', database: { type: 'postgres', config: { host: 'localhost:5432', maxConnections: 10, connectionParameters: { sslmode: 'require' }, }, credentials: { account: 'credo', password: 'credo-password', }, }, }, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() The store id is the database name. On the first initialize() Askar creates that database, so the account needs permission to create databases, or you pass a separate adminAccount and adminPassword in credentials for that. Option Description config.host Host and port, for example localhost:5432. config.maxConnections, config.minConnections Size of the connection pool. Also available for SQLite. config.connectTimeout, config.idleTimeout Timeouts. config.connectionParameters Extra connection string parameters, such as sslmode, sslrootcert and application_name. Parameters that Credo sets itself, such as host, user and dbname, throw. credentials.account, credentials.password The account to connect with. credentials.adminAccount, credentials.adminPassword Optional account for creating and deleting databases.

AskarModule registers storage and a key management backend named askar. Turn either off: enableStorage enableKms Use it when true true Askar stores records and keys. The default. false true Another module stores records, such as Drizzle. Askar still creates its store, for the keys. true false You register AskarKeyManagementService yourself in the KeyManagementModule, for example to make Askar the default next to another backend. See Key management. If you add AskarKeyManagementService to the KeyManagementModule backends and keep enableKms on, registering the module throws.

With the tenants module, multiWalletDatabaseScheme decides where tenant data goes: AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet keeps all tenants in the root store with a profile each, DatabasePerWallet (the default) gives each tenant its own store. This also applies when Askar only keeps the keys. Use ProfilePerWallet. See Where tenant data is stored for the trade-offs, and for why you shouldn't set a SQLite path with DatabasePerWallet.

agent.modules.askar (the module's key in modules) has methods for store-level tasks: Method What it does rotateStoreKey({ newKey, newKeyDerivationMethod? }) Changes the store key. Update your configuration afterwards. exportStore({ exportToStore }) Copies the open store to a new store, for example a backup with its own id, key and path. On SQLite, the target file must not exist yet. importStore({ importFromStore }) Copies another store, such as a backup, to the configured store location. Call closeStore() first. On SQLite, the configured file must not exist yet. deleteStore() Deletes the store and all its data. closeStore(), openStore(), provisionStore(), isStoreOpen Manual control. initialize() and shutdown() already do this. With ProfilePerWallet these methods act on the whole store, including all tenants, so they throw when you call them from a tenant agent.

@credo-ts/drizzle-storage stores the agent's records in regular SQL tables in PostgreSQL or SQLite, through Drizzle ORM. You create the database connection, choose the record bundles and run migrations. Drizzle doesn't store keys, so you also need a key management backend, usually Askar. Drizzle is the storage for servers: records are SQL tables with indexes that the database can query, and many tenants and instances share one database. It doesn't encrypt records, and you run its migrations on every Credo upgrade. To compare it with Askar, see Storage.

PostgreSQL SQLite npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 yarn add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 bun add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 yarn add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 bun add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 @credo-ts/drizzle-storage requires drizzle-orm 0.44 (^0.44.6). Version 0.45 doesn't satisfy the peer dependency. It includes drizzle-kit for the migration CLI, so you don't install that yourself. The Askar packages provide the key management backend. Use PostgreSQL with the pg driver on servers, and always when several instances share the data. SQLite works for a single instance or local development, with libsql on Node.js or expo-sqlite on React Native. For another driver, open an issue in the Credo repository: Credo has to map the driver's error codes.

PostgreSQL SQLite agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle('postgresql://credo:credo-password@localhost:5432/credo'), // The core bundle is always included. Add one bundle per module that stores records. bundles: [openid4vcBundle], }), // Drizzle doesn't store keys: Askar provides the KMS, in its own Postgres database askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { id: 'credo-keys', key: 'my-agent-store-key', database: { type: 'postgres', config: { host: 'localhost:5432' }, credentials: { account: 'credo', password: 'credo-password' }, }, }, }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) // Run the migrations first: the module doesn't create tables await agent.initialize() agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle('file:agent.db'), bundles: [], }), // Drizzle doesn't store keys: Askar provides the KMS askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { id: 'credo-keys', key: 'my-agent-store-key' }, }), }, }) // Run the migrations first: the module doesn't create tables await agent.initialize() database takes any Drizzle PostgreSQL or SQLite database. drizzle() accepts a connection string, or a client or pool you created yourself. The module doesn't create tables. Run the migrations before the first initialize().

A bundle holds the tables for the records of one Credo module. Pass a bundle for every module you use that stores records. Without it, saving or reading such a record throws Could not find a registered drizzle adapter for record type. Bundle Import For coreBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core @credo-ts/core. Always included by the module. didcommBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/didcomm @credo-ts/didcomm actionMenuBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/action-menu @credo-ts/action-menu anoncredsBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/anoncreds @credo-ts/anoncreds openid4vcBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc @credo-ts/openid4vc drpcBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/drpc @credo-ts/drpc tenantsBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/tenants @credo-ts/tenants questionAnswerBundle @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/question-answer @credo-ts/question-answer Order the bundles as in this table, so a bundle comes after the bundles it depends on (actionMenuBundle uses the connection table from didcommBundle). Put your own bundles last.

Without a key management backend the agent still initializes, but every key operation throws. The examples above keep the keys in Askar with enableStorage: false, so Askar creates a store for the keys only. Back that store up together with the Drizzle database: records such as DIDs refer to keys in it. The Node.js backend from @credo-ts/node keeps keys in memory only, so it's for tests. See Key management.

Credo ships the SQL migrations for each bundle. Run them before you start the agent for the first time, and again after every Credo upgrade: Drizzle storage adds migrations in non-breaking releases, and Credo doesn't work until you apply them. Running the migrations when there's nothing new does nothing.

The package has a drizzle-storage command: # PostgreSQL npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle openid4vc migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "postgresql://credo:credo-password@localhost:5432/credo" # SQLite npx drizzle-storage --bundle core migrate --dialect sqlite --database-url "file:agent.db" Option Description --bundle, -b A bundle to migrate. Repeat it for every bundle. Required, and the CLI adds no bundles itself, so always pass --bundle core. Takes the bundle names from the table above, or a path or package name for your own bundles. migrate --dialect postgres or sqlite. migrate --database-url The database to migrate. You can set DRIZZLE_DATABASE_URL instead. Run the CLI with the same Credo version as your agent. The CLI keeps track of applied migrations in a table per bundle, such as credo_migrations__core. drizzle-storage studio --dialect <dialect> --database-url <url> opens Drizzle Studio on the database.

Node.js React Native Each bundle has the absolute path of its migration folders in bundle.migrations. Apply them with the Drizzle migrator for your driver, before you initialize the agent: migrate.ts import { coreBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core' import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator' const database = drizzle('file:agent.db') // The core bundle first, then the bundles you pass to the DrizzleStorageModule for (const bundle of [coreBundle, openid4vcBundle]) { await migrate(database, { migrationsFolder: bundle.migrations.sqlite.migrationsPath, // The table names the drizzle-storage CLI uses, so you can switch between the CLI and this code migrationsTable: `credo_migrations__${bundle.name.replace('-', '_')}`, }) } For PostgreSQL, import migrate from drizzle-orm/node-postgres/migrator and use bundle.migrations.postgres.migrationsPath. On React Native, use expo-sqlite as the driver and the React Native Askar package for the keys: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ expo-sqlite \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ expo-sqlite \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 yarn add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ expo-sqlite \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 bun add \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ expo-sqlite \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 A phone has its own database, so the app applies the migrations itself. Import the SQLite migrations of each bundle from @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/<bundle>/migrations/sqlite and apply them with applyReactNativeMigrations: storage.ts import { applyReactNativeMigrations, DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import coreMigrations from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core/migrations/sqlite' import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc' import openid4vcMigrations from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc/migrations/sqlite' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/expo-sqlite' import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/expo-sqlite/migrator' import { openDatabaseSync } from 'expo-sqlite' const database = drizzle(openDatabaseSync('credo.db')) // Run on every app start, before agent.initialize() await applyReactNativeMigrations({ db: database, migrate, migrations: [coreMigrations, openid4vcMigrations], }) export const storage = new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [openid4vcBundle] }) The migrations import .sql files, so the bundler has to inline them. Install babel-plugin-inline-import as a dev dependency, add the inline-import plugin to your Babel config with extensions: ['.sql'], and add sql to resolver.sourceExts in your Metro config.

For tests, use an in-memory SQLite database and keep the keys in memory with the Node.js backend, so there's nothing to set up or clean up. A new in-memory database is empty, so apply the migrations each time you create an agent: test-agent.ts import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { coreBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core' import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator' export async function createTestAgent() { // Every in-memory database starts empty, so apply the migrations each time const database = drizzle(':memory:') for (const bundle of [coreBundle]) { await migrate(database, { migrationsFolder: bundle.migrations.sqlite.migrationsPath, // A migrations table per bundle, as the drizzle-storage CLI uses migrationsTable: `credo_migrations__${bundle.name.replace('-', '_')}`, }) } return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [] }), // Keys in memory as well, with node:crypto kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())], }), }, }) } The Node.js backend can't encrypt DIDComm messages, which need XSalsa20-Poly1305. For DIDComm tests, keep the keys in Askar on in-memory SQLite, with enableStorage: false.

@credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration copies all records from an Askar store to an empty Drizzle database. Use it when a server that runs on Askar should move to Drizzle, for example to get SQL access to its records. It doesn't move keys: after the migration, Askar stays your key management backend with storage turned off. In 0.7 the migration package requires exactly version 0.6.0 of Askar, so install 0.6.0 of both the Askar platform package and askar-shared for the migration: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.0 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared@0.6.0 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.0 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared@0.6.0 yarn add \ @credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.0 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared@0.6.0 bun add \ @credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.0 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared@0.6.0 Stop the agent and back up the Askar store. The migrator doesn't make a backup. Create the Drizzle database and run the migrations for every bundle you'll use. The database must be empty. Run the migration with your current Askar configuration and your new Drizzle configuration: migrate-to-drizzle.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { AskarToDrizzleStorageMigrator } from '@credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration' import { ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' // The Askar config your agent uses today, with storage still enabled const askarModule = new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'my-agent', key: 'my-agent-store-key' }, }) // The Drizzle config your agent will use: an empty, migrated database and a bundle for // every module that stored records in Askar const drizzleModule = new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle('file:agent.db'), bundles: [], }) const migrator = await AskarToDrizzleStorageMigrator.initialize({ askarModule, drizzleModule, agentDependencies, logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), }) // Copies all records from Askar to Drizzle. The keys stay in Askar. await migrator.migrate() Start the agent with the DrizzleStorageModule and the same Askar store configuration, with enableStorage: false, so Credo still finds the keys. When everything works, you can remove the copied records from the Askar store: migrate-to-drizzle.ts // Removes the copied records from the Askar store, keeping the keys await migrator.deleteStorageRecords() From then on, only open the store with enableStorage: false. With storage on, initialize() fails because the storage version record is gone. If a record in Askar has no bundle in the Drizzle module, the migration throws. skipMigrationForMissingAdapter: true skips such records instead, and they're lost. For a multi-tenant agent, pass tenantsModule and include tenantsBundle to migrate every tenant as well. Tenants that had their own Askar database all end up in the one Drizzle database.

These pages explain the ideas behind Credo: how verifiable credentials work, what an agent is, and where DIDs and DIDComm fit in. Read them if you're new to verifiable credentials or to Credo. If you want to get an agent running first, start with Getting started.
Issuers, holders and verifiers, credentials and presentations, and how exchange protocols, credential formats, key binding, selective disclosure, status and trust fit together in Credo.
What a Credo agent is, how modules add functionality to it, and how agent contexts and tenants keep data apart.
What decentralized identifiers and DID documents are, and how DIDComm uses them for messaging between agents.
The platforms Credo supports, Node.js and React Native, how its packages are published, and which runtimes aren't supported.
Everything you do with Credo goes through an agent. This page explains what an agent holds, how modules extend it, and what agent contexts and tenants are.

An agent is an instance of Agent from @credo-ts/core. It holds the configuration, the storage, the keys and the modules for one party, such as an issuer, a verifier, a wallet or a mediator. These roles all use the same Agent class. What an agent can do depends on the modules you register. You pass three things to the constructor: dependencies: platform-specific dependencies, such as file system access and fetch. Import agentDependencies from @credo-ts/node or @credo-ts/react-native. See Platforms. modules: the modules to register, by key. A storage module is required. config: optional agent-wide settings, such as the logger. import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) await agent.initialize() storage holds the storage and key management modules, such as Drizzle for the records and Askar for the keys on a server. Storage helps you choose, and Your first agent walks through a complete setup step by step.

A module adds functionality to the agent: an API, services, storage records, and sometimes HTTP endpoints or message handlers. Credo is split into packages that each provide one or more modules, so you install only what you use. Default modules are always registered: among others DIDs, W3C credentials, SD-JWT VC, mdoc, X.509 and key management. You use them through properties such as agent.dids, agent.sdJwtVc and agent.kms. Register a module under the same key to configure it, for example dids: new DidsModule({ ... }). Other modules you register yourself, such as DrizzleStorageModule or AskarModule for storage, DidCommModule, OpenId4VcModule, AnonCredsModule and TenantsModule. Their APIs are available under agent.modules.<key>. DidCommModule and OpenId4VcModule are also available as agent.didcomm and agent.openid4vc, but only when you register them under the keys didcomm and openid4vc. The agent's type follows from the modules you pass, so TypeScript knows which APIs exist. Agent configuration covers storage, key management, caching and logging.

Credo keeps the data of one agent or tenant apart from others through an agent context. The context links storage, keys and configuration to an identifier, the contextCorrelationId. An agent has one root context. Credo passes the context along for you, so you only see it in callbacks, such as getTrustedIssuersForVerification(agentContext, ...), and when you write your own modules.

With @credo-ts/tenants, one agent can host many tenants. Each tenant gets its own agent context, so its own storage and keys, while all tenants share the modules, configuration and transports of the root agent. This uses fewer resources than running an agent per tenant, which matters for hosted issuers, verifiers and cloud wallets. See Multi-tenancy.
Credo uses DIDs to identify issuers, holders and the keys they sign with, and DIDComm to exchange messages between agents. This page explains the basics of both.

A decentralized identifier (DID) is an identifier such as did:web:issuer.example.com that you can resolve to a DID document. You create DIDs yourself: no central party issues them. The part after did: is the DID method. It defines where the document lives and how you create and update it: did:key and did:jwk encode a single public key in the DID itself. Nothing is published. did:peer is shared only with the other party of a DIDComm connection. did:web and did:webvh are published on a web server under your domain. did:cheqd, did:indy and did:hedera are anchored on a ledger. DIDs lists the methods Credo supports and shows how to create and resolve DIDs.

A DID document lists: Verification methods: the public keys of the DID. Verification relationships, which say what each key may be used for, for example assertionMethod to sign credentials, authentication to prove control of the DID, and keyAgreement to encrypt messages. Services, such as the endpoint where the DID controller receives DIDComm messages. A verifier resolves the issuer's DID to get the key that signed a credential. Another agent resolves a DID to find out where and how to send it a message.

DIDComm is a way for agents identified by DIDs to send each other messages. A message is encrypted for the recipient's keyAgreement key and sent to its service endpoint, over any transport, such as HTTP or WebSockets. Credo implements DIDComm Messaging v1, the version the Aries protocols use. On top of this messaging layer, protocols define specific exchanges: setting up a connection with Out of Band and DID Exchange, issuing credentials, requesting proofs, mediation and basic messages. Credo also still includes the v1 versions of the Connection, Issue Credential and Present Proof protocols. They're deprecated and removed in 0.8, so use DID Exchange and the v2 protocols. A mobile wallet has no public endpoint, so it uses a mediator: an agent that receives and stores messages until the wallet picks them up. You don't need DIDComm to use DIDs. OpenID4VC uses DIDs or X.509 certificates for keys, and HTTPS and OAuth 2.0 for transport. See Verifiable credentials for how the protocols compare, and DIDComm to set it up.

Credo runs on Node.js and React Native. This page describes what each platform is used for, what you need to know about how Credo is packaged, and which runtimes don't work. Installation has the setup steps.

Use @credo-ts/node for agents that run on a server, such as issuers, verifiers and mediators. Credo requires Node.js 20.19 or later. It's tested on Node.js 22 and 24, so use one of those. Some parts of Credo only run on Node.js: the DIDComm inbound transports from @credo-ts/node, and the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier, which serve their endpoints with Express.

Use @credo-ts/react-native for mobile wallets. It needs react-native-get-random-values, expo-crypto, and a file system package (@dr.pogodin/react-native-fs or react-native-fs). Askar, AnonCreds and Indy VDR are native modules. With Expo, that means you need a development build: Expo Go can't load them.

All @credo-ts/* packages are published as ES modules only. Use import in your code. A CommonJS project can still load them with require() on Node.js versions that support require(esm), but ESM is recommended. In TypeScript, set moduleResolution to nodenext, node16 or bundler. Other settings don't read the exports field of package.json, so subpath imports such as @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm don't resolve.
All @credo-ts/* packages are released together and depend on exact versions of each other. Install the same version of every Credo package you use.

Browsers aren't supported. Credo has no storage, key management or platform dependencies for the browser, and the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier depend on Express. Bun, Deno and Electron aren't tested. Credo's CI only runs on Node.js. They may work through their Node.js compatibility, but there's no guarantee.

A verifiable credential is a set of claims about a subject, such as a name or a date of birth, signed by the party that makes the claims. Anyone who receives it can check that the claims came from that party and weren't changed. This page explains the model and the terms the rest of the docs use, and links to the section that covers each part.

Three roles take part: The issuer signs a credential and gives it to the holder. A government issuing an ID or a university issuing a diploma are issuers. The holder receives the credential, stores it and decides when to share it. The verifier asks the holder for credentials and checks them. The issuer doesn't take part when the holder presents a credential. The verifier only needs the issuer's public key, which it gets from a DID or an X.509 certificate (see Trust). These docs use holder for the role, as the Credo APIs do (agent.openid4vc.holder), and wallet for the application that takes the holder role for a person, such as a mobile wallet app. A Credo agent can take any of these roles, and one agent can take more than one. Issuers and verifiers usually run on a server with Node.js. A holder usually runs in a mobile wallet built with React Native, but it can also be a cloud wallet on a server.

The issuer creates a credential. When the holder shares it, they create a presentation: the credential, or the parts of it the verifier asked for, plus proof that the holder is the one it was issued to. A presentation is bound to the verifier's request, usually through a nonce, so it can't be replayed to another verifier.

Credo separates two things: An exchange protocol defines how the parties talk: how an issuer offers a credential, how the holder requests it, how a verifier asks for a presentation. Credo supports OpenID4VC (OpenID4VCI for issuance, OpenID4VP for presentation), DIDComm (Issue Credential and Present Proof) and the ISO mdoc presentation protocols (in person over BLE or NFC, and online through the Digital Credentials API).
