A credential format defines what a credential looks like and how it's signed: SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C Verifiable Credentials and AnonCreds. Several formats work over more than one protocol, and you can sign, store and verify a credential without any protocol. That's why the docs are split the same way: Protocols covers the flows, Credential formats covers what you can do with a format on its own, and pages such as SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC combine the two. Format OpenID4VC DIDComm ISO mdoc SD-JWT VC Yes No No mdoc Yes No Yes W3C VC Yes Yes No AnonCreds No Yes No Not every W3C data model and signature type works over both OpenID4VC and DIDComm. See Supported standards for the full matrix. Getting started recommends a protocol and format to start with.

Most credentials are bound to a key that the holder controls. The issuer puts the holder's public key (or a DID that resolves to it) in the credential, and the holder signs each presentation with the private key. Someone who copies the credential can't present it without that key. AnonCreds binds credentials to a link secret instead of a key. In Credo the holder's keys live in a key management service (KMS). See Key management.

Selective disclosure lets the holder share some claims of a credential and keep the rest private: SD-JWT VC and mdoc: the issuer signs a salted hash of each claim, and the holder reveals only the claims the verifier asks for. AnonCreds: the holder creates a zero-knowledge proof, which can also prove a predicate, such as being over 18, without revealing the date of birth. W3C VCs: those secured with SD-JWT (data model 2.0) work like SD-JWT VC. Those signed as a plain JWT or with a Linked Data proof are always shared as a whole.

An issuer may need to revoke a credential, or suspend it for a while. With a status list, the issuer publishes a list with one entry per credential, and each credential points to its entry. The verifier fetches the list and checks the entry. Credo supports Token Status Lists for SD-JWT VC and mdoc. AnonCreds uses its own revocation registries, and the holder proves the credential isn't revoked as part of the presentation (see AnonCreds).

A valid signature only proves who signed a credential. The verifier still has to decide whether it trusts that issuer. Credo identifies issuers in two ways: DIDs: the issuer's key is published in a DID document, on a ledger, a web server, or in the DID itself. See DIDs and DIDComm. X.509 certificates: the issuer signs with a certificate that chains up to a root certificate the verifier trusts. mdoc always works this way, and SD-JWT VC often does. You tell Credo which issuers to trust per verification, or with a callback on the agent. See Trusted issuers.

A credential format defines what a credential looks like, how the issuer signs it and how the holder presents it. Formats are separate from exchange protocols: you can sign, store, present and verify a credential with the agent APIs alone, and most formats work over more than one protocol. The pages in this section cover each format on its own. For the flows, see Protocols.

SD-JWT VC mdoc W3C VC AnonCreds Standard IETF ISO/IEC 18013-5 W3C Hyperledger AnonCreds Selective disclosure Per claim Per data element Only data model 2.0 secured as SD-JWT Per attribute, plus predicates such as "age at least 18" Unlinkable presentations With batch issuance With batch issuance With batch issuance Yes Holder binding Key (cnf), as JWK or DID Device key DID of the subject, or key (cnf) in data model 2.0 Link secret Issuer signs with DID or X.509 certificate X.509 certificate DID Keys of a credential definition on a registry Revocation in Credo Token Status List Token Status List None Revocation registry Exchange in Credo OpenID4VC, Digital Credentials API OpenID4VC, Digital Credentials API, ISO 18013-5 proximity OpenID4VC, DIDComm, depending on the variant DIDComm Used in EUDI Wallet (PID and attestations) Mobile driving licence, EUDI Wallet (PID) Open Badges, EBSI Aries and Indy based ecosystems For SD-JWT VC, mdoc and W3C VCs, every presentation of a credential carries the same issuer signature, so verifiers that compare notes can link presentations of it. Batch issuance avoids that: the holder gets several copies, each bound to its own key, and presents each copy once. AnonCreds presentations are zero-knowledge proofs and don't need this. For the protocol versions and the full matrix, see Supported standards.

Follow your ecosystem first. Without a required format: You're building Use An issuer, wallet or verifier for the EUDI Wallet SD-JWT VC and mdoc. The EUDI Wallet uses both, including for the PID. A mobile driving licence, or in-person presentation over NFC or Bluetooth mdoc. It's the only format Credo presents with ISO 18013-5. A new OpenID4VC deployment SD-JWT VC. It has selective disclosure, plain JSON claims, and works with both DIDs and X.509 certificates. Something for an ecosystem built on W3C VCs, such as EBSI or Open Badges W3C VC. Choose a variant explains which one. A DIDComm deployment that needs predicates, or unlinkable presentations without batch issuance AnonCreds.

Bind credentials to a key of the holder, so that a copy of a credential is useless to someone else. For SD-JWT VC and W3C data model 2.0, bind to a JWK by default: the holder needs no DID, and the key can stay in the secure hardware of a phone. Bind to a DID when holders and verifiers already use DIDs. mdocs are always bound to a device key, AnonCreds credentials to the link secret, and W3C data model 1.1 credentials to the DID in credentialSubject.id.

For SD-JWT VC and mdoc, use P-256 keys (ES256) for both issuer and holder. HAIP requires every party to support ES256, and it's the curve that the secure hardware of phones supports. W3C JSON-LD and Data Integrity credentials need Ed25519 keys, because all signature suites that Credo has for them use Ed25519.

Use a status list or revocation registry only if you must be able to revoke credentials before they expire. Short-lived credentials that you reissue don't need one. See Status lists and AnonCreds revocation.

Format Agent API Record SD-JWT VC agent.sdJwtVc SdJwtVcRecord mdoc agent.mdoc MdocRecord W3C VC 1.1 agent.w3cCredentials W3cCredentialRecord W3C VC 2.0 agent.w3cV2Credentials W3cV2CredentialRecord AnonCreds agent.modules.anoncreds (the key you register it under) W3cCredentialRecord All formats except AnonCreds are part of @credo-ts/core, and their modules are registered on every agent. AnonCreds needs @credo-ts/anoncreds and a registry such as a ledger. SD-JWT VC Sign, store, present and verify IETF SD-JWT VCs with agent.sdJwtVc, independent of the exchange protocol. mdoc Sign, store, present and verify ISO 18013-5 mdocs, such as the mobile driving licence, with agent.mdoc. W3C Verifiable Credentials Sign, store, present and verify W3C Verifiable Credentials (data model 1.1 and 2.0) as JWT, SD-JWT, JSON-LD or Data Integrity. AnonCreds Set up AnonCreds in Credo with a registry, register schemas, credential definitions and revocation registries, and manage link secrets and stored credentials. Status lists Revoke and suspend SD-JWT VCs and mdocs with IETF Token Status Lists, using agent.tokenStatusList.
Sign, store, present and verify IETF SD-JWT VCs with agent.sdJwtVc, independent of the exchange protocol.
Sign, store, present and verify ISO 18013-5 mdocs, such as the mobile driving licence, with agent.mdoc.
Sign, store, present and verify W3C Verifiable Credentials (data model 1.1 and 2.0) as JWT, SD-JWT, JSON-LD or Data Integrity.
Set up AnonCreds in Credo with a registry, register schemas, credential definitions and revocation registries, and manage link secrets and stored credentials.
Revoke and suspend SD-JWT VCs and mdocs with IETF Token Status Lists, using agent.tokenStatusList.

AnonCreds credentials are signed with CL signatures, which let a holder present zero-knowledge proofs: reveal only some attributes and prove a predicate such as "age is at least 18" without the value. Verifiers can't link presentations through the signature. Holders bind credentials to a link secret instead of a key. Issuers publish schemas, credential definitions and revocation data on an AnonCreds registry, usually a ledger. This page covers setup and the issuer and holder APIs. Credo exchanges AnonCreds credentials only over DIDComm: see AnonCreds with DIDComm.

const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { // Derive the store key from secure storage or user input, see the Askar page askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: '<store key>' } }), // A holder only resolves objects, so it needs no payer seed cheqd: new CheqdModule({ networks: [{ network: 'testnet' }] }), dids: new DidsModule({ resolvers: [new CheqdDidResolver()] }), anoncreds: new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()], }), }, }) await agent.initialize() Pass the NativeAnoncreds class (supported since Credo 0.7.2): Credo resolves the native binding when it needs it, so import order doesn't matter. The module's API is available as agent.modules.anoncreds under the key you register it with. With Drizzle storage, also register anoncredsBundle, as AnonCreds stores its own records. Each registry handles the identifiers of one DID method, and Credo uses the first registry that matches an identifier. A registry also needs the module of its network, which provides the DID resolver: Registry Import from Identifiers Network setup IndyVdrAnonCredsRegistry @credo-ts/indy-vdr did:indy, and unqualified Indy identifiers for resolving Indy VDR CheqdAnonCredsRegistry @credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds did:cheqd cheqd HederaAnonCredsRegistry @credo-ts/hedera/anoncreds did:hedera Hedera WebVhAnonCredsRegistry @credo-ts/webvh/anoncreds did:webvh did:webvh Import the cheqd and Hedera registries from their /anoncreds subpaths, available since Credo 0.7.2. The package roots still export them, but those exports are deprecated and removed in 0.8. To register objects on Indy, the issuer needs a did:indy.

A schema lists the attribute names of a credential type. An issuer can also use a schema that someone else registered. Issuer issuer.ts const { schemaState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerSchema({ schema: { issuerId, name: 'Employee', version: '1.0', attrNames: ['name', 'role', 'age'], }, // Registry specific, cheqd needs none options: {}, }) if (schemaState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error( `Registering the schema failed: ${schemaState.state === 'failed' ? schemaState.reason : schemaState.state}` ) } issuerId is a DID on the registry that the issuer created or imported in its agent. options depend on the registry. Indy VDR needs endorserMode and endorserDid, and you can type them with registerSchema<IndyVdrRegisterSchemaOptions>. cheqd needs none. The register methods don't throw when registration fails. Check state: finished, failed (with reason), wait, or action (for example when an external Indy endorser has to sign).

A credential definition binds a schema to an issuer and holds the issuer's public keys. You issue against a credential definition. Issuer issuer.ts const { credentialDefinitionState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerCredentialDefinition({ credentialDefinition: { issuerId, schemaId: schemaState.schemaId, tag: 'default', }, options: { supportRevocation: false }, }) if (credentialDefinitionState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Registering the credential definition failed: ${credentialDefinitionState.state}`) } const credentialDefinitionId = credentialDefinitionState.credentialDefinitionId Credo keeps the private keys in the issuer's storage. Without them you can no longer issue with this credential definition. Use tag to create several credential definitions for one schema. Set supportRevocation: true if you want to revoke credentials later: you can't add revocation afterwards.

Revocation is optional and adds work on both sides. The issuer hosts a tails file and writes to the registry for every status list update, and holders download the tails file to prove non-revocation. Enable it when a credential can stop being valid while the holder still has it, such as an employee or membership credential. Leave it off for credentials that stay true, such as a diploma. A revocable credential definition needs a revocation registry and a status list. The revocation registry has a tails file that holders download to prove non-revocation, so the issuer must publish it. The default BasicTailsFileService only downloads tails files. Give issuers a tails file service that uploads: tails.ts import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises' import { AnonCredsModule, type AnonCredsRevocationRegistryDefinition, BasicTailsFileService } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds' import { CheqdDidRegistrar, CheqdDidResolver, CheqdModule } from '@credo-ts/cheqd' import { CheqdAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds' import { Agent, type AgentContext, DidsModule } from '@credo-ts/core' import { anoncredsBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/anoncreds' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs' import { exampleStorage } from './example-storage.js' class TailsServerFileService extends BasicTailsFileService { public async uploadTailsFile( _agentContext: AgentContext, { revocationRegistryDefinition }: { revocationRegistryDefinition: AnonCredsRevocationRegistryDefinition } ) { // Before the upload, `tailsLocation` is the path of the tails file Credo generated const tailsFile = await readFile(revocationRegistryDefinition.value.tailsLocation) const tailsFileUrl = `https://tails.example.com/${revocationRegistryDefinition.value.tailsHash}` const response = await fetch(tailsFileUrl, { method: 'PUT', body: tailsFile }) if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Uploading the tails file failed with status ${response.status}`) return { tailsFileUrl } } } agent.ts anoncreds: new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()], tailsFileService: new TailsServerFileService(), }), Then create the revocation registry and its first status list: Issuer issuer.ts const { credentialDefinitionState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerCredentialDefinition({ credentialDefinition: { issuerId, schemaId, tag: 'revocable' }, options: { supportRevocation: true }, }) if (credentialDefinitionState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Registering the credential definition failed: ${credentialDefinitionState.state}`) } const { revocationRegistryDefinitionState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerRevocationRegistryDefinition({ revocationRegistryDefinition: { issuerId, credentialDefinitionId: credentialDefinitionState.credentialDefinitionId, tag: 'default', maximumCredentialNumber: 1000, }, options: {}, }) if (revocationRegistryDefinitionState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Registering the revocation registry failed: ${revocationRegistryDefinitionState.state}`) } const revocationRegistryDefinitionId = revocationRegistryDefinitionState.revocationRegistryDefinitionId // The initial list, in which no credential is revoked const { revocationStatusListState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerRevocationStatusList({ revocationStatusList: { issuerId, revocationRegistryDefinitionId }, options: {}, }) if (revocationStatusListState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Registering the revocation status list failed: ${revocationStatusListState.state}`) } Credo marks the registry as active, and you can issue up to maximumCredentialNumber credentials with it. Each credential gets an index in the registry, which you choose when you issue and must track yourself. To revoke, publish a new status list with the revoked indexes: Issuer issuer.ts // Revoke the credentials issued with revocationRegistryIndex 1 and 2 const { revocationStatusListState: updatedState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.updateRevocationStatusList({ revocationStatusList: { revocationRegistryDefinitionId, revokedCredentialIndexes: [1, 2] }, options: {}, }) if (updatedState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error(`Revoking failed: ${updatedState.state}`) Indy VDR in 0.7.2 In Credo 0.7.2, issuing revocable credentials with the Indy VDR registry can fail, because the issuer can't resolve the status list of its own revocation registry. AnonCreds with DIDComm shows how to issue revocable credentials, notify holders and request proof of non-revocation.

A link secret is the holder's secret that all its AnonCreds credentials are bound to. By default (autoCreateLinkSecret: true) Credo creates one on the first credential request. The first link secret becomes the default. You can also create one yourself, and getLinkSecretIds lists them: Holder holder.ts // Optional: without a link secret, one is created on the first credential request const linkSecretId = await agent.modules.anoncreds.createLinkSecret({ setAsDefault: true }) const credentials = await agent.modules.anoncreds.getCredentials({ credentialDefinitionId }) for (const credential of credentials) { console.log(credential.credentialId, credential.attributes, credential.linkSecretId === linkSecretId) } The holder stores AnonCreds credentials as W3C VCDM 1.1 credentials (W3cCredentialRecord) with a DataIntegrityProof using the anoncreds-2023 cryptosuite. getCredentials filters them by credential definition, schema or issuer and returns the attributes and identifiers, and getCredential(id) returns one. agent.w3cCredentials lists the same records, but its verifyCredential rejects AnonCreds proofs.

A verifier checks AnonCreds presentations during the Present Proof exchange. It resolves the schemas, credential definitions and status lists from the registries. Which issuers you accept is part of the proof request, through restrictions. The agent's trusted issuers configuration doesn't apply to AnonCreds.

An mdoc is the credential format of ISO/IEC 18013-5, used for the mobile driving licence (mDL) and the EU PID. The issuer signs a salted digest of each data element with an X.509 certificate, and binds the mdoc to a device key of the holder. To present, the holder signs a device response that contains only the requested elements. This page covers agent.mdoc and MdocDeviceResponse. To issue and present mdocs over OpenID4VC, see mdoc with OpenID4VC. To present them in person or in the browser with the ISO protocols, see Proximity (ISO 18013-5) and Digital Credentials API (ISO 18013-7).

Everything on this page is in @credo-ts/core. MdocModule is a default module without options, so every agent has agent.mdoc. The agent also needs storage and key management. The examples use three agents: an issuer, a holder and a verifier. mdoc.ts import { Agent, DateOnly, Mdoc, MdocDeviceResponse, MdocRecord, X509ExtendedKeyUsage, X509KeyUsage, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { PublicJwk } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' function createAgent(storage: ExampleStorage) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup }, }) }

mdocs are always signed with an X.509 certificate, never with a DID. This example creates a self-signed document signer certificate from a key in the issuer's KMS: Issuer mdoc.ts const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) // A self-signed document signer certificate. Production issuers use a certificate issued by their IACA. const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk), // Verification fails when the subject has no country (C) issuer: { commonName: 'Example mDL Issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) }, extensions: { keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature] }, extendedKeyUsage: { usages: [X509ExtendedKeyUsage.MdlDs] }, }, }) The certificate subject must include a country (C). Verification fails without it, and also when the mdoc has an issuing_country element that doesn't match. In production, the document signer certificate is issued by your IACA root certificate, and verifiers trust the root. See X.509 certificates.

Issuer mdoc.ts // The device key of the wallet. In a real flow the wallet sends the public key, for example in an OpenID4VCI proof. const deviceKey = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const mdoc = await issuer.mdoc.sign({ docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', namespaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: 'Doe', given_name: 'Jane', birth_date: new DateOnly('1990-01-01'), issuing_country: 'NL', age_over_18: true, }, }, // `signed` and `validFrom` default to the time of signing validityInfo: { validUntil: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) }, issuerCertificate, holderKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(deviceKey.publicJwk), }) // base64url encoded IssuerSigned structure, as returned over OpenID4VCI const issued = mdoc.base64Url docType is the document type, such as org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL, and namespaces maps each namespace to its data elements. Use DateOnly from @credo-ts/core for elements that are a date without a time, such as birth_date. validityInfo.validUntil is required. signed and validFrom default to the time of signing. If you set validFrom, also set signed to a time no later than it, because signing fails when validFrom is before signed. issuerCertificate is the signing certificate, or a chain with the signing certificate first. Its key must be in the issuer's KMS. holderKey is the public device key the mdoc is bound to. keyAuthorizations lists the namespaces or elements the holder may sign itself (device-signed elements). By default there are none. statusInfo points to a status list entry, see Status lists. The signature algorithm follows from the certificate key: ES256, ES384, ES512 or EdDSA. Use P-256 keys (ES256) for the certificate and the device key unless your ecosystem asks for something else: HAIP requires every party to support ES256, and the secure hardware of phones supports P-256. Element digests always use SHA-256.

The holder parses the received mdoc, verifies it, and stores it as an MdocRecord: Holder mdoc.ts const receivedMdoc = Mdoc.fromBase64Url(issued) // The KMS key id is not part of the mdoc. Set it so Credo can sign device responses. receivedMdoc.deviceKeyId = deviceKey.keyId const verification = await holder.mdoc.verify(receivedMdoc, { trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')], }) if (verification.isValid === false) throw new Error(verification.error) const record = await holder.mdoc.store({ record: MdocRecord.fromMdoc(receivedMdoc) }) const [mdl] = await holder.mdoc.findAllByQuery({ docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL' }) console.log(mdl.firstCredential.issuerSignedNamespaces) deviceKeyId is the KMS key id of the device key. It isn't part of the mdoc, so set it before you store the mdoc. MdocRecord.fromMdoc copies it to the record. verify returns { isValid: true } or { isValid: false, error }, with error as a message. Without trustedCertificates it uses the agent's trusted issuers configuration, and throws when no trusted certificates are configured at all. Records are tagged with docType and alg. agent.mdoc also has getById, getAll, update and deleteById. A record can hold several instances of the same mdoc, each bound to its own key, for batch issuance. With OpenID4VCI, the holder flow verifies the mdoc and returns the MdocRecord for you. You only store it.

A presentation is a device response: the mdoc with only the requested elements, signed with the device key. Over OpenID4VP, Credo builds it for you. To build one yourself, use MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse: Holder mdoc.ts // Values the verifier sends in its OpenID4VP request const sessionTranscriptOptions = { type: 'openId4Vp', clientId: 'x509_san_dns:verifier.example.com', responseUri: 'https://verifier.example.com/response', verifierGeneratedNonce: 'b5c2f9e1-3a7d-4c8b-9e0f-1d2a3b4c5d6e', } as const const deviceResponse = await MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse(holder.context, { mdocs: [record.firstCredential], documentRequests: [ { docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', // Element identifier mapped to intent to retain nameSpaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: false, age_over_18: false } }, }, ], sessionTranscriptOptions, }) const encodedDeviceResponse = deviceResponse.encoded documentRequests lists the elements to disclose per namespace. Every element of an mdoc is selectively disclosable, so the response contains these elements and nothing else. The boolean is the verifier's intent to retain the element. sessionTranscriptOptions binds the response to one exchange. The openId4Vp and openId4VpDcApi types take the values from an OpenID4VP request. For other transports, such as ISO 18013-5 proximity, compute the session transcript yourself and pass { type: 'sessionTranscriptBytes', sessionTranscriptBytes }. deviceNameSpaces adds device-signed elements. They're only included when requested and authorized by keyAuthorizations. Only device signatures are supported. Device MAC authentication fails.

Verifier mdoc.ts const receivedResponse = MdocDeviceResponse.fromBase64Url(encodedDeviceResponse) // Throws when the response is invalid. Pass the trusted certificates explicitly: // this method does not use the agent trust configuration. await receivedResponse.verify(verifier.context, { trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')], sessionTranscriptOptions, }) // { 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL': { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: 'Doe', age_over_18: true } } } console.log(receivedResponse.issuerClaims) verify resolves when the response is valid and throws an MdocError when it isn't. It checks the issuer signature and certificate chain, the element digests, the device signature over the session transcript, the validity period (with the agent's validitySkewSeconds) and the status. issuerClaims and deviceClaims hold the disclosed elements per document type and namespace. Pass the trusted certificates MdocDeviceResponse.verify doesn't use the agent's trusted issuers configuration or the trusted certificates of the X.509 module. Without trustedCertificates, every response fails verification. The OpenID4VP verifier and the DC API flow resolve trust for you. trustedCertificates takes certificates as PEM or base64 strings. To trust a separate certificate for signing status lists, pass [{ issuance: [...], status: [...] }] instead.
mdoc with OpenID4VC Proximity (ISO 18013-5) Digital Credentials API (ISO 18013-7) Status lists X.509 certificates

An SD-JWT VC (IETF SD-JWT VC) is a JWT signed by the issuer, in which the holder can disclose claims one by one. It's usually bound to a key the holder controls. This page covers agent.sdJwtVc: signing, storing, presenting and verifying SD-JWT VCs yourself. To issue and present them over OpenID4VC, see SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC. The protocol calls these same APIs for you.

Everything on this page is in @credo-ts/core. SdJwtVcModule is a default module, so every agent has agent.sdJwtVc. The agent also needs storage and key management. The examples use three agents: an issuer, a holder and a verifier. sd-jwt-vc.ts import { Agent, DidKey, type KeyDidCreateOptions, SdJwtVcModule, SdJwtVcRecord } from '@credo-ts/core' import { PublicJwk } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' function createAgent(storage: ExampleStorage, sdJwtVc?: SdJwtVcModule) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // SdJwtVcModule is a default module. Register it yourself only to configure it. ...(sdJwtVc ? { sdJwtVc } : {}), }, }) }

The issuer signs with a key of a DID it created (or imported with its keys), and binds the credential to the holder's public key: Issuer sd-jwt-vc.ts // The issuer signs with a key of a DID it created const { didState } = await issuer.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the issuer DID failed') const issuerDid = didState.did const issuerDidUrl = `${issuerDid}#${DidKey.fromDid(issuerDid).publicJwk.fingerprint}` // The holder key. In a real flow the wallet sends the public key, for example in an OpenID4VCI proof. const holderKey = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const holderJwk = PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(holderKey.publicJwk) const credential = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({ payload: { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', given_name: 'Jane', family_name: 'Doe', birthdate: '1990-01-01', address: { street_address: 'Main Street 1', locality: 'Utrecht', country: 'NL' }, nationalities: ['NL', 'DE'], }, issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl }, holder: { method: 'jwk', jwk: holderJwk }, disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name', 'family_name', 'birthdate'], _sd_decoy: 2, address: { _sd: ['street_address', 'locality'] }, nationalities: { _sd: [0, 1] }, }, hashingAlgorithm: 'sha-256', }) // The compact SD-JWT VC: issuer-signed JWT followed by the disclosures console.log(credential.compact) payload holds the claims and needs a vct, the credential type. Credo sets iss, cnf and iat (pass iat: null to leave iat out). Add exp, nbf or status yourself. issuer is { method: 'did', didUrl } with a DID URL that points to a key, or { method: 'x5c', x5c } with a certificate chain (see below). holder is { method: 'jwk', jwk }, which sets cnf.jwk, or { method: 'did', didUrl }, which sets cnf.kid. disclosureFrame lists the claims the holder can disclose one by one (see below). hashingAlgorithm sets the digest algorithm of the disclosures: sha-256 (default), sha-384 or sha-512. headerType sets the typ header. Keep the default dc+sd-jwt, and use vc+sd-jwt only for verifiers that don't support dc+sd-jwt yet.

Bind to a JWK by default. The holder doesn't need a DID, and the key can stay in the secure hardware of a phone. Bind to a DID when holders and verifiers already work with DIDs. Without holder the credential is a bearer credential: anyone with a copy can present it, and a verifier can't require key binding.

Each _sd lists the claims of one object that the holder can disclose separately: property names, or positions for array elements. Claims that aren't listed are always disclosed, and iss, nbf, exp, cnf, vct and status can't be listed. List every claim about the person, so the holder shares only what a verifier asks for. Leave claims visible that every verifier needs and that say nothing about the person. For a nested object, give it its own _sd, as for address above, so the holder can disclose the locality without the street. Also list the object in the parent _sd if even its presence says something about the person. Set _sd_decoy to add fake digests, so verifiers can't tell how many claims are hidden.

Sign with X.509 when your verifiers expect certificates, as HAIP and the EUDI Wallet do. Otherwise a DID is simpler. Put the certificate chain in x5c, leaf certificate first. Credo signs with the leaf certificate's key, so that key must be in the agent's KMS. A certificate you create with agent.x509.createCertificate from a KMS key is ready to use. For certificate chains and trust anchors, see X.509 certificates. Issuer sd-jwt-vc.ts const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk), issuer: { commonName: 'Example Issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, extensions: { subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'issuer.example.com' }] } }, }) const x509Credential = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({ payload: { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', given_name: 'Jane' }, // `issuer` is optional. When set, it must match a SAN of the leaf certificate. issuer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate], issuer: 'https://issuer.example.com' }, holder: { method: 'jwk', jwk: holderJwk }, disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name'] }, })

The holder verifies a received credential, then stores it as an SdJwtVcRecord: Holder sd-jwt-vc.ts const verification = await holder.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact }) if (verification.isValid === false) throw verification.error const record = await holder.sdJwtVc.store({ record: new SdJwtVcRecord({ // The KMS key id lets Credo sign the key binding JWT when presenting credentialInstances: [{ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact, kmsKeyId: holderKey.keyId }], }), }) const [identityRecord] = await holder.sdJwtVc.findAllByQuery({ vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity' }) console.log(identityRecord.firstCredential.prettyClaims) kmsKeyId is the KMS key the credential is bound to. Credo signs the key binding JWT with it when presenting. A DID-bound credential doesn't need it, because Credo finds the key through the DID. credentialInstances can hold several copies of the same credential, each bound to its own key, as issued with batch issuance. Records are tagged with vct, alg and sdAlg for queries. agent.sdJwtVc also has getById, getAll, update and deleteById, and fromCompact decodes a credential without verifying it. With OpenID4VCI, the holder flow returns the SdJwtVcRecord with kmsKeyId set, and you only store it.

The holder chooses which claims to disclose with a presentation frame, and adds a key binding JWT for the verifier: Holder sd-jwt-vc.ts // Received from the verifier const audience = 'https://verifier.example.com' const nonce = 'f8b4a1d2-7c1e-4b0a-9d3e-2a6c5e8f1b90' const presentation = await holder.sdJwtVc.present({ // firstCredential carries the kmsKeyId of the record sdJwtVc: record.firstCredential, presentationFrame: { given_name: true, address: { locality: true } }, verifierMetadata: { audience, nonce, issuedAt: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) }, }) presentationFrame sets true for each selectively disclosable claim to disclose, nested like the payload. Claims that aren't selectively disclosable are always included. verifierMetadata creates the key binding JWT with the verifier's audience and nonce, and additionalPayload adds claims to it. Key binding fails for a credential without cnf. Leave verifierMetadata out to present without key binding. Pass record.firstCredential rather than the compact string, so Credo knows which key to sign with. For records with several instances, useInstanceFromCredentialRecord from @credo-ts/core picks an unused one.

Verifier sd-jwt-vc.ts const result = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: presentation, keyBinding: { audience, nonce }, requiredClaimKeys: ['given_name', 'address.locality'], fetchTypeMetadata: true, trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid }], }) if (result.isValid === false) throw result.error // { vct, iss, cnf, iat, given_name, address: { locality, country }, nationalities: [] } console.log(result.sdJwtVc.prettyClaims) console.log(result.sdJwtVc.typeMetadata?.name) verify returns { isValid: true, sdJwtVc } or { isValid: false, error }, and sdJwtVc.prettyClaims holds the disclosed claims. Verification checks the issuer signature, the digests of the disclosures, iat, nbf and exp (with the agent's validitySkewSeconds), the typ header and the status. Options: Option Effect keyBinding Requires a key binding JWT signed by the cnf key, with this audience and nonce. requiredClaimKeys Claims that must be disclosed, as dot paths such as address.locality. trustedIssuers The issuers to accept for this call. fetchTypeMetadata Resolves the type metadata of the vct into sdJwtVc.typeMetadata. A failed fetch doesn't fail verification. disableStatusValidation Skips the status check. now The time to verify against. Trust depends on how the credential is signed: DID: any issuer DID is accepted unless trustedIssuers or the agent's getTrustedIssuersForVerification callback returns a list. With a list, the issuer DID must be on it. X.509: verification fails unless a trust anchor is configured, per call or on the agent. Verifier sd-jwt-vc.ts const x509Result = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: x509Credential.compact, trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')] }], }) if (x509Result.isValid === false) throw x509Result.error To configure trust once for all verifications, see Trusted issuers. If the credential has a status claim, verify fetches the status list and fails when the credential is revoked or suspended. See Status lists.

error is the error of the first check that failed. Read its message to see why: sd-jwt-vc.ts const expired = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({ payload: { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 3600 }, issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl }, }) const expiredResult = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: expired.compact }) if (expiredResult.isValid === false) { console.log(expiredResult.error.message) }

SD-JWT VC type metadata describes a vct: display names, claim labels and rendering. By default Credo only resolves vct values that are HTTPS URLs, by fetching them. To serve type metadata yourself, or resolve other vct values, register SdJwtVcModule with a customTypeMetadataResolver: sd-jwt-vc.ts const identityTypeMetadata = { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', name: 'Identity credential', display: [{ locale: 'en-US', name: 'Identity credential' }], claims: [{ path: ['given_name'], display: [{ locale: 'en-US', label: 'Given name' }] }], } const sdJwtVcModule = new SdJwtVcModule({ // Called for the `vct` of a credential and for every `extends` value in its type metadata customTypeMetadataResolver: async (vct, _integrity, { defaultResolver }) => { if (vct === identityTypeMetadata.vct) return identityTypeMetadata return defaultResolver({}) }, }) customTypeMetadataResolver is called for the vct, and for each extends value in the type metadata. Return the type metadata document, undefined for none, or call defaultResolver for the HTTPS fetch. If the credential has a vct#integrity claim, your resolver has to check it; IntegrityVerifier from @credo-ts/core does that. The default resolver checks integrity itself. Pass the module under the sdJwtVc key, which replaces the default module. agent.sdJwtVc.fetchTypeMetadata(sdJwtVc) resolves type metadata outside of verification.
SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC Status lists Trusted issuers

A Token Status List is a signed, compressed list with one status entry per credential, which the issuer publishes at a URL. Each credential points to its entry with the URL and an index, and the verifier fetches the list to check the entry. Credo uses status lists for SD-JWT VC (as a JWT) and mdoc (as a CWT). This page covers creating and updating lists with agent.tokenStatusList, referencing them from credentials, and how verification checks them.

Use a status list when you must be able to revoke or suspend credentials before they expire. Credentials that are short-lived and reissued often don't need one: their expiry does the job, and you have no list to host. Use 1 bit per entry if you only revoke, and 2 bits if you also suspend. Credo supports Token Status Lists for SD-JWT VC and mdoc only. It doesn't support the W3C Bitstring Status List, so W3C credentials have no revocation in Credo (see W3C Verifiable Credentials). AnonCreds uses its own revocation registries, published on the ledger, and the holder proves non-revocation in the presentation (see AnonCreds).

agent.tokenStatusList creates, updates and fetches status list tokens, and verification checks them. Everything around that is up to your app: Host each token at its URL, with content type application/statuslist+jwt or application/statuslist+cwt. Store the current token, and publish a new one after each change and before the current one expires. Allocate an index for each credential and remember which credential has which index. Pick unused indexes at random: indexes handed out in order reveal when a credential was issued. The examples run an issuer, a holder and a verifier in one process, with a small HTTP server that stands in for your hosting: status-list.ts // Your app hosts the status list tokens. This is a minimal stand-in for that endpoint. const hostedStatusLists = new Map<string, { contentType: string; body: string | Uint8Array }>() const server = createServer((request, response) => { const hosted = hostedStatusLists.get(request.url ?? '') if (!hosted) return response.writeHead(404).end() response.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': hosted.contentType }).end(hosted.body) }) await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(4070, resolve))

Issuer status-list.ts const statusListUri = 'http://localhost:4070/status-lists/1' const { statusList: statusListJwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.createTokenStatusList<'jwt'>({ format: 'jwt', signer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl }, alg: 'EdDSA', // A new list has every entry set to 0 (valid) statusList: { statusListLength: 100_000, bitsPerStatus: 1 }, statusListUri, expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000), // Seconds a verifier may cache the list timeToLive: 60 * 60, }) hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+jwt', body: statusListJwt }) format is jwt for SD-JWT VC and cwt for mdoc. statusList sets the number of entries and the bits per entry (1, 2, 4 or 8). The statuses are 0 (valid), 1 (invalid) and 2 (suspended), so suspension needs at least 2 bits. Every entry starts at 0. statusListUri is the URL where you host the token. It becomes the sub claim, and verification fails when it doesn't match the URL in the credential. signer is { method: 'did', didUrl } or { method: 'x5c', x5c }, with a key in the agent's KMS. CWT lists need x5c. expiresAt and timeToLive set exp and ttl, where ttl tells verifiers how long they may cache the list. The result has the encoded token in statusList and the parsed token in parsed. Pass the format as type parameter, such as createTokenStatusList<'jwt'>, to get the matching result type.

For an SD-JWT VC, add a status claim to the payload: Issuer status-list.ts // Your app allocates the index and remembers which credential uses it const statusListIndex = 4821 const credential = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({ payload: { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', given_name: 'Jane', status: { status_list: { idx: statusListIndex, uri: statusListUri } }, }, issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl }, holder: { method: 'jwk', jwk: holderJwk }, disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name'] }, }) The status claim can't be selectively disclosable. For an mdoc, pass statusInfo: { index, uri } to agent.mdoc.sign (see mdoc below).
documents.s: Reference the list from a credential

documents.t: Set the new status in the current token, and host the result: Issuer status-list.ts // Load the current token (from your own storage, or fetch it), then set the new status const { statusList: currentToken } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.fetchTokenStatusList<'jwt'>({ uri: statusListUri, acceptedFormats: ['jwt'], }) const { statusList: updatedStatusListJwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.updateTokenStatusList<'jwt'>({ format: 'jwt', token: currentToken, // 0 = valid, 1 = invalid (revoked), 2 = suspended. Needs `bitsPerStatus: 2` or more for 2. status: { index: statusListIndex, status: 1 }, signer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl }, alg: 'EdDSA', expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000), }) hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+jwt', body: updatedStatusListJwt }) status takes one { index, status } or an array, so you can change many entries in one update. The update keeps the URL, sets a new iat, and keeps exp and ttl unless you pass new values, so pass expiresAt again when the list should stay valid longer. fetchTokenStatusList downloads and parses a token, but doesn't verify its signature: load the current token from your own storage if you can.

agent.sdJwtVc.verify fetches the status list of a credential with a status claim, verifies its signature and reads the entry: Verifier status-list.ts const validResult = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact }) console.log(validResult.isValid) // true After the update the same credential fails: Verifier status-list.ts const revokedResult = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact }) if (revokedResult.isValid === false) { // 'Status is not valid' console.log(revokedResult.error.message) } Any status other than 0 fails verification, including suspended, and disableStatusValidation: true skips the check. Credo fetches the list on every verification, with the agent's fetch. Which key may sign the status list depends on the trusted issuer that matched the credential: No trusted issuers configured (DID issuers only): the list must be signed with the credential issuer's key. A trusted DID: the list's iss must be that DID. A trusted X.509 issuer: the list's certificate chain must chain to the status certificates of the trusted issuer. Without status, it must chain to the issuance certificates and be the same chain that signed the credential.

mdoc status lists are CWTs signed with an X.509 certificate, and need an expiration time. Verification of an mdoc, and of a device response, checks the status the same way: any status other than valid fails. status-list.ts // mdoc status lists are CWTs, signed with the issuer certificate const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk), issuer: { commonName: 'Example mDL Issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, }) const mdocStatusListUri = 'http://localhost:4070/status-lists/mdoc-1' const { statusList: statusListCwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.createTokenStatusList<'cwt'>({ format: 'cwt', signer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] }, alg: 'ES256', statusList: { statusListLength: 100_000, bitsPerStatus: 1 }, statusListUri: mdocStatusListUri, // Required for mdoc expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000), }) hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/mdoc-1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+cwt', body: statusListCwt }) const mdoc = await issuer.mdoc.sign({ docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', namespaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: 'Doe', issuing_country: 'NL' } }, validityInfo: { validUntil: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) }, issuerCertificate, holderKey: holderJwk, statusInfo: { index: statusListIndex, uri: mdocStatusListUri }, }) const { statusList: updatedStatusListCwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.updateTokenStatusList<'cwt'>({ format: 'cwt', token: statusListCwt, status: { index: statusListIndex, status: 1 }, signer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] }, alg: 'ES256', }) hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/mdoc-1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+cwt', body: updatedStatusListCwt }) const mdocResult = await verifier.mdoc.verify(Mdoc.fromBase64Url(mdoc.base64Url), { trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')], }) console.log(mdocResult.isValid) // false As with SD-JWT VC, the status list must be signed by the same certificate chain as the mdoc, unless you trust a separate status list certificate with trustedCertificates: [{ issuance: [...], status: [...] }].

The W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model defines a JSON structure for credentials and presentations. It doesn't fix how they're signed: the same credential can be secured as a JWT, an SD-JWT, or with an embedded proof. Credo supports data model 1.1 on agent.w3cCredentials and data model 2.0 on agent.w3cV2Credentials. This page covers signing, storing, presenting and verifying with both. For exchange, see W3C VCs with OpenID4VC and W3C VCs with DIDComm.

Data model Secured as Claim format Selective disclosure Holder binding Exchange 1.1 JWT jwt_vc (jwt_vc_json in OpenID4VC) No DID in credentialSubject.id OpenID4VC, DIDComm presentation only 1.1 JSON-LD with an Ed25519 Linked Data proof ldp_vc No DID in credentialSubject.id DIDComm (OpenID4VC has known problems) 2.0 JWT vc+jwt No cnf claim None, sign and verify only 2.0 SD-JWT vc+sd-jwt Yes cnf claim OpenID4VC, DIDComm issuance 2.0 Data Integrity (eddsa-jcs-2022) di_vc No DID in credentialSubject.id DIDComm issuance The issuer always signs with a key of a DID it created (or imported with its keys). X.509 issuers aren't supported. W3C 2.0 vc+sd-jwt is a different format from SD-JWT VC (dc+sd-jwt), even though both use SD-JWT. For the protocol details, see W3C VCs with OpenID4VC and W3C VCs with DIDComm.

Use the variant your ecosystem or verifiers ask for. Without such a requirement: Over OpenID4VC, use data model 1.1 as JWT (jwt_vc_json). Use 2.0 as SD-JWT (vc+sd-jwt) when you need selective disclosure. Over DIDComm, use 1.1 as JSON-LD (ldp_vc), the only 1.1 variant that DIDComm can issue, or 2.0 as SD-JWT for selective disclosure. Avoid 2.0 as plain JWT and with Data Integrity. Credo can't exchange vc+jwt over any protocol, can't present di_vc over any protocol, and doesn't check the issuer trust and validity period of di_vc credentials. If you don't need W3C VCs, SD-JWT VC is simpler and has selective disclosure.

Everything on this page is in @credo-ts/core, and both modules are default modules. The agent also needs storage and key management. The examples use an issuer, a holder and a verifier, each with an Ed25519 did:key: w3c.ts import { Agent, ClaimFormat, DidKey, defaultDocumentLoader, JsonTransformer, type KeyDidCreateOptions, purposes, utils, W3cCredential, W3cCredentialRecord, W3cCredentialsModule, W3cJsonLdVerifiablePresentation, w3cDate, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' const membershipContext = { '@context': { MembershipCredential: 'https://example.com/vocab#MembershipCredential', name: 'https://schema.org/name', memberSince: { '@id': 'https://example.com/vocab#memberSince', '@type': 'http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#date' }, }, } function createAgent(storage: ExampleStorage) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // Serve your own JSON-LD contexts instead of fetching them from the network w3cCredentials: new W3cCredentialsModule({ documentLoader: (agentContext) => defaultDocumentLoader(agentContext, { 'https://example.com/contexts/membership/v1': membershipContext }), }), }, }) } async function createDidKey(agent: Agent) { const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the DID failed') return { did: didState.did, didUrl: `${didState.did}#${DidKey.fromDid(didState.did).publicJwk.fingerprint}` } }

Every property of a JSON-LD credential must be defined in one of its @contexts, and signing and verifying load those contexts through a document loader. The default loader has copies of the common contexts (credentials v1 and v2, the security suites, DIDs, ODRL, schema.org, Open Badges 3.0), resolves DIDs, and fetches every other URL from the network. Pass your own contexts to defaultDocumentLoader as shown above, or set your own documentLoader to control what is fetched. Register W3cCredentialsModule under the w3cCredentials key to replace the default module. Data model 2.0 uses the same document loader.

w3c.ts const issuerDid = await createDidKey(issuer) const holderDid = await createDidKey(holder) const credential = W3cCredential.fromJson({ '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://example.com/contexts/membership/v1'], type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'MembershipCredential'], issuer: issuerDid.did, issuanceDate: w3cDate(Date.now()), // The subject id binds the credential to the holder DID credentialSubject: { id: holderDid.did, name: 'Jane Doe', memberSince: '2024-01-01' }, }) const jwtVc = await issuer.w3cCredentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.JwtVc>({ format: ClaimFormat.JwtVc, credential, alg: 'EdDSA', verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl, }) console.log(jwtVc.serializedJwt) const ldpVc = await issuer.w3cCredentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.LdpVc>({ format: ClaimFormat.LdpVc, credential, // did:key Ed25519 keys are Ed25519VerificationKey2018 verification methods proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl, }) console.log(ldpVc.toJson()) verificationMethod is the DID URL of an assertionMethod key of the issuer DID. For jwt_vc, alg must fit the key. A JWT VC can have only one credentialSubject. For ldp_vc, proofType is Ed25519Signature2018 for Ed25519VerificationKey2018 verification methods (such as did:key) or Ed25519Signature2020 for Ed25519VerificationKey2020. These are the only Linked Data suites. There is no BBS+ suite, so 1.1 credentials have no selective disclosure. caution Build JSON-LD credentials with W3cCredential.fromJson, as above. A new W3cCredential({ ... }) without expirationDate fails to sign as ldp_vc with "expirationDate" must be a valid date: undefined.

Holder w3c.ts const jwtResult = await holder.w3cCredentials.verifyCredential({ credential: jwtVc.serializedJwt }) const ldpResult = await holder.w3cCredentials.verifyCredential({ credential: ldpVc }) if (!jwtResult.isValid || !ldpResult.isValid) throw new Error('Received an invalid credential') await holder.w3cCredentials.store({ record: W3cCredentialRecord.fromCredential(jwtVc) }) await holder.w3cCredentials.store({ record: W3cCredentialRecord.fromCredential(ldpVc) }) // Returns credentials, not records const memberships = await holder.w3cCredentials.findAllByQuery({ types: ['MembershipCredential'], claimFormat: ClaimFormat.LdpVc, }) console.log(memberships.length) findAllByQuery returns the credentials, not the records. Records are tagged with claimFormat, types, issuerId, subjectIds, schemaIds and contexts. getById and getAll return records, and deleteById removes one. There is no update. Store JSON-LD credentials with agent.w3cCredentials.store: it adds the expanded types that OpenID4VP queries on.

The holder wraps credentials in a presentation and signs it with an authentication key of its DID, the DID in credentialSubject.id: Holder w3c.ts // Received from the verifier const challenge = 'c0ffee12-3456-4789-abcd-ef0123456789' const domain = 'https://verifier.example.com' const jwtPresentation = await holder.w3cCredentials.createPresentation({ credentials: [jwtVc], holder: holderDid.did, }) const jwtVp = await holder.w3cCredentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.JwtVp>({ format: ClaimFormat.JwtVp, presentation: jwtPresentation, alg: 'EdDSA', verificationMethod: holderDid.didUrl, challenge, domain, }) const ldpPresentation = await holder.w3cCredentials.createPresentation({ // Signing a JSON-LD presentation without an id fails id: `urn:uuid:${utils.uuid()}`, credentials: [ldpVc], holder: holderDid.did, }) const ldpVp = await holder.w3cCredentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.LdpVp>({ format: ClaimFormat.LdpVp, presentation: ldpPresentation, proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', proofPurpose: new purposes.AuthenticationProofPurpose({ challenge, domain }), verificationMethod: holderDid.didUrl, challenge, domain, }) challenge and domain come from the verifier. In a JWT VP they're the nonce and aud claims. A JWT VP can only contain JWT VCs, and a JSON-LD VP only JSON-LD VCs. A JSON-LD presentation needs a proofPurpose, and an id: signing fails without one.

Verifier w3c.ts const jwtVpResult = await verifier.w3cCredentials.verifyPresentation({ presentation: jwtVp.serializedJwt, challenge, domain, trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid.did }], }) // A JSON-LD presentation must be passed as an instance, not as JSON const ldpVpResult = await verifier.w3cCredentials.verifyPresentation({ presentation: JsonTransformer.fromJSON(ldpVp.toJson(), W3cJsonLdVerifiablePresentation), challenge, domain, trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid.did }], }) if (!jwtVpResult.isValid) console.error(jwtVpResult.error, jwtVpResult.validations) console.log(jwtVpResult.isValid, ldpVpResult.isValid) verifyCredential and verifyPresentation return { isValid, validations, error }, where validations shows which check failed. For a presentation, Credo checks the holder signature, challenge and domain, every credential in it, and that the holder is the subject of each credential. A JSON-LD credential or presentation must be passed as an instance, such as from JsonTransformer.fromJSON. The date checks of JSON-LD credentials don't use the agent's validitySkewSeconds. Without trustedIssuers and without a trusted issuers callback on the agent, any issuer DID is accepted.

The 2.0 examples use the same agents and DIDs, and these imports: w3c-v2.ts import { Agent, ClaimFormat, DidKey, type KeyDidCreateOptions, W3cV2Credential, W3cV2CredentialRecord, W3cV2EnvelopedVerifiableCredential, W3cV2Presentation, W3cV2SdJwtCredentialService, w3cDate, } from '@credo-ts/core'

Issuer w3c-v2.ts const credential = new W3cV2Credential({ type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'MembershipCredential'], issuer: issuerDid.did, validFrom: w3cDate(Date.now()), credentialSubject: { id: holderDid.did, name: 'Jane Doe', memberSince: '2024-01-01' }, }) // vc+jwt const jwtVc = await issuer.w3cV2Credentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.JwtW3cVc>({ format: ClaimFormat.JwtW3cVc, credential, alg: 'EdDSA', verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl, }) // vc+sd-jwt: `cnf` binds the credential to the holder key const sdJwtVc = await issuer.w3cV2Credentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVc>({ format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVc, credential, alg: 'EdDSA', verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl, holder: { method: 'did', didUrl: holderDid.didUrl }, disclosureFrame: { credentialSubject: { _sd: ['name', 'memberSince'] } }, }) // di_vc with a Data Integrity proof const diVc = await issuer.w3cV2Credentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.DiVc>({ format: ClaimFormat.DiVc, credential, cryptosuite: 'eddsa-jcs-2022', verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl, }) // `encoded` is a compact string for vc+jwt and vc+sd-jwt, and JSON for di_vc console.log(sdJwtVc.encoded, diVc.encoded) verificationMethod is the DID URL of an assertionMethod key of the issuer DID, and alg must fit the key. holder adds a cnf claim with a DID URL or a JWK, for vc+jwt and vc+sd-jwt. Choose as for SD-JWT VC. A di_vc credential is bound through credentialSubject.id. disclosureFrame works as for SD-JWT VC. @context, type, credentialStatus, credentialSchema and relatedResource can't be selectively disclosable at the top level. cryptosuite for di_vc is eddsa-jcs-2022, the only cryptosuite, which needs an Ed25519 key.

Holder w3c-v2.ts const sdJwtResult = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.verifyCredential({ credential: sdJwtVc.encoded }) const diResult = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.verifyCredential({ credential: diVc }) if (!sdJwtResult.isValid || !diResult.isValid) throw new Error('Received an invalid credential') const record = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.store({ record: W3cV2CredentialRecord.fromCredential(sdJwtVc) }) // Returns credentials, not records const memberships = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.findAllByQuery({ claimFormat: ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVc, types: ['MembershipCredential'], }) console.log(memberships.length) As in 1.1, findAllByQuery returns credentials and there is no update. A record can hold several instances of the same credential for batch issuance.

There is no key binding JWT for 2.0. The holder proves possession by signing a presentation that contains the credential: Holder w3c-v2.ts // Received from the verifier const challenge = '9d0e4c6a-2b1f-4e8d-a7c3-5f6b8e9d0a1c' const domain = 'https://verifier.example.com' // Selective disclosure is only available on the service const sdJwtService = holder.dependencyManager.resolve(W3cV2SdJwtCredentialService) const disclosed = await sdJwtService.present(holder.context, { credential: record.encoded, presentationFrame: { credentialSubject: { name: true } }, }) const sdJwtVp = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVp>({ format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVp, presentation: new W3cV2Presentation({ holder: holderDid.did, verifiableCredential: [W3cV2EnvelopedVerifiableCredential.fromVerifiableCredential(disclosed)], }), challenge, domain, }) const diVp = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.DiVp>({ format: ClaimFormat.DiVp, presentation: new W3cV2Presentation({ holder: holderDid.did, verifiableCredential: [diVc] }), cryptosuite: 'eddsa-jcs-2022', verificationMethod: holderDid.didUrl, challenge, domain, }) Selective disclosure for vc+sd-jwt is only on W3cV2SdJwtCredentialService. Wrap the result with W3cV2EnvelopedVerifiableCredential to put it in a presentation. For vp+jwt and vp+sd-jwt, Credo signs with the authentication key of the holder DID. The DID must be created in this agent, with exactly one authentication key in its KMS. Without holder, Credo signs with the key in the credentials' cnf. For di_vp, pass the verificationMethod and cryptosuite.

Verifier w3c-v2.ts const sdJwtVpResult = await verifier.w3cV2Credentials.verifyPresentation({ presentation: sdJwtVp.encoded, challenge, domain, }) const diVpResult = await verifier.w3cV2Credentials.verifyPresentation({ presentation: diVp, challenge, domain }) if (!sdJwtVpResult.isValid) console.error(sdJwtVpResult.presentation.validations, sdJwtVpResult.credentialEntries) console.log(sdJwtVpResult.isValid, diVpResult.isValid) The result has presentation.validations for the presentation itself and credentialEntries with a result per credential. verifyCredential verifies a single credential, and takes trustedIssuers: Verifier w3c-v2.ts const jwtVcResult = await verifier.w3cV2Credentials.verifyCredential({ credential: jwtVc.encoded, trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid.did }], }) console.log(jwtVcResult.isValid) Trust in 2.0 trustedIssuers on verifyPresentation isn't applied to the credentials in the presentation. Configure a trusted issuers callback on the agent instead. For di_vc credentials, Credo checks neither trusted issuers nor validFrom and validUntil. Check them yourself.

Credo doesn't verify credentialStatus for W3C credentials. There is no support for Bitstring Status List or Status List 2021. Data model 1.1: verifying a credential with a credentialStatus, or a presentation that contains one, fails by default. Pass verifyCredentialStatus: false and check the status yourself. Data model 2.0: credentialStatus is ignored, unless you pass verifyCredentialStatus: true, which makes verification fail. For revocation with SD-JWT VC and mdoc, see Status lists.
W3C VCs with OpenID4VC W3C VCs with DIDComm Trusted issuers

Credo uses DIDs to sign and verify credentials, as AnonCreds issuer identifiers, and for DIDComm connections. agent.dids creates, resolves and imports DIDs, and keeps track of the ones your agent controls. For what DIDs are, see DIDs and DIDComm.

An issuer signs with a key that's bound to an X.509 certificate or to a DID. The credential format and the ecosystem usually decide which one: You issue Identify the issuer with mdoc An X.509 certificate. mdoc doesn't support DIDs. SD-JWT VC for HAIP or EUDI wallets An X.509 certificate chain (x5c) that leads to a root the verifier trusts. SD-JWT VC in other ecosystems An X.509 certificate or a DID. W3C VC A DID. W3C credentials can't be signed with a certificate. AnonCreds A DID on the network of the AnonCreds registry. As a rule of thumb: use X.509 certificates for OpenID4VC, and DIDs for DIDComm and AnonCreds. OpenID4VP verifiers make the same choice for their client identifier, see Verifying credentials. How a verifier decides whether to accept the signer is on Trusted issuers.

You need Use A holder DID, or a DID for tests did:key (default) or did:jwk. The DID contains the public key, so there's nothing to publish. DIDComm connections did:peer. DIDComm creates these for each connection. A public issuer DID without a ledger did:web (default) to host a DID document under your domain. did:webvh adds a verifiable history of the document, and can hold AnonCreds objects. An AnonCreds issuer on a ledger The method of the network your ecosystem uses: did:indy (Indy networks such as Sovrin), did:cheqd or did:hedera.

Method Create Update Deactivate Resolve Package did:key Yes No No Yes @credo-ts/core did:jwk Yes No No Yes @credo-ts/core did:peer Yes No No Yes @credo-ts/core did:web Import only No No Yes @credo-ts/core did:webvh Yes Yes No Yes @credo-ts/webvh did:cheqd Yes Yes Yes Yes @credo-ts/cheqd did:indy Yes No No Yes @credo-ts/indy-vdr did:sov No No No Yes @credo-ts/indy-vdr did:hedera Yes Yes Yes Yes @credo-ts/hedera

agent.dids.create creates the DID and its keys, registers it when the method needs that, and stores a DidRecord. The record links the verification methods to the keys in the KMS, so the agent can sign with the DID later. dids.ts const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } }, }) // Registrars report failures in the result instead of throwing if (didState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Creating the did failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`) } // A did:key has one verification method, identified by the key fingerprint const didKey = DidKey.fromDid(didState.did) const verificationMethodId = `${didKey.did}#${didKey.publicJwk.fingerprint}` The generic parameter (KeyDidCreateOptions, JwkDidCreateOptions, CheqdDidCreateOptions, and so on) types the options for the method. Registrars return failures instead of throwing, so always check didState.state: finished: didState.did and didState.didDocument are set. failed: didState.reason says why. action or wait: the method needs another step, for example an endorsement of an Indy transaction. To use a key that's already in the KMS, pass its keyId instead of createKey: dids.ts const { keyId } = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const jwkResult = await agent.dids.create<JwkDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'jwk', options: { keyId }, }) if (jwkResult.didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the did:jwk failed') // The verification method of a did:jwk is always `#0` const jwkVerificationMethodId = `${jwkResult.didState.did}#0`

dids.ts const resolution = await agent.dids.resolve(didState.did) if (!resolution.didDocument) { throw new Error(`Resolving failed: ${resolution.didResolutionMetadata.error}`) } // resolveDidDocument returns the document, or throws when resolution fails const didDocument = await agent.dids.resolveDidDocument(didState.did) const verificationMethod = didDocument.dereferenceKey(verificationMethodId, ['assertionMethod']) resolve returns the full resolution result, with didResolutionMetadata.error when resolution fails. resolveDidDocument returns only the document and throws on failure. Credo caches resolved documents for 5 minutes for methods whose resolver allows it (did:web, did:webvh, did:cheqd, did:indy, did:sov and did:hedera). Pass { useCache: false } to resolve to skip the cache, or cacheDurationInSeconds to change the duration. For DIDs that you created or imported, these resolvers (except did:sov) return the document from your DidRecord instead of fetching it.

Import a DID that you created outside Credo, such as a did:web (there's no did:web registrar) or an existing ledger DID. keys links verification methods in the document to keys in the KMS. Without it the agent can resolve the DID, but not sign with it. dids.ts const did = 'did:web:issuer.example.com' const webKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const webVerificationMethod = getMultikey({ did, verificationMethodId: `${did}#key-1`, publicJwk: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(webKey.publicJwk), }) const webDidDocument = new DidDocumentBuilder(did) .addContext('https://w3id.org/security/multikey/v1') .addVerificationMethod(webVerificationMethod) .addAuthentication(webVerificationMethod.id) .addAssertionMethod(webVerificationMethod.id) .build() await agent.dids.import({ did, didDocument: webDidDocument, // Links the verification method to the KMS key, so the agent can sign with this did keys: [{ didDocumentRelativeKeyId: '#key-1', kmsKeyId: webKey.keyId }], }) // Host this JSON at https://issuer.example.com/.well-known/did.json const didJson = webDidDocument.toJSON() PublicJwk comes from @credo-ts/core/kms. Without didDocument, Credo resolves the DID to get the document. Importing a DID that already exists throws, unless you pass overwrite: true. To list the DIDs your agent created or imported, use getCreatedDids, optionally filtered by method or did: dids.ts const createdWebDids = await agent.dids.getCreatedDids({ method: 'web' })

DidsModule is registered by default under the key dids, with these registrars and resolvers: Registrars: did:key, did:peer and did:jwk. Resolvers: did:web, did:key, did:peer and did:jwk. To add a method, register DidsModule yourself. The packages for ledger and web methods don't add their registrar and resolver to DidsModule, so you always list them: agent.ts import { Agent, DidsModule, JwkDidRegistrar, JwkDidResolver, KeyDidRegistrar, KeyDidResolver, PeerDidRegistrar, PeerDidResolver, WebDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { WebVhDidRegistrar, WebVhDidResolver, WebVhModule } from '@credo-ts/webvh' const didModules = { webvh: new WebVhModule(), dids: new DidsModule({ // These lists replace the defaults, so include the built-in methods you still need registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new PeerDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar(), new WebVhDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [ new KeyDidResolver(), new PeerDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver(), new WebVhDidResolver(), ], }), } Your lists replace the defaults Passing registrars or resolvers replaces the default list. Credo adds the did:key and did:peer registrar and resolver back, because DIDComm needs them, but not did:web and did:jwk. Include WebDidResolver, JwkDidResolver and JwkDidRegistrar yourself if you still need them. publicDidMethods lists the methods whose documents are the same for every agent context. With multi-tenancy, their documents are cached once for all tenants instead of per tenant. The default is ['web', 'indy', 'sov', 'cheqd', 'hedera', 'webvh'].

X.509 certificates Create self-signed and CA-issued X.509 certificates and certificate signing requests with agent.x509, parse certificates, validate chains and check revocation. Trusted issuers How Credo decides whether to trust the issuer of a credential or the signer of a request, what it does by default, and how to configure trust with getTrustedIssuersForVerification and trusted X.509 certificates. cheqd Create, update and deactivate did:cheqd DIDs, publish DID-linked resources, and use cheqd as an AnonCreds registry with @credo-ts/cheqd. Indy VDR Connect to Hyperledger Indy networks with @credo-ts/indy-vdr to resolve did:indy and did:sov, register did:indy DIDs with an endorser, and use Indy as an AnonCreds registry. Hedera Create, update, deactivate and resolve did:hedera DIDs, and use Hedera as an AnonCreds registry with @credo-ts/hedera. did:webvh Create, update and resolve did:webvh DIDs with @credo-ts/webvh, host the DID log, and use did:webvh as an AnonCreds registry.

Connect to Hyperledger Indy networks with @credo-ts/indy-vdr to resolve did:indy and did:sov, register did:indy DIDs with an endorser, and use Indy as an AnonCreds registry.

cheqd is a Cosmos-based network for DIDs and DID-linked resources: data such as logos, schemas or status lists, published under a DID and controlled with its keys. @credo-ts/cheqd adds the did:cheqd method, DID-linked resources and an AnonCreds registry. Ledger writes cost CHEQ tokens, paid by a Cosmos account that you configure. Use did:cheqd when your ecosystem uses cheqd, for example to issue AnonCreds credentials on cheqd, or to publish resources under a DID on a public network. For a public issuer DID without a ledger, did:web is simpler, see Choose a DID method.
npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/cheqd@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/cheqd@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/cheqd@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/cheqd@^0.7.2

Register CheqdModule with the networks you use, and add the cheqd registrar and resolver to DidsModule: agent.ts import { type CheqdDidCreateOptions, CheqdDidRegistrar, CheqdDidResolver, CheqdModule } from '@credo-ts/cheqd' import { Agent, DidDocumentService, DidsModule, JwkDidRegistrar, JwkDidResolver, KeyDidRegistrar, KeyDidResolver, PeerDidRegistrar, PeerDidResolver, utils, WebDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' const cheqdModules = { cheqd: new CheqdModule({ networks: [ // The payer account pays the fees for ledger writes { network: 'testnet', cosmosPayerSeed: process.env.CHEQD_TESTNET_PAYER_MNEMONIC }, // Without a payer seed you can resolve, but not write { network: 'mainnet' }, ], }), dids: new DidsModule({ registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new PeerDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar(), new CheqdDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [ new KeyDidResolver(), new PeerDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver(), new CheqdDidResolver(), ], }), } Spread these modules into the modules of your agent. Each network takes: Option Description network 'testnet' or 'mainnet'. cosmosPayerSeed Mnemonic, or a 32-character seed, of the Cosmos account that pays for writes. Without it, Credo generates a new empty account on every start: you can resolve, but writes fail. rpcUrl RPC endpoint. Defaults to https://rpc.cheqd.network for testnet and https://rpc.cheqd.net for mainnet. The agent connects to the networks in the background when it starts. CheqdModule doesn't register the did:cheqd registrar and resolver itself, so list them in DidsModule. Your lists replace the default registrars and resolvers, see Configure DID methods.

issuer.ts const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<CheqdDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'cheqd', options: { network: 'testnet', methodSpecificIdAlgo: 'uuid', createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } }, }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Creating the did failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`) } const did = didState.did Credo creates an Ed25519 key and a DID document with one JsonWebKey2020 verification method, #key-1. To use an Ed25519 key that's already in the KMS, pass keyId instead of createKey. methodSpecificIdAlgo picks the identifier format: uuid (default) or base58btc. To publish your own DID document, pass didDocument instead, with options.keys linking each authentication verification method to a KMS key. cheqd accepts Ed25519VerificationKey2018, Ed25519VerificationKey2020 and JsonWebKey2020 verification methods. All write operations accept fee and feeOptions for the ledger transaction, and versionId for the new version of the DID document (a random UUID by default).

Resolve the document, change it, and pass the full new document to update: issuer.ts const didDocument = await agent.dids.resolveDidDocument(did) didDocument.service = [ new DidDocumentService({ id: `${did}#website`, type: 'LinkedDomains', serviceEndpoint: 'https://issuer.example.com', }), ] const updateResult = await agent.dids.update({ did, didDocument }) if (updateResult.didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Updating the did failed') The keys of all authentication verification methods sign the update, so they must be in the agent's KMS.
issuer.ts const deactivateResult = await agent.dids.deactivate({ did }) A deactivated DID still resolves, and its document metadata marks it as deactivated. You can't update it anymore.

Create a resource under a DID with agent.modules.cheqd, where cheqd is the key you registered the module under: issuer.ts const resourceId = utils.uuid() const resourceResult = await agent.modules.cheqd.createResource(did, { id: resourceId, name: 'issuer-logo', resourceType: 'Logo', version: '1.0', data: { uri: 'https://issuer.example.com/logo.png' }, }) if (resourceResult.resourceState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the resource failed') id must be a UUID. data can be an object (stored as JSON), a Uint8Array, or a base64 string: Credo always decodes a string as base64. All verification methods of the DID sign the resource, so the agent needs all their keys. A resource with the same name and resourceType as an existing one becomes a new version of it. Resolve a resource by its id, or by name and type: issuer.ts // By resource id const byId = await agent.modules.cheqd.resolveResource(`${did}/resources/${resourceId}`) // By name and type: the latest version, or add &version=1.0 or &resourceVersionTime=<unix time> const byName = await agent.modules.cheqd.resolveResource(`${did}?resourceName=issuer-logo&resourceType=Logo`) The result has resource and resourceMetadata, or error and message when the resource can't be resolved.

CheqdAnonCredsRegistry registers and resolves AnonCreds schemas, credential definitions and revocation data as DID-linked resources. Import it from the @credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds subpath: the export from the @credo-ts/cheqd root is deprecated, and removed in 0.8. Set up AnonCreds as described in AnonCreds, with the cheqd registry: agent.ts import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds' import { CheqdAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds' import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs' const anoncreds = new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()], }) The registry also needs CheqdModule, and the issuer needs a did:cheqd.

Hedera is a public network whose Consensus Service (HCS) stores did:hedera DID documents and AnonCreds objects. @credo-ts/hedera adds the did:hedera method and an AnonCreds registry, built on the Hiero DID SDK. Writes cost HBAR, paid by an operator account that you configure. Use did:hedera when your ecosystem uses Hedera, for DIDs or as an AnonCreds registry. Experimental The Hedera module is experimental and may have breaking changes in any release. Pin exact versions of all @credo-ts/* packages when you use it.
npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/hedera@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/hedera@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/hedera@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/hedera@^0.7.2
