Register HederaModule with the networks you use, and add the Hedera registrar and resolver to DidsModule: agent.ts import { Agent, DidDocumentService, DidsModule, JwkDidRegistrar, JwkDidResolver, KeyDidRegistrar, KeyDidResolver, PeerDidRegistrar, PeerDidResolver, WebDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { type HederaDidCreateOptions, HederaDidRegistrar, HederaDidResolver, type HederaDidUpdateOptions, HederaModule, } from '@credo-ts/hedera' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' // The operator account pays the Hedera transaction fees const operatorId = process.env.HEDERA_OPERATOR_ID const operatorKey = process.env.HEDERA_OPERATOR_KEY if (!operatorId || !operatorKey) throw new Error('HEDERA_OPERATOR_ID and HEDERA_OPERATOR_KEY must be set') const hederaModules = { hedera: new HederaModule({ networks: [{ network: 'testnet', operatorId, operatorKey }], }), dids: new DidsModule({ registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new PeerDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar(), new HederaDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [ new KeyDidResolver(), new PeerDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver(), new HederaDidResolver(), ], }), } Spread these modules into the modules of your agent. Each network takes: Option Description network 'mainnet', 'testnet', 'previewnet', 'local-node', or a custom network { name, nodes, mirrorNodes }. operatorId Account id of the operator account, such as 0.0.12345. operatorKey Private key of the operator account. HederaModule doesn't register the DID registrar and resolver itself, so list them in DidsModule. Your lists replace the default registrars and resolvers, see Configure DID methods.

issuer.ts const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<HederaDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'hedera', options: { network: 'testnet' }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Creating the did failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`) } const did = didState.did Credo creates an Ed25519 root key in the KMS and publishes a DID document with it as #did-root-key. The root key signs every later update. Pass secret.rootKeyId to use an Ed25519 key that's already in the KMS. With more than one network configured, options.network picks the network for the new DID. To publish a full DID document right away, pass didDocument, and list the KMS keys of its verification methods in secret.keys as { kmsKeyId, didDocumentRelativeKeyId }.

issuer.ts const updateResult = await agent.dids.update<HederaDidUpdateOptions>({ did, didDocumentOperation: 'addToDidDocument', didDocument: { service: [ new DidDocumentService({ id: `${did}#website`, type: 'LinkedDomains', serviceEndpoint: 'https://issuer.example.com', }), ], }, }) if (updateResult.didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Updating the did failed') didDocumentOperation is required: addToDidDocument adds the services and verification methods in didDocument. removeFromDidDocument removes them. setDidDocument replaces the document. Credo finds the network from the DID and signs with the root key from the DidRecord. Every verification method in the update needs its KMS key: Credo uses the keys in the DidRecord, and you pass keys for new verification methods in secret.keys.
issuer.ts const deactivateResult = await agent.dids.deactivate({ did })

HederaAnonCredsRegistry registers and resolves AnonCreds schemas, credential definitions and revocation data on HCS. Import it from the @credo-ts/hedera/anoncreds subpath: the export from the @credo-ts/hedera root is deprecated, and removed in 0.8. The Hiero DID SDK needs a Zstandard library to store the objects, and a crypto library on React Native: Node.js React Native npm pnpm yarn bun npm install zstd-napi pnpm add zstd-napi yarn add zstd-napi bun add zstd-napi npm pnpm yarn bun npm install react-native-zstd react-native-quick-crypto pnpm add react-native-zstd react-native-quick-crypto yarn add react-native-zstd react-native-quick-crypto bun add react-native-zstd react-native-quick-crypto Set up AnonCreds as described in AnonCreds, with the Hedera registry: agent.ts import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds' import { HederaAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/hedera/anoncreds' import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs' // HederaModule must be registered as well, the registry uses its network configuration const anoncreds = new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new HederaAnonCredsRegistry()], }) The registry uses the network configuration of HederaModule, so register that module as well. The issuer needs a did:hedera.

Hyperledger Indy networks, such as BCovrin Test and Sovrin, store DIDs and AnonCreds objects. @credo-ts/indy-vdr connects to one or more Indy networks through Indy VDR. It resolves did:indy and did:sov, registers did:indy DIDs, and provides an AnonCreds registry. Use it when your ecosystem uses an Indy network, usually to issue or verify AnonCreds credentials.

Node.js React Native npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-nodejs@^0.3.0 pnpm add @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-nodejs@^0.3.0 yarn add @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-nodejs@^0.3.0 bun add @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-nodejs@^0.3.0 npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-react-native@^0.3.0 pnpm add @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-react-native@^0.3.0 yarn add @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-react-native@^0.3.0 bun add @credo-ts/indy-vdr@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/indy-vdr-react-native@^0.3.0 This version of Credo needs version 0.3 of the native Indy VDR packages: @credo-ts/indy-vdr has a peer dependency on @hyperledger/indy-vdr-shared ^0.3.0.

Register IndyVdrModule with the networks you use, and add the Indy registrar and resolvers to DidsModule: agent.ts import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises' import { DidsModule, JwkDidRegistrar, JwkDidResolver, KeyDidRegistrar, KeyDidResolver, PeerDidRegistrar, PeerDidResolver, WebDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { IndyVdrIndyDidRegistrar, IndyVdrIndyDidResolver, IndyVdrModule, IndyVdrSovDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/indy-vdr' import { indyVdr } from '@hyperledger/indy-vdr-nodejs' const indyVdrModules = { indyVdr: new IndyVdrModule({ indyVdr, networks: [ { indyNamespace: 'bcovrin:test', isProduction: false, genesisTransactions: await readFile('genesis/bcovrin-test.txn', 'utf8'), connectOnStartup: true, }, ], }), dids: new DidsModule({ registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new PeerDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar(), new IndyVdrIndyDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [ new KeyDidResolver(), new PeerDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver(), new IndyVdrIndyDidResolver(), new IndyVdrSovDidResolver(), ], }), } On React Native, import indyVdr from the React Native package instead, and bundle the genesis transactions with your app: import { indyVdr } from '@hyperledger/indy-vdr-react-native' Pass the indyVdr object itself: unlike Askar and AnonCreds, Indy VDR has no Native* class. Each network takes: Option Description indyNamespace Namespace of the network in did:indy identifiers, such as bcovrin:test in did:indy:bcovrin:test:.... genesisTransactions Contents of the network's genesis file, as a string. isProduction Whether this is a production network. connectOnStartup Connect when the agent starts instead of on first use. Defaults to false. transactionAuthorAgreement { version, acceptanceMechanism }, required to write to networks with a transaction author agreement. acceptanceMechanism is a label from the network's acceptance mechanism list. IndyVdrModule doesn't register the DID registrar and resolvers itself, so list them in DidsModule. Your lists replace the default registrars and resolvers, see Configure DID methods.

With the resolvers registered, agent.dids.resolve handles both methods. For did:indy, Credo uses the network whose indyNamespace matches the DID. A did:sov or unqualified Indy identifier doesn't say which network it's on, so Credo queries all networks and prefers a production network when the DID exists on more than one.

Writing to an Indy network needs a DID that the network allows to write, usually with the ENDORSER role. To use a DID that was registered from a seed, import its key and the DID: endorser.ts // The seed the DID was registered with on the ledger. Keep it secret. const endorserSeed = process.env.ENDORSER_SEED if (!endorserSeed) throw new Error('ENDORSER_SEED is not set') const { privateJwk } = transformPrivateKeyToPrivateJwk({ type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' }, privateKey: TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String(endorserSeed), }) const { keyId, publicJwk } = await endorser.kms.importKey({ privateJwk }) // A DID registered from a seed is the base58 encoding of the first 16 bytes of the public key const publicKey = PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(publicJwk).publicKey.publicKey const endorserDid = `did:indy:bcovrin:test:${TypedArrayEncoder.toBase58(publicKey.slice(0, 16))}` await endorser.dids.import({ did: endorserDid, // did:indy documents reference the main key as #verkey keys: [{ didDocumentRelativeKeyId: '#verkey', kmsKeyId: keyId }], }) transformPrivateKeyToPrivateJwk comes from @credo-ts/askar. Without a didDocument, import resolves the DID from the network.

With an endorser DID in the agent's wallet, register a new DID and let the same agent endorse it: endorser.ts const { didState } = await endorser.dids.create<IndyVdrDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'indy', options: { endorserDid, endorserMode: 'internal', }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Registering the did failed') The new DID gets an Ed25519 key, or the key you pass as keyId. Other options are alias, role (STEWARD, TRUSTEE, ENDORSER or NETWORK_MONITOR) and services. Services are written to the DID document on the ledger, or as a legacy endpoint attribute with useEndpointAttrib: true. Updating and deactivating did:indy DIDs isn't supported.

When the endorser is a different agent, the author prepares the transaction, the endorser signs it, and the author submits it: author.ts // Author: prepare the transaction. The returned state asks for an endorsement. const authorResult = (await author.dids.create<IndyVdrDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'indy', options: { endorserDid, endorserMode: 'external' }, })) as IndyVdrDidCreateResult const authorState = authorResult.didState if (authorState.state !== 'action' || authorState.action !== 'endorseIndyTransaction') { throw new Error('Expected an endorsement request') } // Endorser: sign the transaction it received from the author const endorsedNymRequest = await endorser.modules.indyVdr.endorseTransaction( authorState.nymRequest, authorState.endorserDid ) // Author: submit the endorsed transaction const submitResult = await author.dids.create<IndyVdrDidCreateOptions>({ did: authorState.did, options: { endorserMode: 'external', endorsedTransaction: { nymRequest: endorsedNymRequest } }, }) With endorserMode: 'external', the registrar returns the state action with action: 'endorseIndyTransaction'. Cast the result to IndyVdrDidCreateResult to read nymRequest and, when you pass services with useEndpointAttrib, attribRequest. Send these to the endorser, who signs each one with agent.modules.indyVdr.endorseTransaction. The author then calls create again with the DID and the endorsed transactions.

IndyVdrAnonCredsRegistry registers and resolves AnonCreds schemas, credential definitions and revocation data on Indy. It's exported from the @credo-ts/indy-vdr root. Set up AnonCreds as described in AnonCreds, with the Indy registry: agent.ts import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds' import { IndyVdrAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/indy-vdr' import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs' const anoncreds = new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new IndyVdrAnonCredsRegistry()], }) The registry needs IndyVdrModule. To register objects, the issuer needs a did:indy with write permission, and passes endorserMode and endorserDid in the registration options.

A valid signature shows that a credential is intact and who signed it. Whether you accept that signer is a separate decision: when Credo verifies a credential or a signed request, it looks up the issuers you trust for that verification and checks the signer against them.

Credo checks these sources in order, and the first one that returns trusted issuers decides: Trusted issuers or certificates passed to the verify call, such as trustedIssuers on agent.sdJwtVc.verify. The agent's getTrustedIssuersForVerification callback. The X.509 module's getTrustedCertificatesForVerification callback (deprecated, X.509 only). The X.509 module's trustedCertificates (X.509 only). What happens when no source returns trusted issuers depends on how the object is signed: Signer No trusted issuers found (default) Trusted issuers found X.509 certificate chain Verification fails. The chain must lead to one of the trusted certificates. DID Any DID is accepted. The DID (without fragment) must be in the list. So an agent without trust configuration accepts credentials signed with any DID, and rejects all X.509-signed credentials. Return an empty list ({ trustedIssuers: [] }) to reject every signer, including DIDs. OpenID4VC objects signed with a bare jwk header, without a DID or certificate, aren't checked against trusted issuers. This applies to SD-JWT VCs, mdocs, W3C credentials signed as JWT, SD-JWT or with JSON-LD proofs, and to the signed objects in OpenID4VC. AnonCreds and Data Integrity credentials don't use it.

In production, set getTrustedIssuersForVerification and return a list for every signer type you accept: the root certificates for X.509 signers, for example from a trust list, and the DIDs you accept for DID signers. For signer types you don't accept, return { trustedIssuers: [] }. Returning undefined for a DID signer accepts any DID. The X.509 module's trustedCertificates are enough when the agent trusts one fixed set of root certificates for everything, for example in tests. Pass trustedIssuers to a verify call for a one-off check.

Set the callback in the agent config. Credo calls it for each verification with the signer and the verification context: agent.ts const trustedRootCertificates = [rootCertificatePem] const trustedIssuerDids = ['did:web:issuer.example.com'] const agent = new Agent({ config: { getTrustedIssuersForVerification: async (_agentContext, { signer, verification }) => { // Fall through to the X.509 module configuration for anything other than credentials if (verification.type !== 'credential') return undefined if (signer.method === 'x509') { return { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: trustedRootCertificates }] } } return { trustedIssuers: trustedIssuerDids.map((did) => ({ method: 'did', issuance: did })) } }, }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup }, }) signer is either { method: 'x509', certificateChain } with the parsed certificates, leaf first, or { method: 'did', didUrl }. Return one of: { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: [...] }] }: the PEM or base64 DER certificates that X.509 chains must lead to. { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: 'did:...' }, ...] }: the DIDs you trust. { trustedIssuers: [] } to reject the signer. undefined to fall through to the X.509 module configuration, or, for a DID signer, to accept it. All returned entries must use the same method as the signer, otherwise verification throws. verification.type tells you what Credo is verifying: Type When Package credential Verifying a credential, including credentials the holder receives over OpenID4VCI. @credo-ts/core mdocReaderAuth The holder checks the reader certificate of an mdoc request over the Digital Credentials API. @credo-ts/core openId4VpCredential A verifier checks a credential in an OpenID4VP response. Includes the openId4VcVerificationSessionRecord. @credo-ts/openid4vc oauth2SecuredAuthorizationRequest The holder checks a signed OpenID4VP authorization request. @credo-ts/openid4vc openId4VciCredentialIssuerMetadata The holder checks signed credential issuer metadata. @credo-ts/openid4vc openId4VciKeyAttestation An issuer checks a key attestation. @credo-ts/openid4vc oauth2ClientAttestation An issuer checks a wallet (client) attestation. @credo-ts/openid4vc To get the OpenID4VC verification types, type the callback as GetTrustedIssuersForVerification<VerificationSigner, OpenId4VcVerificationTypes>, as in the examples below. A separate callback typed as plain GetTrustedIssuersForVerification can't be assigned to the agent config in strict mode, so in agents without OpenID4VC define it inline as above. When the signer isn't trusted, isValid is false and error says why: verify.ts const result = await agent.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: x509SignedCredential.compact }) if (!result.isValid) { console.error('Credential not trusted or invalid', result.error) } To change the callback at runtime, for example after loading a trust list, call agent.config.setTrustedIssuersForVerification: agent.ts // Reject everything until the trust list is loaded agent.config.setTrustedIssuersForVerification(async () => ({ trustedIssuers: [] }))

Trusted issuers passed to a verify call take precedence, and Credo doesn't call the callback for that verification: verify.ts // Trusted issuers passed to the call replace the callback for this verification const perCallResult = await agent.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: x509SignedCredential.compact, trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: [otherRoot.certificate.toString('pem')] }], }) Other calls take trusted certificates directly: agent.mdoc.verify(mdoc, { trustedCertificates }), and the holder's agent.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest(request, { trustedCertificates }). The trustedCertificates option of agent.sdJwtVc.verify is deprecated in favour of trustedIssuers. MdocDeviceResponse.verify only uses the trustedCertificates you pass, see mdoc.

Use the openId4VpCredential type to give each verifier its own trust list. The examples read trust lists from JSON files: trust.ts import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises' import type { GetTrustedIssuersForVerification, VerificationSigner } from '@credo-ts/core' import type { OpenId4VcVerificationTypes } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' // A JSON array of PEM encoded certificates, for example exported from a trust list async function loadTrustList(name: string): Promise<string[]> { return JSON.parse(await readFile(`trust-lists/${name}.json`, 'utf8')) } Verifier verifier-trust.ts const trustedRootsByVerifier: Record<string, string[]> = { 'pid-verifier': await loadTrustList('pid-providers'), 'diploma-verifier': await loadTrustList('universities'), } export const getVerifierTrustedIssuers: GetTrustedIssuersForVerification< VerificationSigner, OpenId4VcVerificationTypes > = async (_agentContext, { signer, verification }) => { if (verification.type !== 'openId4VpCredential') return undefined // Each verifier only accepts credentials from its own trust list const { verifierId } = verification.openId4VcVerificationSessionRecord const trustedRoots = trustedRootsByVerifier[verifierId] ?? [] if (signer.method === 'x509') { return { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: trustedRoots }] } } // This verifier doesn't accept did-signed credentials return { trustedIssuers: [] } } A credential from an issuer outside the verifier's list fails verification, and the verification session ends in the Error state. See Verifying credentials for the flow.

The holder verifies the credentials it receives, and the authorization requests that verifiers sign with a certificate: Holder wallet-trust.ts const trustedIssuerRoots = await loadTrustList('issuers') const trustedVerifierRoots = await loadTrustList('relying-parties') export const getHolderTrustedIssuers: GetTrustedIssuersForVerification< VerificationSigner, OpenId4VcVerificationTypes > = async (_agentContext, { signer, verification }) => { // Did-signed objects are accepted, as no list is returned for them if (signer.method !== 'x509') return undefined switch (verification.type) { // Credentials received over OpenID4VCI case 'credential': return { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: trustedIssuerRoots }] } // Signed OpenID4VP authorization requests case 'oauth2SecuredAuthorizationRequest': return { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: trustedVerifierRoots }] } default: return undefined } } Without trusted certificates, receiving an X.509-signed SD-JWT VC or mdoc over OpenID4VCI fails, and so does resolving an authorization request signed with x509_san_dns or x509_hash. See Receiving credentials and Presenting credentials.

An OpenID4VCI issuer that requires wallet or key attestations uses the oauth2ClientAttestation and openId4VciKeyAttestation types to trust the wallet providers that sign them. See Wallet and key attestations.

If the agent trusts the same root certificates for every X.509 signer, list them on the X.509 module: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem] }) Credo only uses them for X.509 signers, and only when no earlier source returns trusted issuers, for example when the callback returns undefined. See X.509 certificates. The X.509 module's getTrustedCertificatesForVerification(agentContext, { certificateChain, verification }) callback is deprecated. It works like getTrustedIssuersForVerification for X.509 signers only, returning certificates instead of trusted issuers. Move its logic to getTrustedIssuersForVerification.
documents.s: Trusted certificates in the X.509 module

documents.t: An X.509 trusted issuer can also list the certificates that may sign status lists for its credentials, in status: { method: 'x509', issuance: [issuerRootPem], status: [statusListSignerPem] } Without status, the status list must be signed with the same certificate chain as the credential. See Status lists.

did:webvh is hosted on your own web server, like did:web, but every version of the DID document is recorded in a signed log. Resolvers verify the whole log, so they can check the history of the DID and who changed it. @credo-ts/webvh creates and updates did:webvh DIDs and their log, resolves them, and provides an AnonCreds registry. You host the log yourself. Use did:webvh instead of did:web when verifiers should be able to check how your DID document changed over time, or when you want to publish AnonCreds objects without a ledger.
npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/webvh@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/webvh@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/webvh@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/webvh@^0.7.2

Register WebVhModule and add the did:webvh registrar and resolver to DidsModule: agent.ts import { Agent, DidDocumentService, DidsModule, JwkDidRegistrar, JwkDidResolver, KeyDidRegistrar, KeyDidResolver, PeerDidRegistrar, PeerDidResolver, WebDidResolver, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { type WebVhDidCreateOptions, type WebVhDidLog, WebVhDidRecordMetadataKeys, WebVhDidRegistrar, WebVhDidResolver, type WebVhDidUpdateOptions, WebVhModule, } from '@credo-ts/webvh' import express from 'express' const webVhModules = { webvh: new WebVhModule(), dids: new DidsModule({ registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new PeerDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar(), new WebVhDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [ new KeyDidResolver(), new PeerDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver(), new WebVhDidResolver(), ], }), } Spread these modules into the modules of your agent. WebVhModule has no options, and doesn't register the registrar and resolver with DidsModule. Your lists replace the default registrars and resolvers, see Configure DID methods.

issuer.ts const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<WebVhDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'webvh', domain: 'issuer.example.com', }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Creating the did failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`) } const did = didState.did domain, and the optional path, go at the top level of the options. Credo creates an Ed25519 key that signs the log, and adds it to the DID document as a Multikey verification method for authentication and assertionMethod. The result is a DID such as did:webvh:<scid>:issuer.example.com, where the self-certifying identifier (SCID) is derived from the first log entry. With path: 'issuers/acme', the DID ends in issuer.example.com:issuers:acme. Credo stores the DID and its log in a DidRecord, and publishes nothing. An agent can have one did:webvh per domain and path.

Serve the log as JSON Lines, one entry per line, at: https://<domain>/.well-known/did.jsonl for a DID without a path. https://<domain>/<path>/did.jsonl for a DID with a path. The log is in the metadata of the DidRecord. This Express route reads it on every request, so it always serves the latest version: server.ts const app = express() app.get('/.well-known/did.jsonl', async (_request, response) => { const [didRecord] = await agent.dids.getCreatedDids({ did }) const log: WebVhDidLog | null = didRecord?.metadata.get(WebVhDidRecordMetadataKeys.DidLog) if (!log) { response.sendStatus(404) return } // One log entry per line response.type('text/jsonl').send(log.map((entry: unknown) => JSON.stringify(entry)).join('\n')) }) Resolvers fetch the log over HTTPS, verify every entry, and return the latest DID document. For a DID that your agent created, agent.dids.resolve returns the document from the DidRecord.

Resolve the document, change it, and pass the full new document to update: issuer.ts const didDocument = await agent.dids.resolveDidDocument(did) didDocument.service = [ new DidDocumentService({ id: `${did}#website`, type: 'LinkedDomains', serviceEndpoint: 'https://issuer.example.com', }), ] const updateResult = await agent.dids.update<WebVhDidUpdateOptions>({ did, didDocument }) if (updateResult.didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Updating the did failed') Credo signs a new log entry with the update key and stores the new log. If you leave out assertionMethod, Credo keeps the one from the previous version. Deactivating a did:webvh isn't supported.

A did:webvh can link resources, such as AnonCreds objects, at <did>/resources/<resourceId>. Resolve one with the API of the module, under the key you registered it with: const result = await agent.modules.webvh.resolveResource(`${did}/resources/${resourceId}`) Credo fetches the resource from https://<domain>/resources/<resourceId> (or under the path of the DID). The result has content, or error and message when the resource can't be resolved.

WebVhAnonCredsRegistry registers and resolves AnonCreds objects as resources of a did:webvh. Import it from the @credo-ts/webvh/anoncreds subpath. Set up AnonCreds as described in AnonCreds, with the did:webvh registry: agent.ts import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds' import { WebVhAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/webvh/anoncreds' import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs' const anoncreds = new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new WebVhAnonCredsRegistry()], }) Registering a schema, credential definition, revocation registry definition or status list publishes nothing. The result has the object id, <did>/resources/<resourceId>, and in registrationMetadata.attestedResource a resource signed with the DID's assertionMethod key. Store it, and serve it as JSON at https://<domain>/resources/<resourceId>, so others can resolve the object.

mdoc issuers, SD-JWT VC issuers and OpenID4VP verifiers often sign with a key that's bound to an X.509 certificate instead of a DID. agent.x509 creates certificates and certificate signing requests (CSRs), validates certificate chains and creates certificate revocation lists (CRLs). How a verifier decides which certificates to trust is on Trusted issuers. In the examples, one agent plays the certificate authority (CA) and a second agent is a verifier. They use these imports: ca.ts import { Agent, CredoWebCrypto, X509Certificate, X509CertificateRevocationListEntryReason, X509ExtendedKeyUsage, X509KeyUsage, X509Module, X509RevocationCheckMode, X509ValidationError, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { PublicJwk } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

A CA signs the certificates of issuers or verifiers, and whoever checks those certificates trusts the root certificate of the CA. For mdoc issuers, this root is the issuing authority CA (IACA). Create a key in the KMS and a self-signed certificate for it: ca.ts const rootKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const rootPublicJwk = PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(rootKey.publicJwk) // Without a subjectPublicKey the certificate is self-signed const rootCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: rootPublicJwk, issuer: { commonName: 'Example Root CA', countryName: 'NL' }, validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + 5 * oneYear) }, extensions: { subjectKeyIdentifier: { include: true }, keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.KeyCertSign, X509KeyUsage.CrlSign], markAsCritical: true }, basicConstraints: { ca: true, pathLenConstraint: 0, markAsCritical: true }, }, }) const rootCertificatePem = rootCertificate.toString('pem') Without subjectPublicKey, the authorityKey signs its own certificate and issuer is also the subject. Passing subject for a self-signed certificate throws. pathLenConstraint: 0 lets this CA sign end-entity certificates, but no intermediate CAs. issuer and subject take commonName, countryName, stateOrProvinceName and organizationalUnit. For other name attributes, pass a distinguished name string such as 'CN=Example Root CA, O=Example, C=NL'.

Sign a certificate for another key with the CA key. This one is an issuer certificate: ca.ts const issuerKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const issuerCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: rootPublicJwk, subjectPublicKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk), issuer: rootCertificate.subject, subject: { commonName: 'Example Issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + oneYear) }, extensions: { authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true }, subjectKeyIdentifier: { include: true }, keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature], markAsCritical: true }, // Document signer usage, required for mdoc issuer certificates extendedKeyUsage: { usages: [X509ExtendedKeyUsage.MdlDs], markAsCritical: true }, // An SD-JWT VC `iss` must match a SAN URI, or its host a SAN DNS name subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'issuer.example.com' }] }, }, }) // The certificate keeps the KMS key id of the subject key, so Credo can sign with it console.log(issuerCertificate.keyId === issuerKey.keyId) Credo signs with authorityKey, so it must be a key in the agent's KMS. The certificate gets the key id of subjectPublicKey, which lets the agent that holds that key sign with the certificate. The extensions and subject alternative names (SANs) depend on what the certificate is for: Certificate What it needs CA, or mdoc IACA basicConstraints with ca: true, and a key usage with KeyCertSign, plus CrlSign if the CA signs CRLs. Credo rejects a CA certificate without basicConstraints, or with a key usage that lacks these. mdoc issuer (document signer) A country (countryName) in the subject, DigitalSignature key usage, and the MdlDs extended key usage. Credo checks the country but not the extended key usage, which ISO 18013-5 requires. See mdoc. SD-JWT VC issuer When the credential has an iss, a SAN URI equal to it, or a SAN DNS name equal to its host. Without iss, no SAN is needed. See SD-JWT VC. OpenID4VP verifier (access certificate) With the x509_san_dns client id prefix (the default), the host of the verifier's baseUrl as a SAN DNS name. With x509_hash, no SAN is needed. See Verifying credentials. mdoc reader (DC API reader authentication) No specific extensions: the wallet checks that the chain leads to a reader certificate it trusts. See Digital Credentials API.

X509Module is registered by default under the key x509. Register it yourself to pass options: verifier.ts const verifierAgent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup x509: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem], revocationCheck: { mode: X509RevocationCheckMode.SoftFail }, }), }, }) Option Description trustedCertificates PEM or base64 DER strings, or X509Certificate instances. Credo uses them as trust anchors when nothing else decides trust, see Trusted issuers. getTrustedCertificatesForVerification Deprecated. Use the agent's getTrustedIssuersForVerification callback instead. revocationCheck Enables CRL checking during chain validation. See Revocation. To change the trusted certificates at runtime, use agent.x509.config.addTrustedCertificate(certificate) or agent.x509.config.setTrustedCertificates(certificates).

When the key holder and the CA are different parties, the key holder sends a CSR. Here the verifier requests an access certificate: ca.ts // Verifier: create a key and a certificate signing request (CSR) for it const verifierKey = await verifierAgent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const csr = await verifierAgent.x509.createCertificateSigningRequest({ subjectPublicKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(verifierKey.publicJwk), subject: { commonName: 'Example Verifier', countryName: 'NL' }, extensions: { // With the x509_san_dns client id prefix, the verifier's host must be a SAN DNS name subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'verifier.example.com' }] }, }, }) const encodedCsr = csr.toString('pem') // CA: parse the CSR and check its signature, which proves possession of the key const receivedCsr = agent.x509.parseCertificateSigningRequest({ encodedCertificateSigningRequest: encodedCsr }) await receivedCsr.verify(new CredoWebCrypto(agent.context)) const accessCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: rootPublicJwk, subjectPublicKey: receivedCsr.publicJwk, issuer: rootCertificate.subject, subject: receivedCsr.subject, validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + oneYear) }, extensions: { authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true }, keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature], markAsCritical: true }, subjectAlternativeName: { name: receivedCsr.sanDnsNames.map((value) => ({ type: 'dns', value })) }, }, }) const accessCertificatePem = accessCertificate.toString('pem') parseCertificateSigningRequest doesn't check the CSR signature. Call verify to make sure the requester holds the private key. The CA decides which extensions go into the certificate: copy only the values from the CSR that you've checked.

X509Certificate.fromEncodedCertificate parses a PEM or base64 DER certificate. A parsed certificate has no key id, so set keyId to the KMS key id before you sign with it: verifier.ts // Verifier: parse the certificate returned by the CA and link it to the KMS key const verifierCertificate = X509Certificate.fromEncodedCertificate(accessCertificatePem) verifierCertificate.keyId = verifierKey.keyId console.log(verifierCertificate.subject, verifierCertificate.sanDnsNames) Getters include subject, issuer, sanDnsNames, sanUriNames, keyUsage, extendedKeyUsage, isCertificateAuthority, crlDistributionPoints and publicJwk. Encode a certificate with toString('pem') or toString('base64'), and compare two with equal.

verifier.ts const validatedChain = await verifierAgent.x509.validateCertificateChain({ // Leaf first, as in an x5c header. The root may be left out when it is a trusted certificate. certificateChain: [issuerCertificate.toString('base64')], trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem], }) // The chain starts at the trust anchor and ends with the leaf console.log( validatedChain[0].equal(rootCertificate), validatedChain[validatedChain.length - 1].equal(issuerCertificate) ) Pass the chain leaf first, as in an x5c header. The chain may leave out the root if it's in trustedCertificates. On success Credo returns the chain from the trust anchor to the leaf. On failure it throws an X509ValidationError, whose validationResult.validations shows which check failed. Credo checks the signatures and validity periods, basic constraints, the keyCertSign key usage of CA certificates, path length constraints, critical extensions, and revocation when enabled. It doesn't check OCSP, name constraints or certificate policies, and it doesn't enforce extended key usage. caution Without trustedCertificates, Credo validates the chain but doesn't check that it ends at a certificate you trust. The module's trustedCertificates aren't used here. allowNonRootTrustedCertificate defaults to true: a trusted intermediate or leaf certificate acts as the trust anchor, and Credo doesn't verify its signature. ISO 18013-5 needs this, because mdoc issuers don't include the root in the chain. Set it to false to require that trusted certificates are verified up to a self-signed root. The default may change in a future version.

Credo checks revocation with CRLs, from the URLs in a certificate's crlDistributionPoints. Revocation checking is off unless you set revocationCheck on the module: Mode Behaviour X509RevocationCheckMode.SoftFail Default when revocationCheck is set. Rejects revoked certificates and invalid CRLs, and skips the check when the CRL can't be downloaded. X509RevocationCheckMode.Require Also fails when the CRL can't be downloaded. X509RevocationCheckMode.Disabled No revocation checks. Certificates without a CRL distribution point pass the check. Credo checks every certificate in the chain except the root (checkFullChain), and caches a CRL for an hour (crlCacheExpirySeconds), but never past its nextUpdate. Large CRLs Credo 0.7 parses CRLs with the default node limit of the ASN.1 parser (asn1js), which rejects CRLs with more than about 2,000 entries. Validation of a certificate whose CRL is that large fails, also in SoftFail mode. To revoke certificates, create a CRL signed by the CA key and publish it at the distribution point URL: ca.ts const revokedKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) const revokedCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: rootPublicJwk, subjectPublicKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(revokedKey.publicJwk), issuer: rootCertificate.subject, subject: { commonName: 'Revoked Issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + oneYear) }, extensions: { authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true }, keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature], markAsCritical: true }, crlDistributionPoints: { urls: [crlUrl] }, }, }) const crl = await agent.x509.createCertificateRevocationList({ authorityKey: rootPublicJwk, issuer: rootCertificate.subject, validity: { nextUpdate: new Date(Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) }, entries: [{ certificate: revokedCertificate, reason: X509CertificateRevocationListEntryReason.KeyCompromise }], extensions: { crlNumber: { value: 1 }, authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true } }, }) // Serve the DER encoded CRL at the URL in the certificate's crlDistributionPoints const crlBytes = crl.rawCertificateRevocationList Validating the revoked certificate now fails on the revocation check: verifier.ts try { await verifierAgent.x509.validateCertificateChain({ certificateChain: [revokedCertificate.toString('base64')], trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem], }) } catch (error) { if (!(error instanceof X509ValidationError)) throw error // The validations show which check failed, here revocationStatus console.log('Rejected:', error.message, error.validationResult.validations.revocationStatus?.isValid) }
Credo is a project of the OpenWallet Foundation. This page lists the repositories that make up Credo, the libraries it builds on, and projects built with it.

credo-ts: the framework, published as the @credo-ts/* packages. credo-ts-docs: this documentation. credo-ts-ext: extension packages, such as a REST API, React hooks and push notifications. They haven't been updated for recent Credo versions. See Extensions.

Credo doesn't implement every standard itself. It uses these libraries: Library Packages Used for Identity Common TS @openid4vc/* OpenID4VCI, OpenID4VP and OAuth 2.0 @sd-jwt/* SD-JWT and SD-JWT VC @owf/mdoc, @owf/cose mdoc (ISO 18013-5) @owf/token-status-list Token Status Lists dcql Digital Credentials Query Language (DCQL) queries Askar @openwallet-foundation/askar-* (wrapper) Encrypted storage and key management AnonCreds @hyperledger/anoncreds-* (wrapper) AnonCreds credentials Indy VDR @hyperledger/indy-vdr-* Reading from and writing to Indy ledgers Askar, AnonCreds and Indy VDR are written in Rust. Their JavaScript wrappers have separate packages for Node.js and React Native.

Paradym: Animo's platform for issuing and verifying credentials, built on Credo. Paradym Wallet: an open source React Native wallet that uses Credo, made as a companion to Paradym. Bifold: an open source React Native wallet that uses Credo, which you can adapt to build your own wallet. DIDComm Mediator Credo: a DIDComm mediator built on Credo, with a Docker image you can deploy.
Ask questions in the Credo channel on Discord. Join the Credo working group calls. Read the contributing guide before you open a pull request.

The credo-ts-ext repository hosts packages built on top of Credo that aren't part of the framework itself. warning All extension packages require Credo 0.5 (@credo-ts/core@^0.5) and don't work with the Credo version these docs describe. The pages in this section describe their 0.5 APIs. Package Latest release Description @credo-ts/rest 0.10.0 A REST API and CLI around a Credo agent @credo-ts/react-hooks 0.6.1 React hooks for the records of a Credo agent @credo-ts/redux-store 0.5.1 A Redux Toolkit store for the state of a Credo agent @credo-ts/push-notifications 0.7.1 DIDComm protocols to share an APNs or Firebase push notification token @credo-ts/transport-ble 0.3.0 DIDComm over Bluetooth Low Energy for React Native

warning @credo-ts/push-notifications 0.7.1, the latest release, requires Credo 0.5 (@credo-ts/core@^0.5.0) and hasn't been updated for later versions of Credo. @credo-ts/push-notifications lets a mobile agent send its push notification token to another agent, usually its mediator, over a DIDComm connection. The other agent can then wake the app with a push notification when a message arrives. It implements Aries RFC 0699 for Apple Push Notification service (APNs) and Aries RFC 0734 for Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM).
npm install @credo-ts/push-notifications@0.7.1

Register the module for each service you use: import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { PushNotificationsApnsModule, PushNotificationsFcmModule } from '@credo-ts/push-notifications' const agent = new Agent({ // ...config and dependencies modules: { pushNotificationsApns: new PushNotificationsApnsModule(), pushNotificationsFcm: new PushNotificationsFcmModule(), }, }) await agent.initialize() Then send the token that you got from the operating system over a connection: // iOS await agent.modules.pushNotificationsApns.setDeviceInfo(connectionId, { deviceToken }) // Android, or iOS through Firebase await agent.modules.pushNotificationsFcm.setDeviceInfo(connectionId, { deviceToken, devicePlatform: 'android' }) getDeviceInfo(connectionId) asks the other agent for the device info it has stored for the connection.

warning @credo-ts/react-hooks 0.6.1, the latest release, requires Credo 0.5 (@credo-ts/core@^0.5.0) and hasn't been updated for later versions of Credo. @credo-ts/react-hooks exposes the DIDComm records of a Credo agent, such as connections, credential exchanges and proof exchanges, as React hooks that update when the records change.
npm install @credo-ts/react-hooks@0.6.1 @credo-ts/question-answer@^0.5 @credo-ts/question-answer is a peer dependency.

Wrap your app in AgentProvider and pass it an initialized agent: import type { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import AgentProvider from '@credo-ts/react-hooks' export function App({ agent }: { agent: Agent }) { return <AgentProvider agent={agent}>{/* your app */}</AgentProvider> } Inside the provider, useAgent() returns { agent, loading }, and the record hooks return the records and a loading flag: import { useConnections } from '@credo-ts/react-hooks' function ConnectionList() { const { records: connections, loading } = useConnections() return <FlatList data={connections} renderItem={({ item }) => <ConnectionItem connection={item} />} /> } useConnections, useCredentials, useProofs and useBasicMessages each have variants that select records, such as useConnectionById(id), useCredentialByState(state) and useProofsByConnectionId(connectionId). See the package source for the full list.

warning @credo-ts/redux-store 0.5.1, the latest release, requires Credo 0.5 (@credo-ts/core@^0.5.0) and hasn't been updated for later versions of Credo. @credo-ts/redux-store keeps the DIDComm state of a Credo agent in a Redux Toolkit store, so the UI of a React or React Native app stays in sync with the agent. It has slices, thunks and selectors for connections, credentials, proofs and mediation. initializeStore(agent) creates the store, and startRecordListeners keeps it in sync with the agent's records.
npm install @credo-ts/redux-store@0.5.1

warning @credo-ts/rest 0.10.0, the latest release, runs Credo 0.5 (@credo-ts/core@^0.5.1) and hasn't been updated for later versions of Credo. @credo-ts/rest runs a Credo agent behind HTTP endpoints, so you can create connections, issue credentials and request proofs from any language. It includes a CLI to start the server, a WebSocket or webhook feed of agent events, and optional multi-tenancy.

npx -p @credo-ts/rest@0.10.0 credo-rest start \ --label "Credo Rest" \ --wallet-id "walletId" \ --wallet-key "walletKey" \ --endpoint http://localhost:5000 \ --admin-port 3000 \ --outbound-transport http \ --inbound-transport http 5000 The admin API listens on --admin-port, and DIDComm messages arrive on the inbound transport. The OpenAPI documentation is served with Swagger UI at /docs on the admin port, for example http://localhost:3000/docs. Run npx -p @credo-ts/rest@0.10.0 credo-rest start --help to list all options, such as PostgreSQL storage, ledgers, auto-accept settings and webhooks.

Credo is a TypeScript framework for issuing, holding and verifying verifiable credentials. It supports OpenID4VC and DIDComm, and formats such as SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C Verifiable Credentials and AnonCreds. This section takes you from an empty project to a running agent.

Node.js 20.19 or later (Credo is tested on Node.js 22 and 24), or React Native. These pages use Expo for React Native. A TypeScript project that uses ES modules. Credo is published as ES modules only. Browsers aren't supported, and Bun and Deno aren't tested. See Platforms.

Four choices come up before you write any code. If you're not sure, start with the default. You can add a protocol or format later, and an agent can use several at once. Choice Default Pick the other option when Details Platform Node.js, for issuers, verifiers, mediators and cloud wallets You build a mobile wallet: use React Native with Expo Platforms Protocol OpenID4VC Use DIDComm if you need a lasting connection with messaging between agents, or AnonCreds, or your ecosystem is built on Aries. A wallet can support both Protocols Credential format SD-JWT VC Your ecosystem asks for another one: mdoc for mobile driving licences, W3C VCs for Open Badges or EBSI, AnonCreds (DIDComm only) for predicates and unlinkable presentations. The EUDI Wallet uses SD-JWT VC and mdoc Credential formats Storage On a server, Drizzle on PostgreSQL for the records, as SQL tables that scale to many tenants and instances, and Askar for the keys. In a mobile wallet, Askar for both Use SQLite instead of PostgreSQL for a single server instance or local development. A mobile wallet can also use Drizzle on expo-sqlite Storage The getting started pages use Drizzle on SQLite with Askar for the keys on Node.js, and Askar on React Native. They work for any protocol and format.

1. Installation Set up a Node.js or Expo project and install Credo and its storage. 2. Your first agent Create an agent, initialize it, create a DID and shut it down. 3. Example setups Complete configurations for wallets, issuers, verifiers, mediators and tests.
Set up a Node.js or Expo project and install Credo and its storage.
Create an agent, initialize it, create a DID and shut it down.
Complete configurations for wallets, issuers, verifiers, mediators and tests.

Once your agent runs, pick the guide for what you're building: Issue credentials Run an OpenID4VCI issuer that wallets receive credentials from. Verify credentials Request and verify presentations with OpenID4VP. Build a wallet Receive, store and present credentials in a mobile or server wallet. Use DIDComm Connect to other agents and exchange messages and credentials over DIDComm. If you're new to verifiable credentials, start with Concepts. If you use an AI coding assistant, see AI coding agents.
Run an OpenID4VCI issuer that wallets receive credentials from.
Request and verify presentations with OpenID4VP.
Receive, store and present credentials in a mobile or server wallet.
Connect to other agents and exchange messages and credentials over DIDComm.
AI coding agents often know an older Credo version from their training data. They write better Credo code when they read these docs, so the docs are also published as Markdown.

URL Contents https://credo.js.org/llms.txt Index of the Credo 0.7 docs, with a link to the Markdown version of each page https://credo.js.org/llms-full.txt All Credo 0.7 docs in one file https://credo.js.org/guides/next/llms.txt Index of the Credo 0.8 docs (unreleased) https://credo.js.org/guides/next/llms-full.txt All Credo 0.8 docs in one file Every page is also available as Markdown: add .md to its URL, for example https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/installation.md. Code examples in the Markdown are the same type-checked snippets as on the site. The Copy page button at the top of each page copies its Markdown. Its menu opens the page in Claude or ChatGPT.

Add a line like this to the AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md of your project: This project uses Credo 0.7 (`@credo-ts/*` packages). Before writing or changing Credo code, read https://credo.js.org/llms.txt and the Markdown pages it links to.
documents.s: Point your agent at the docs

documents.t: Each recipe on this page is a complete, type-checked agent configuration for a common deployment. Start from the one closest to what you build. The linked pages explain the options.

Start here if you build a wallet app for phones. This React Native app receives and presents credentials with OpenID4VC, and connects to other agents over DIDComm through a mediator. Askar stores the data and keys, and keys that must stay in the device's secure hardware use the secure environment backend. Install the packages from Installation, and: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 yarn add \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 bun add \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5 agent.ts import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy, DidCommModule, DidCommWsOutboundTransport, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { agentDependencies, SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' interface WalletAgentOptions { // A raw key from Store.generateRawKey(), kept in the device keychain walletKey: string // Invitation URL of the mediator that receives DIDComm messages for this wallet mediatorInvitationUrl: string } export function createWalletAgent({ walletKey, mediatorInvitationUrl }: WalletAgentOptions) { return new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Warn), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw' }, // The Askar backend is registered in the kms module below, so it can be the default enableKms: false, }), kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [new AskarKeyManagementService(), new SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService()], defaultBackend: 'askar', }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), didcomm: new DidCommModule({ // No inbound transports: messages for the wallet go through the mediator transports: { outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, mediationRecipient: { mediatorInvitationUrl, mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode, }, mediator: false, }), }, }) } export type WalletAgent = ReturnType<typeof createWalletAgent> Askar is the default key management backend. A key goes to the secure environment only when you create it with backend: 'secureEnvironment', which supports P-256 keys and ES256 signatures. walletKey is a raw key that you generate once and keep in the device keychain, see Askar. If the wallet only uses OpenID4VC, leave out the didcomm module and package. Mediation explains the pickup strategies.

Start here if your organization issues or verifies credentials from its own backend. This Node.js service issues credentials with OpenID4VCI and verifies presentations with OpenID4VP. It stores its records in PostgreSQL with Drizzle, its keys in Askar and its cache in Redis, so you can run several instances of it. npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ express@^5 \ ioredis pnpm add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ express@^5 \ ioredis yarn add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ express@^5 \ ioredis bun add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ express@^5 \ ioredis npm pnpm yarn bun npm install --save-dev @types/express@^5 pnpm add -D @types/express@^5 yarn add -D @types/express@^5 bun add -d @types/express@^5 server.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, CacheModule, ClaimFormat, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile, type OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper, OpenId4VcModule, } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres' import express from 'express' import { Redis } from 'ioredis' function env(name: string) { const value = process.env[name] if (!value) throw new Error(`Environment variable ${name} is not set`) return value } // The URL wallets use to reach this service, for example https://issuer.example.com const publicUrl = env('PUBLIC_URL') // Issues an SD-JWT VC with the claims you set as issuanceMetadata when creating the offer const credentialRequestToCredentialMapper: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper = ({ credentialConfiguration, holderBinding, issuanceSession, }) => { if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc) { throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format '${credentialConfiguration.format}'`) } return { type: 'credentials', format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc, credentials: holderBinding.keys.map((holder) => ({ payload: { vct: credentialConfiguration.vct, ...issuanceSession.issuanceMetadata }, holder, issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: env('ISSUER_DID_URL') }, })), } } const app = express() const redis = new Redis(env('REDIS_URL')) const agent = new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { // Records go in PostgreSQL tables. Run the migrations of the core and openid4vc bundles first. storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle(env('DATABASE_URL')), bundles: [openid4vcBundle], }), // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar keeps them, in a PostgreSQL database of its own askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { // Also the name of the PostgreSQL database id: 'issuer-verifier-keys', key: env('STORE_KEY'), database: { type: 'postgres', config: { host: env('POSTGRES_HOST') }, credentials: { account: env('POSTGRES_USER'), password: env('POSTGRES_PASSWORD') }, }, }, }), // Shared by all instances of the service cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new RedisCache(redis) }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, issuer: { baseUrl: `${publicUrl}/oid4vci`, credentialRequestToCredentialMapper }, verifier: { baseUrl: `${publicUrl}/oid4vp` }, }), }, }) // Mounts the OpenID4VC routes on the Express app await agent.initialize() const server = app.listen(4000) process.on('SIGTERM', async () => { server.close() await agent.shutdown() // The agent doesn't close the Redis connection await redis.quit() }) credentialRequestToCredentialMapper decides which credential the issuer signs for a request. This one signs SD-JWT VCs with a DID that the agent created before, set in ISSUER_DID_URL. Before you can offer credentials, create an issuer record. Issuing credentials covers the mapper, issuer records and offers. agent.initialize() adds the OpenID4VC routes to the Express app, so start the server after it. Drizzle doesn't create tables. Run the migrations before every deploy: npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle openid4vc migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "$DATABASE_URL"

Start here if you host issuers or verifiers for many organizations in one deployment. Each organization is a tenant with its own DIDs, keys and records. See Multi-tenancy. Install the packages of the issuer and verifier service, and: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2 server.ts import { AskarModule, AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, CacheModule, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc' import { tenantsBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/tenants' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache' import { TenantsModule } from '@credo-ts/tenants' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres' import express from 'express' import { Redis } from 'ioredis' function env(name: string) { const value = process.env[name] if (!value) throw new Error(`Environment variable ${name} is not set`) return value } const app = express() const redis = new Redis(env('REDIS_URL')) const modules = { // The records of all tenants in one PostgreSQL database. Run the migrations of the core, // openid4vc and tenants bundles first. storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle(env('DATABASE_URL')), bundles: [openid4vcBundle, tenantsBundle], }), // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar keeps them: one database, with a profile per tenant askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, multiWalletDatabaseScheme: AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet, store: { id: 'multi-tenant-keys', key: env('STORE_KEY'), database: { type: 'postgres', config: { host: env('POSTGRES_HOST') }, credentials: { account: env('POSTGRES_USER'), password: env('POSTGRES_PASSWORD') }, }, }, }), // Required: the default cache throws as soon as a second agent context (a tenant) uses it cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new RedisCache(redis) }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, verifier: { baseUrl: `${env('PUBLIC_URL')}/oid4vp` }, }), } const agent = new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...modules, // Tenant agents share the modules of the root agent. The type argument types their API. tenants: new TenantsModule<typeof modules>({ sessionLimit: 500 }), }, }) await agent.initialize() app.listen(4000) Replace the default cache: it works with one agent context only, and throws as soon as a tenant uses it. Use InMemoryLruCache for a single instance or RedisCache for several, see Caching. Drizzle keeps the records of all tenants in one database. ProfilePerWallet does the same for the keys, with an Askar profile per tenant. Run the migrations with the tenants bundle: npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle openid4vc --bundle tenants migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" Tenant agents use the modules of the root agent, and the OpenID4VC endpoints route each request to the tenant that owns the issuer or verifier. Create a tenant and set it up through a tenant agent: export async function createVerifierTenant(label: string) { const tenant = await agent.modules.tenants.createTenant({ config: { label } }) const verifier = await agent.modules.tenants.withTenantAgent({ tenantId: tenant.id }, (tenantAgent) => tenantAgent.openid4vc.verifier.createVerifier({ clientMetadata: { client_name: label } }) ) return { tenantId: tenant.id, verifierId: verifier.verifierId } }

Start here if the mobile wallets in your DIDComm ecosystem need a mediator. This public Node.js service receives DIDComm messages for wallets without an endpoint of their own, and holds them until the wallet picks them up. It stores records in PostgreSQL with Drizzle, keeps keys in Askar and caches in Redis. See Mediation. npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ ioredis pnpm add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ ioredis yarn add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ ioredis bun add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ pg \ ioredis mediator.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, CacheModule, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommModule, DidCommWsOutboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { didcommBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/didcomm' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport, DidCommWsInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres' import { Redis } from 'ioredis' function env(name: string) { const value = process.env[name] if (!value) throw new Error(`Environment variable ${name} is not set`) return value } const redis = new Redis(env('REDIS_URL')) const agent = new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), autoUpdateStorageOnStartup: true, }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { // Run the Drizzle migrations for the core and didcomm bundles before you start the agent storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle(env('DATABASE_URL')), bundles: [didcommBundle], }), // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar provides the KMS askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { id: 'mediator-keys', key: env('STORE_KEY'), database: { type: 'postgres', config: { host: env('POSTGRES_HOST') }, credentials: { account: env('POSTGRES_USER'), password: env('POSTGRES_PASSWORD') }, }, }, }), cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new RedisCache(redis) }), didcomm: new DidCommModule({ // The public URLs of the HTTP and WebSocket transports, for example behind a reverse proxy endpoints: [env('HTTP_ENDPOINT'), env('WS_ENDPOINT')], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port: 4000 }), new DidCommWsInboundTransport({ port: 4001 })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport(), new DidCommWsOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, mediator: { autoAcceptMediationRequests: true }, // Message pickup is enabled by default. A mediator doesn't need the other protocols. mediationRecipient: false, credentials: false, proofs: false, basicMessages: false, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() process.on('SIGTERM', async () => { await agent.shutdown() await redis.quit() }) Run the migrations before you start it: npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle didcomm migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "$DATABASE_URL" Queued messages are kept in memory by default, so they're lost on restart and not shared between instances. For production, pass a persistent queueTransportRepository to the DidCommModule. DIDComm Mediator Credo is a complete mediator that can keep the queue in PostgreSQL or DynamoDB. autoUpdateStorageOnStartup migrates the storage when you upgrade Credo. Back up the database first, see Updating.

Start here for unit and integration tests of your own code. Each agent gets its own in-memory SQLite database and keeps its keys in memory, so tests don't share state and nothing is written to disk. agent.test.ts import { after, before, test } from 'node:test' import { Agent, type KeyDidCreateOptions } from '@credo-ts/core' import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { coreBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core' import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node' import { createClient } from '@libsql/client' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator' export async function createTestAgent() { // A new in-memory database for every agent keeps parallel tests apart const database = drizzle(createClient({ url: ':memory:' })) await migrate(database, { migrationsFolder: coreBundle.migrations.sqlite.migrationsPath, // Give every bundle you add its own migrations table migrationsTable: 'credo_migrations__core', }) return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [] }), // Keeps the keys in memory kms: new KeyManagementModule({ backends: [new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())], }), }, }) } The Node.js key management backend is lighter than Askar and needs no store. DIDComm needs XSalsa20-Poly1305, which only Askar has, so tests that use DIDComm keep the keys in Askar with an in-memory store. A test with Node.js's test runner: const agent = await createTestAgent() before(() => agent.initialize()) after(() => agent.shutdown()) test('creates a did:key', async () => { const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the DID failed') })

This page builds the smallest complete agent: it stores records in an SQLite file with Drizzle and keys in Askar, creates a did:key, resolves it and shuts down. On React Native, Askar stores both. You need the packages from Installation.

Node.js React Native src/index.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, type KeyDidCreateOptions, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' const agent = new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { // Records go in the tables of an SQLite file storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle('file:agent.db'), bundles: [], }), // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar keeps them askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { id: 'my-first-agent', // Use a secret from your environment or a secure store in a real application key: 'my-first-agent-key', }, }), }, }) agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, type KeyDidCreateOptions, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' const agent = new Agent({ config: { logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info), }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'my-first-agent', // Use a key from the device's secure storage in a real app key: 'my-first-agent-key', }, }), }, }) The Agent constructor takes three options: dependencies are the platform implementations of the file system, fetch, WebSocket and events. Import agentDependencies from @credo-ts/node or @credo-ts/react-native. modules adds features to the agent. On Node.js, the DrizzleStorageModule stores the records, and the AskarModule with enableStorage: false is the key management backend. On React Native, the AskarModule does both. An agent needs a storage module: without one, new Agent() throws Missing required dependency: 'StorageService'. config holds agent-wide settings, such as the logger. See Agent configuration. drizzle('file:agent.db') opens agent.db in the current directory. For PostgreSQL and the record bundles of other modules, see Drizzle. store.id names the Askar database and store.key encrypts it. On Node.js the Askar database is created at ~/.afj/data/wallet/<id>/sqlite.db. See Askar for the options and how to choose the key.

The key you register a module under is the name of its API: agent.modules.askar for the module above. didcomm and openid4vc are also available as agent.didcomm and agent.openid4vc when you register them under those keys. Default modules, such as DIDs, key management and SD-JWT VC, are always registered and have their APIs at the top level, for example agent.dids and agent.kms. TypeScript infers these APIs from the modules you pass, so using a module you didn't register is a type error. Agent configuration lists the default modules and shows how to type an agent you pass around.

await agent.initialize() initialize() opens the storage and the Askar store, creates the store on the first run, and checks that the storage is up to date for this version of Credo. Call it once, before you use the agent.

const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } }, }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') { throw new Error(`Creating the DID failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`) } const didDocument = await agent.dids.resolveDidDocument(didState.did) console.log(JSON.stringify(didDocument.toJSON(), null, 2)) agent.dids.create() creates an Ed25519 key in Askar, stores a DID record that links the DID to the key, and returns the did:key. resolveDidDocument() resolves the DID to its DID document, and throws if that fails. See DIDs for other DID methods.
await agent.shutdown() shutdown() stops the modules and closes the storage. Call it before your process exits or your app is closed.

Node.js React Native Drizzle doesn't create tables, so apply the migrations of the core bundle first, and again after every Credo upgrade. Without them, initialize() fails with no such table: StorageVersion. npx drizzle-storage --bundle core migrate --dialect sqlite --database-url file:agent.db Then run the agent: npx tsx src/index.ts The agent logs its startup at the info level and prints the DID document: INFO: Creating agent with config { ... } INFO: Agent storage is up to date. { "@context": [ "https://www.w3.org/ns/did/v1", ... ], "id": "did:key:z6Mkg...", "verificationMethod": [ ... ], ... } Run it again and the agent adds a second DID to the same database. Metro doesn't support top-level await, so the React Native version wraps the steps in runFirstAgent(). Call it from your app, for example in a useEffect of your root component, and check the Metro logs for the DID document.
Example setups shows complete configurations for wallets, issuers, verifiers and mediators. Agent configuration describes all agent options.

This page sets up a project and installs Credo, its platform package, and the packages for storage and keys. Every agent needs a storage module. On Node.js the next pages store records with Drizzle in SQLite and keys with Askar. On React Native, Askar stores both. Use Node.js for a server and React Native for a mobile wallet. Choose your setup covers the other choices to make first.

Node.js React Native Credo needs Node.js 20.19 or later. It's published as ES modules only, so create a project with "type": "module": mkdir my-agent cd my-agent npm init -y npm pkg set type=module Add TypeScript and tsx to run TypeScript files: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install --save-dev typescript tsx pnpm add -D typescript tsx yarn add -D typescript tsx bun add -d typescript tsx tsconfig.json { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext", "strict": true, "skipLibCheck": true } } "module": "nodenext" resolves the exports of the Credo packages, including subpaths such as @credo-ts/core/kms. "moduleResolution": "bundler" works too. The older "node" resolution doesn't find subpaths. skipLibCheck is needed because some of Credo's dependencies ship type definitions that don't type-check. Create an Expo app, or use an existing one: npx create-expo-app@latest my-wallet Credo uses native modules, so it doesn't run in Expo Go. Build the app with Continuous Native Generation, for example with npx expo run:android and npx expo run:ios or with EAS Build. Expo's TypeScript and Metro defaults work with Credo's ES modules, so you don't need to change them.

Keep all @credo-ts/* packages on the same version. They depend on each other with exact versions. Node.js React Native npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 yarn add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 bun add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 \ drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 \ @libsql/client \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 @libsql/client is the SQLite driver for Drizzle. Keep drizzle-orm on the version range shown, which @credo-ts/drizzle-storage requires. Install the peer dependencies of @credo-ts/react-native with npx expo install, so you get the versions that match your Expo SDK: npx expo install expo-crypto react-native-get-random-values @dr.pogodin/react-native-fs Package Why Credo needs it react-native-get-random-values Secure random numbers. @credo-ts/react-native imports it for you, so you don't need a polyfill in your entry file. expo-crypto Hashing in the JSON-LD libraries Credo uses. @dr.pogodin/react-native-fs File system access. react-native-fs works too. Importing @credo-ts/react-native throws if neither is installed. @credo-ts/react-native declares expo-crypto@^15 as its peer range, which only matches Expo SDK 54. With a newer SDK, npm refuses to install Credo with an ERESOLVE error. Add an override to your package.json first: package.json { "overrides": { "@credo-ts/react-native": { "expo-crypto": "$expo-crypto" } } } pnpm and Yarn print a peer dependency warning instead. Then install Credo: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/react-native@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/react-native@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 yarn add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/react-native@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 bun add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/react-native@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 \ @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native is linked automatically and doesn't need a config plugin. Rebuild the native app after you install it. The Askar platform package depends on @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared with its exact version, and @credo-ts/askar needs the same copy. Install a single Askar version: with two versions of askar-shared in your project, agent.initialize() fails with Native askar has not been registered yet. pnpm and Bun The Askar packages download their native library in an install script. pnpm and Bun don't run install scripts of dependencies unless you allow them. With pnpm, run pnpm approve-builds. With Bun, add the package to trustedDependencies in your package.json.
Your first agent configures the agent and runs it. Storage compares Drizzle with Askar.
An exchange protocol defines how issuers, holders and verifiers talk to each other. Credo supports OpenID4VC, DIDComm and the ISO mdoc protocols.
