Use When OpenID4VC By default, for new issuers, wallets and verifiers. It only needs HTTPS, carries SD-JWT VC and mdoc, and is what the EU Digital Identity Wallet and the HAIP profile use. ISO mdoc A wallet presents mdocs, such as a mobile driving licence, in person to a reader over BLE or NFC. A wallet usually receives those mdocs with OpenID4VCI. DIDComm You join an ecosystem built on DIDComm and AnonCreds, or the parties need a lasting connection to exchange messages beyond a single issuance or presentation.

OpenID4VC builds on OAuth 2.0 and plain HTTPS. OpenID4VCI covers issuance and OpenID4VP covers presentation. An issuer or verifier starts each exchange with a QR code or link, and the wallet completes it with a few HTTPS requests. Nothing persists between exchanges. This is the protocol family of the EU Digital Identity Wallet and its HAIP profile, and of mobile driving licences (mDL) presented online.

DIDComm is a messaging protocol between agents that identify each other with DIDs. Two agents first set up a connection, usually from an out-of-band invitation. Over that connection either side can then offer credentials, request proofs or send other messages, for as long as the connection lasts. Mobile wallets can't accept incoming connections, so they receive messages through a mediator. DIDComm is used in ecosystems built on Hyperledger Aries and AnonCreds.

ISO mdoc covers the presentation protocols of ISO/IEC 18013-5 and 18013-7, which carry only mdocs, such as the mobile driving licence. A wallet presents in person to a reader over BLE or NFC (proximity), or to a website through the browser (ISO 18013-7 Annex C). Like OpenID4VC, each presentation stands alone. These protocols don't cover issuance.

The W3C Digital Credentials API lets a website request credentials through the browser, which passes the request to a wallet. It's a channel for other protocols: Credo supports it with OpenID4VP and with ISO 18013-7 Annex C.

OpenID4VC DIDComm ISO mdoc Transport HTTPS requests from the wallet to the issuer or verifier Encrypted messages over HTTP or WebSocket, through a mediator for mobile wallets BLE or NFC in person, or the browser with the Digital Credentials API Relationship None: each exchange stands alone A connection that both agents keep None: each presentation stands alone Starts with A credential offer or authorization request An out-of-band invitation A QR code or NFC tap, or a website calling the Digital Credentials API Issuer and verifier Node.js Node.js No issuer. Verifier on Node.js Holder Node.js and React Native Node.js and React Native Node.js and React Native Typical ecosystems EU Digital Identity Wallet, HAIP, mDL Aries and AnonCreds ecosystems mDL and EU PID, in person and online

Format OpenID4VC DIDComm ISO mdoc SD-JWT VC Yes No No mdoc Yes No Yes W3C VC Yes Yes No AnonCreds No Yes No Which W3C data models and proof types work depends on the protocol and on whether you issue or present. Supported standards has the full matrix.

Protocol pages cover each role. For OpenID4VC these are Issuing credentials, Receiving credentials, Presenting credentials and Verifying credentials. For DIDComm they're Connections, Issuing credentials and Requesting proofs. The ISO mdoc pages cover proximity presentation (ISO 18013-5). Pages named "… with OpenID4VC" or "… with DIDComm", such as SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC and AnonCreds with DIDComm, cover what's specific to one format on one protocol. What you can do with a format on its own, such as signing, storing and verifying credentials or checking their status, is under Credential formats. The W3C Digital Credentials API lets a website request credentials through the browser. The browser and the operating system let the user pick a wallet and a credential, on the same device or on a phone nearby, without QR codes or redirects. The API only carries the request and the response, and another protocol defines what they contain. Credo supports two, OpenID4VP and ISO 18013-7 Annex C, on both the verifier and the wallet side. This page explains how the API works and what to choose. To build one side, see Building a verifier or Building a wallet.

The wallet registers its credentials with the operating system beforehand, so the browser only offers wallets that hold a matching credential. The verifier's backend creates the request with Credo, and its web page passes it to navigator.credentials.get(). The page can pass several requests in one call, one per protocol, and the wallet answers one of them. The browser tells the wallet the origin of the page that asked. The wallet binds its response to that origin, and the backend verifies the response for its own origin, so a response can't be relayed to another website. Nothing goes over the network between the wallet and the verifier: the response comes back through the page.

OpenID4VP ISO 18013-7 Annex C Protocol identifier openid4vp-v1-unsigned or openid4vp-v1-signed org-iso-mdoc Credential formats SD-JWT VC and mdoc mdoc Request A DCQL query, which can express alternatives A device request: document types and data elements Verifier identity The origin, or a signed request The origin, or reader authentication Response encryption With response mode dc_api.jwt Always Platforms Android Android and iOS Credo API agent.openid4vc in @credo-ts/openid4vc agent.mdoc in @credo-ts/core, since Credo 0.7.1 OpenID4VC and ISO mdoc explain the protocols themselves.

Which browsers support the API, and which protocols they accept, differs per platform and changes quickly. Check the current support before you depend on it. At the time of writing: Platform Protocols How wallets take part Android OpenID4VP and org-iso-mdoc The wallet registers its credentials, with their claim values, in Credential Manager. A matcher compares each request with them in a sandbox, and the system picker shows the matching credentials. iOS 26 and later org-iso-mdoc only The wallet is a document provider of the Identity Document Services framework. It registers only mdocs of a fixed set of document types, such as the mDL and the EU PID, and iOS matches requests on the document type alone. Chrome supports both protocols, and Safari only org-iso-mdoc. On desktop, the browser can pass the request to a phone nearby.

As a verifier: Choice Default When to pick the other Protocol For mdocs, pass an OpenID4VP and an org-iso-mdoc request in one call, so wallets on both platforms can answer. For SD-JWT VCs, OpenID4VP. org-iso-mdoc alone reaches wallets on both platforms without the OpenID4VC module, but misses Android wallets that only support OpenID4VP. Signed requests Unsigned. The wallet identifies you by the origin of your website, which the browser verified through its TLS certificate. Sign when wallets or your ecosystem need to know who you are beyond the origin, for example a registered verifier. Use x509_hash for OpenID4VP, as HAIP does, and reader authentication for org-iso-mdoc. Some wallets only answer signed requests. Response encryption (OpenID4VP) dc_api.jwt. Only your backend can read the response, not the page and the browser it passes through. HAIP requires it. dc_api only for testing. org-iso-mdoc always encrypts. As a wallet, support org-iso-mdoc for mdocs, as it's the only protocol iOS passes on, and OpenID4VP on Android for SD-JWT VCs and for verifiers that only send OpenID4VP. Credo answers signed and unsigned requests of both protocols, encrypted or not. HAIP also asks wallets to accept multi-signed OpenID4VP requests (openid4vp-v1-multisigned), which Credo doesn't support.
Building a verifier: create the requests, call the API from a web page, and verify the response. Building a wallet: answer requests in a React Native wallet.

A verifier for the Digital Credentials API has two parts: a Node.js backend with a Credo agent, which creates the requests and verifies the responses, and a web page that passes them through the browser. This page builds both. The example asks for the given name and age over 18 from an mDL, with OpenID4VP and with ISO 18013-7 Annex C (org-iso-mdoc) in one call, so wallets on Android and iOS can answer. Digital Credentials API explains the flow and the choices.

npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ express pnpm add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ express yarn add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ express bun add \ @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 \ express The agent also needs storage, see Storage. The backend creates the requests, verifies the responses, and serves the web page: dc-api-verifier.ts import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs' import { Agent, ClaimFormat, X509Module } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import express from 'express' // The origin of the web page that calls the Digital Credentials API. This server serves the page. const origin = 'http://localhost:4037' const app = express() // The web page, with the code from dc-api-verifier-browser.ts app.use(express.static('public')) const verifier = new Agent({ config: { // Allows the http://localhost URLs of this example. Never enable this in production. allowInsecureHttpUrls: true, }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // Certificates (or root CAs) of the issuers you accept, as PEM or base64. For an mDL, the IACA certificates. x509: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates: [readFileSync('issuer-certificate.pem', 'utf8')] }), // Only needed for OpenID4VP. ISO 18013-7 Annex C uses `agent.mdoc`, which every agent has. openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, verifier: { baseUrl: `${origin}/oid4vp` } }), }, }) await verifier.initialize() const { verifierId } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.createVerifier() origin is the origin of the page that calls the API. Here the backend serves the page, so it's the backend's own origin. The verifier accepts credentials from the issuers in its trust configuration. See Trusted issuers. Only OpenID4VP needs OpenId4VcModule. If you only use org-iso-mdoc, leave it out.

Create a request for each protocol you offer. Both ask for the same data elements: OpenID4VP ISO 18013-7 Annex C dc-api-verifier.ts async function createOpenId4VpRequest() { const { verificationSession, authorizationRequestObject } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.createAuthorizationRequest({ verifierId, // Unsigned: the wallet identifies the verifier by the origin the browser passes on requestSigner: { method: 'none' }, // Encrypt the response to the verifier responseMode: 'dc_api.jwt', dcql: { query: { credentials: [ { id: 'mdl', format: 'mso_mdoc', meta: { doctype_value: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL' }, claims: [{ path: ['org.iso.18013.5.1', 'given_name'] }, { path: ['org.iso.18013.5.1', 'age_over_18'] }], }, ], }, }, }) // The page passes `request` to navigator.credentials.get() return { verificationSessionId: verificationSession.id, request: authorizationRequestObject } } responseMode is dc_api.jwt, which encrypts the response to the verifier, or dc_api, which doesn't. An unsigned request (method: 'none') has no client id. The wallet identifies the verifier as origin:<origin>. Return authorizationRequestObject to the page, not the openid4vp:// URI in authorizationRequest. authorizationResponseRedirectUri can't be used, as the response goes back to the page. To request an SD-JWT VC instead, change the DCQL query (see SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC) and pass only this request. Annex C only carries mdocs. dc-api-verifier.ts async function createIsoMdocRequest() { const { verificationSession, request } = await verifier.mdoc.createDcApiVerificationSession({ docRequests: [ { docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', // Element identifier mapped to intent to retain nameSpaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { given_name: false, age_over_18: false } }, }, ], }) // The page passes `request` to navigator.credentials.get() return { verificationSessionId: verificationSession.id, request } } nameSpaces maps each data element to its intent to retain. Pass { intentToRetain, optional, source } instead of a boolean to accept a response without the element (optional: true), or with the element signed by the device instead of the issuer (source: 'deviceSigned' or 'any'). By default the response must contain every requested element, issuer signed. With several docRequests, set treatAmbiguousMultipleDocRequestsAsAlternatives if one of them is enough. The flag isn't sent, so a wallet may still answer all of them. Each session has its own encryption key in the KMS, and expires after 5 minutes (expiresInSeconds). The page gets both requests from one route: dc-api-verifier.ts // The page passes both requests in one call, and the wallet answers one of them app.post('/dc-api/request', async (_request, response) => { response.json({ openid4vp: await createOpenId4VpRequest(), isoMdoc: await createIsoMdocRequest() }) })

Unsigned requests identify the verifier by its origin. To let wallets verify who you are beyond that, sign the request with a certificate whose key is in the verifier's KMS: OpenID4VP ISO 18013-7 Annex C requestSigner: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [verifierCertificate], clientIdPrefix: 'x509_hash' }, expectedOrigins: [origin], The wallet rejects a signed request when expectedOrigins doesn't include the origin the browser passed. On the page, use protocol openid4vp-v1-signed. Verifying credentials explains the client identifier prefixes. readerAuth: { certificate: readerCertificate, origin }, The signature covers one origin, so create a session per origin. The wallet only accepts a signed request when it trusts your certificate or its CA.

The page posts the response to the backend, which verifies it for the protocol the wallet answered: OpenID4VP ISO 18013-7 Annex C dc-api-verifier.ts async function verifyOpenId4VpResponse(verificationSessionId: string, data: Record<string, unknown>) { const { dcql } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.verifyAuthorizationResponse({ verificationSessionId, authorizationResponse: data, origin, }) const [mdl] = dcql?.presentations.mdl ?? [] if (mdl?.claimFormat !== ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc) throw new Error('Expected an mdoc presentation') return mdl.issuerClaims['org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL'] } With the dc_api response modes, Credo doesn't receive the response at its endpoint, so you pass it to verifyAuthorizationResponse. The result is the same as for other response modes, see mdoc with OpenID4VC for reading mdoc claims. dc-api-verifier.ts async function verifyIsoMdocResponse(verificationSessionId: string, data: { response: string }) { const { deviceResponse } = await verifier.mdoc.verifyDcApiResponse({ verificationSessionId, response: data, origin }) return deviceResponse.issuerClaims['org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL'] } Credo decrypts the response, verifies each mdoc (issuer signature and certificate chain, element digests, device signature, validity and status), and checks the response against the request. When an element is missing or isn't signed as required, it throws MdocDeviceRequestNotSatisfiedError, with the details in deviceRequestMatch. A response for an expired session throws MdocVerificationSessionExpiredError. Create a new request. issuerClaims has the disclosed elements per document type and namespace, deviceClaims the device-signed ones. The route picks the protocol from the response: dc-api-verifier.ts app.post('/dc-api/response', express.json(), async (request, response) => { const { protocol, data, openid4vpSessionId, isoMdocSessionId } = request.body if (typeof openid4vpSessionId !== 'string' || typeof isoMdocSessionId !== 'string') { return response.status(400).end() } // Some browsers return the response as a JSON string const responseData = typeof data === 'string' ? JSON.parse(data) : data try { const claims = protocol === 'org-iso-mdoc' ? await verifyIsoMdocResponse(isoMdocSessionId, responseData) : await verifyOpenId4VpResponse(openid4vpSessionId, responseData) response.json(claims) } finally { // Also deletes the encryption key of the session, whichever request the wallet answered await verifier.mdoc.deleteVerificationSessionById(isoMdocSessionId) } }) app.listen(4037) origin is the origin of your page. Use the value you know, never one from the request: verification fails for any other origin, which is what stops a relayed response. Credo doesn't delete mdoc verification sessions or their keys by itself. Delete each session with deleteVerificationSessionById, also when the wallet answered the OpenID4VP request or verification failed.

The web page gets the requests from the backend, passes them to navigator.credentials.get(), and posts the response back: dc-api-verifier-browser.ts export async function verifyWithWallet() { const { openid4vp, isoMdoc } = await postJson('/dc-api/request') const options: DigitalCredentialRequestOptions = { mediation: 'required', digital: { requests: [ // Use 'openid4vp-v1-signed' for a signed request { protocol: 'openid4vp-v1-unsigned', data: openid4vp.request }, { protocol: 'org-iso-mdoc', data: isoMdoc.request }, ], }, } // The browser and the operating system let the user pick a wallet and a credential. // Throws a NotAllowedError when the user cancels or no wallet has a matching credential. const credential = await navigator.credentials.get(options) if (!credential || !('data' in credential) || !('protocol' in credential)) { throw new Error('No digital credential returned') } return postJson('/dc-api/response', { // The protocol of the request the wallet answered protocol: credential.protocol, data: credential.data, openid4vpSessionId: openid4vp.verificationSessionId, isoMdocSessionId: isoMdoc.verificationSessionId, }) } The wallet answers one of the requests, and credential.protocol says which. Post credential.data to your backend as it is. TypeScript's DOM types don't have the digital option yet. The full example declares it. The call throws a NotAllowedError when the user cancels or no wallet has a matching credential. The browser doesn't say which, so a website can't find out what a wallet holds without the user's consent. Call it when the user clicks a button: dc-api-verifier-browser.ts const button = document.querySelector('button') // The API needs a secure context (https or localhost) and a browser that supports it if (!('DigitalCredential' in window)) { button?.replaceWith('Your browser does not support the Digital Credentials API') } // The browser only opens the wallet in response to a user action, such as a click button?.addEventListener('click', async () => { const claims = await verifyWithWallet() console.log(claims) }) The browser only opens the wallet shortly after a user action. A single request to your backend before the call is quick enough. For slower work, get the requests before the click. The API only exists in a secure context (https, or http://localhost) and in browsers that support it. Elsewhere, fall back to a QR code or a link, see Verifying credentials.
documents.s: Call the API from the browser

documents.t: The backend serves the page from public/. Put the certificate of the issuer you trust in issuer-certificate.pem, then start it with npx tsx dc-api-verifier.ts and open http://localhost:4037. Backend Web page dc-api-verifier.ts // The verifier backend. It creates the requests that the web page in dc-api-verifier-browser.ts passes // to the Digital Credentials API, and verifies the response the page posts back. import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc' import { exampleStorage } from './example-storage.js' const storage = await exampleStorage([openid4vcBundle]) import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs' import { Agent, ClaimFormat, X509Module } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import express from 'express' // The origin of the web page that calls the Digital Credentials API. This server serves the page. const origin = 'http://localhost:4037' const app = express() // The web page, with the code from dc-api-verifier-browser.ts app.use(express.static('public')) const verifier = new Agent({ config: { // Allows the http://localhost URLs of this example. Never enable this in production. allowInsecureHttpUrls: true, }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // Certificates (or root CAs) of the issuers you accept, as PEM or base64. For an mDL, the IACA certificates. x509: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates: [readFileSync('issuer-certificate.pem', 'utf8')] }), // Only needed for OpenID4VP. ISO 18013-7 Annex C uses `agent.mdoc`, which every agent has. openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, verifier: { baseUrl: `${origin}/oid4vp` } }), }, }) await verifier.initialize() const { verifierId } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.createVerifier() async function createOpenId4VpRequest() { const { verificationSession, authorizationRequestObject } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.createAuthorizationRequest({ verifierId, // Unsigned: the wallet identifies the verifier by the origin the browser passes on requestSigner: { method: 'none' }, // Encrypt the response to the verifier responseMode: 'dc_api.jwt', dcql: { query: { credentials: [ { id: 'mdl', format: 'mso_mdoc', meta: { doctype_value: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL' }, claims: [{ path: ['org.iso.18013.5.1', 'given_name'] }, { path: ['org.iso.18013.5.1', 'age_over_18'] }], }, ], }, }, }) // The page passes `request` to navigator.credentials.get() return { verificationSessionId: verificationSession.id, request: authorizationRequestObject } } async function createIsoMdocRequest() { const { verificationSession, request } = await verifier.mdoc.createDcApiVerificationSession({ docRequests: [ { docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', // Element identifier mapped to intent to retain nameSpaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { given_name: false, age_over_18: false } }, }, ], }) // The page passes `request` to navigator.credentials.get() return { verificationSessionId: verificationSession.id, request } } // The page passes both requests in one call, and the wallet answers one of them app.post('/dc-api/request', async (_request, response) => { response.json({ openid4vp: await createOpenId4VpRequest(), isoMdoc: await createIsoMdocRequest() }) }) async function verifyOpenId4VpResponse(verificationSessionId: string, data: Record<string, unknown>) { const { dcql } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.verifyAuthorizationResponse({ verificationSessionId, authorizationResponse: data, origin, }) const [mdl] = dcql?.presentations.mdl ?? [] if (mdl?.claimFormat !== ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc) throw new Error('Expected an mdoc presentation') return mdl.issuerClaims['org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL'] } async function verifyIsoMdocResponse(verificationSessionId: string, data: { response: string }) { const { deviceResponse } = await verifier.mdoc.verifyDcApiResponse({ verificationSessionId, response: data, origin }) return deviceResponse.issuerClaims['org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL'] } app.post('/dc-api/response', express.json(), async (request, response) => { const { protocol, data, openid4vpSessionId, isoMdocSessionId } = request.body if (typeof openid4vpSessionId !== 'string' || typeof isoMdocSessionId !== 'string') { return response.status(400).end() } // Some browsers return the response as a JSON string const responseData = typeof data === 'string' ? JSON.parse(data) : data try { const claims = protocol === 'org-iso-mdoc' ? await verifyIsoMdocResponse(isoMdocSessionId, responseData) : await verifyOpenId4VpResponse(openid4vpSessionId, responseData) response.json(claims) } finally { // Also deletes the encryption key of the session, whichever request the wallet answered await verifier.mdoc.deleteVerificationSessionById(isoMdocSessionId) } }) app.listen(4037) Compile the script into public/, for example with npx esbuild dc-api-verifier-browser.ts --outdir=public. public/index.html <button>Verify with your wallet</button> <script type="module" src="dc-api-verifier-browser.js"></script> dc-api-verifier-browser.ts // Runs in the browser, on the verifier's web page. Talks to the routes in dc-api-verifier.ts. // TypeScript's DOM types don't include the Digital Credentials API yet type DigitalCredentialRequestOptions = CredentialRequestOptions & { digital: { requests: Array<{ protocol: string; data: unknown }> } } async function postJson(path: string, body: unknown = {}) { const response = await fetch(path, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(body), }) if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${path} failed with status ${response.status}`) return response.json() } export async function verifyWithWallet() { const { openid4vp, isoMdoc } = await postJson('/dc-api/request') const options: DigitalCredentialRequestOptions = { mediation: 'required', digital: { requests: [ // Use 'openid4vp-v1-signed' for a signed request { protocol: 'openid4vp-v1-unsigned', data: openid4vp.request }, { protocol: 'org-iso-mdoc', data: isoMdoc.request }, ], }, } // The browser and the operating system let the user pick a wallet and a credential. // Throws a NotAllowedError when the user cancels or no wallet has a matching credential. const credential = await navigator.credentials.get(options) if (!credential || !('data' in credential) || !('protocol' in credential)) { throw new Error('No digital credential returned') } return postJson('/dc-api/response', { // The protocol of the request the wallet answered protocol: credential.protocol, data: credential.data, openid4vpSessionId: openid4vp.verificationSessionId, isoMdocSessionId: isoMdoc.verificationSessionId, }) } const button = document.querySelector('button') // The API needs a secure context (https or localhost) and a browser that supports it if (!('DigitalCredential' in window)) { button?.replaceWith('Your browser does not support the Digital Credentials API') } // The browser only opens the wallet in response to a user action, such as a click button?.addEventListener('click', async () => { const claims = await verifyWithWallet() console.log(claims) })

Building a wallet: the other side of the flow. Verifying credentials: OpenID4VP requests, client identifiers and verification sessions. mdoc with OpenID4VC and SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC: request and read each format. Trusted issuers: decide which issuers you trust.

When a website calls the Digital Credentials API, the operating system offers the wallets that hold a matching credential, and opens the one the user picks with the request and the origin of the website. In a React Native wallet, @animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api handles the platform side: it registers credentials with Credential Manager on Android and Identity Document Services on iOS, and shows your request UI. Credo resolves the request and creates the response. This page builds a minimal wallet that answers both OpenID4VP and org-iso-mdoc requests. Digital Credentials API explains the flow and which protocols to support, and the module README has all options and platform details. Paradym Wallet, an open source wallet built on Credo, supports the API this way. See its request handling, credential registration and request UI for a complete implementation.

The wallet is a React Native agent, see Installation. Add the module, and expo-secure-store for the wallet key: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api expo-secure-store pnpm add @animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api expo-secure-store yarn add @animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api expo-secure-store bun add @animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api expo-secure-store Add the config plugin to app.json and run npx expo prebuild: app.json { "expo": { "plugins": [ [ "@animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api", { "entry": "src/dc-api-wallet-request", "ios": { "documentTypes": ["org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL"] } } ] ] } } The module needs Expo SDK 55 and React Native 0.83 or later. On these SDKs, npm only installs Credo with the expo-crypto override from Installation. It works on Android devices whose Credential Manager has the registry API, and on iOS 26 and later. The app itself can still support older iOS versions. entry is the file with the request UI, without extension. ios.documentTypes are the mdoc document types the wallet can present on iOS, from the set Apple allows: org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL, eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1, eu.europa.ec.av.1, org.iso.23220.photoid.1 and org.iso.23220.1.jp.mnc. Without it, the plugin doesn't add the iOS app extension. Android needs no options.

The app and the request UI open the same wallet: dc-api-wallet-agent.ts import { type DcApiClaimValue, type DcApiCredential, getRegistrationStatus, getSharedContainerPath, isSupported, registerCredentials, type SdJwtClaims, } from '@animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api' import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, DateOnly } from '@credo-ts/core' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar, Store } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' import * as SecureStore from 'expo-secure-store' import { Platform } from 'react-native' // Used by both the app and the request UI export async function initializeWalletAgent() { // On iOS, the config plugin shares the keychain with the request UI let walletKey = await SecureStore.getItemAsync('wallet-key') if (!walletKey) { walletKey = Store.generateRawKey() await SecureStore.setItemAsync('wallet-key', walletKey) } const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw', // On iOS the request UI runs in an app extension, which can only read files in the // shared app group container. On Android it runs in the app's process. database: Platform.OS === 'ios' ? { type: 'sqlite', config: { path: `${getSharedContainerPath()}/wallet.sqlite` } } : undefined, }, }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) await agent.initialize() return agent } export type WalletAgent = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof initializeWalletAgent>> On iOS, the request UI runs in an app extension, a separate process that can't read the app's files. The config plugin creates an app group, and getSharedContainerPath() returns a directory that both can use. A wallet that already has a store elsewhere has to move it there first. The plugin also shares the keychain between the app and the extension, so both read the same wallet key. On Android, the request UI runs in the app's process.
documents.s: Share the wallet with the request UI

documents.t: The operating system only offers the wallet for a request that matches a registered credential: dc-api-wallet-agent.ts // Call this on start and whenever the wallet stores or deletes a credential. // Each call replaces the credentials registered before. export async function registerWalletCredentials(agent: WalletAgent) { if (!isSupported()) return // iOS asks the user for permission on the first registration. Registering after they denied it throws. if ((await getRegistrationStatus()) === 'notAuthorized') return const mdocs = (await agent.mdoc.getAll()).map( (record): DcApiCredential => ({ // Comes back in the request when the user picks this credential id: record.id, display: { title: record.firstCredential.docType }, credential: { format: 'mso_mdoc', doctype: record.firstCredential.docType, namespaces: Object.fromEntries( Object.entries(record.firstCredential.issuerSignedNamespaces).map(([namespace, elements]) => [ namespace, Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(elements).map(([element, value]) => [element, claimValue(value)])), ]) ), }, }) ) const sdJwtVcs = (await agent.sdJwtVc.getAll()).map( (record): DcApiCredential => ({ id: record.id, display: { title: record.getTags().vct }, credential: { format: 'dc+sd-jwt', vct: record.getTags().vct, claims: sdJwtClaims(record.firstCredential.prettyClaims), }, }) ) // iOS only registers the mdocs whose document type is in the config plugin's `ios.documentTypes` await registerCredentials({ credentials: [...mdocs, ...sdJwtVcs] }) } On Android, a matcher runs in a sandbox and compares each request with the registered claims. The system picker shows the matching credentials with their values, so register the values: the full example converts them. Each call replaces the registered set, so pass all credentials. iOS only registers mdocs whose document type is in ios.documentTypes, and only keeps their id and document type. It matches on the document type, so a request can reach the wallet for elements the mdoc doesn't have. SD-JWT VCs aren't registered there. The first registration on iOS asks the user for permission.

When the user picks a credential of the wallet, the operating system starts the request UI. Credo resolves the request for the origin and creates the response: OpenID4VP ISO 18013-7 Annex C dc-api-wallet-response.ts export async function createOpenId4VpResponse( agent: WalletAgent, { protocol, data }: Openid4vpProtocolRequest, origin: string ): Promise<Openid4vpResponseOptions> { // The request arrives as a JSON string const resolved = await agent.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest(JSON.parse(data), { origin }) if (!resolved.dcql?.queryResult.can_be_satisfied) throw new Error('No matching credentials') const { authorizationResponse } = await agent.openid4vc.holder.acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest({ authorizationRequestPayload: resolved.authorizationRequestPayload, dcql: { credentials: agent.openid4vc.holder.selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest(resolved.dcql.queryResult) }, origin, }) // Answer with the protocol of the request return { protocol, data: authorizationResponse } } Pass the origin to both resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest and acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest. The holder rejects a DC API request without it, and a signed request whose expected_origins doesn't include it. A signed request only resolves when the wallet trusts the verifier's certificate. See Presenting credentials. acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest doesn't send anything. It returns authorizationResponse for you to hand back to the platform, with the protocol of the request. dc-api-wallet-response.ts export async function createIsoMdocResponse( agent: WalletAgent, { data }: IsoMdocProtocolRequest, origin: string ): Promise<IsoMdocResponseOptions> { const resolved = await agent.mdoc.resolveDcApiRequest({ request: data, origin }) if (!resolved.success || resolved.docRequestsAsAlternatives) throw new Error('No matching mdoc') const { response } = await agent.mdoc.createDcApiResponse({ resolvedRequest: resolved, credentials: resolved.docRequests.map(({ docRequestIndex, validCredentials }) => ({ docRequestIndex, record: validCredentials[0].record, })), }) return { protocol: 'org-iso-mdoc', data: { response } } } resolveDcApiRequest rejects a request without an origin. It verifies reader authentication and matches the stored mdocs against each document request. success is false when they can't satisfy the request. A signed request from a reader you don't trust throws. Trust readers through the agent's trust configuration with verification type mdocReaderAuth, or pass trustedReaderCertificates. readerAuth.certificateChain on each document request has the verified chain, leaf first, to show the verifier to the user. createDcApiResponse discloses every requested element. Pass elements per credential to disclose fewer, for example to leave out the ones the user declined. It sends nothing: hand the returned response back to the platform. Both functions present the first stored credential that matches. On Android, request.selection.credentialIds has the ids of the credentials the user picked in the system picker, so a full wallet presents those.

The request UI calls these functions when the user shares: dc-api-wallet-request.tsx async function share() { // Always use the origin from the operating system. On Android it's undefined when an app asks // for itself instead of a website. const { origin } = request if (!origin) return request.decline('No website origin') const agent = await initializeWalletAgent() try { if (request.platform === 'ios') { // iOS only hands over the request once the user approved, and only as org-iso-mdoc const [isoMdocRequest] = await request.approve() if (!isoMdocRequest) return request.decline('No org-iso-mdoc request') return await request.respond(await createIsoMdocResponse(agent, isoMdocRequest, origin)) } // On Android, the request that the credentials picked in the system picker were matched against const { requests, selection } = request const protocolRequest = requests[selection?.requestIndex ?? selection?.candidateRequestIndexes[0] ?? 0] if (!protocolRequest) return request.decline('No supported protocol') await request.respond( protocolRequest.protocol === 'org-iso-mdoc' ? await createIsoMdocResponse(agent, protocolRequest, origin) : await createOpenId4VpResponse(agent, protocolRequest, origin) ) } catch (shareError) { // The request stays open, so the user can try again or decline setError(shareError instanceof Error ? shareError.message : String(shareError)) } finally { await agent.shutdown() } } Always use the origin from the operating system, never one from the request. On Android it's undefined when an app asks for itself instead of a website. On Android, requests has the requests the page passed, and selection what the user picked in the system picker and the request it matched. With several requests of the same protocol, the matcher only reports the protocol, so the example takes the first candidate. iOS has no picker, and hands over the request only after approve(), always as org-iso-mdoc. Before that, request.presentmentRequests has the document types and elements the operating system parsed from it, to show on the consent screen. respond() sends the response through the operating system to the page, decline() cancels. Until then the request stays open, so the user can try again after an error. The entry file registers the screen: dc-api-wallet-request.tsx // The entry file registers the screen export default registerDcApiScreen(DcApiScreen) The request UI is bundled separately from the app. Import only what it needs: on iOS the extension gets little memory, and ios.excludedPackages or ios.includedPackages limit which native modules it links. The module README also lists known issues with some native modules in the request UI, and patches for them.

Render the app's screens as usual and call registerWalletCredentials after the wallet stores or deletes a credential. The request UI is dc-api-wallet-request.tsx. dc-api-wallet-agent.ts dc-api-wallet-response.ts dc-api-wallet-request.tsx dc-api-wallet-agent.ts // The wallet app: a React Native agent, and the credentials it registers with the operating system. // The request UI in dc-api-wallet-request.tsx opens the same wallet. import { type DcApiClaimValue, type DcApiCredential, getRegistrationStatus, getSharedContainerPath, isSupported, registerCredentials, type SdJwtClaims, } from '@animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api' import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, DateOnly } from '@credo-ts/core' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar, Store } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' import * as SecureStore from 'expo-secure-store' import { Platform } from 'react-native' // Used by both the app and the request UI export async function initializeWalletAgent() { // On iOS, the config plugin shares the keychain with the request UI let walletKey = await SecureStore.getItemAsync('wallet-key') if (!walletKey) { walletKey = Store.generateRawKey() await SecureStore.setItemAsync('wallet-key', walletKey) } const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw', // On iOS the request UI runs in an app extension, which can only read files in the // shared app group container. On Android it runs in the app's process. database: Platform.OS === 'ios' ? { type: 'sqlite', config: { path: `${getSharedContainerPath()}/wallet.sqlite` } } : undefined, }, }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) await agent.initialize() return agent } export type WalletAgent = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof initializeWalletAgent>> // Call this on start and whenever the wallet stores or deletes a credential. // Each call replaces the credentials registered before. export async function registerWalletCredentials(agent: WalletAgent) { if (!isSupported()) return // iOS asks the user for permission on the first registration. Registering after they denied it throws. if ((await getRegistrationStatus()) === 'notAuthorized') return const mdocs = (await agent.mdoc.getAll()).map( (record): DcApiCredential => ({ // Comes back in the request when the user picks this credential id: record.id, display: { title: record.firstCredential.docType }, credential: { format: 'mso_mdoc', doctype: record.firstCredential.docType, namespaces: Object.fromEntries( Object.entries(record.firstCredential.issuerSignedNamespaces).map(([namespace, elements]) => [ namespace, Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(elements).map(([element, value]) => [element, claimValue(value)])), ]) ), }, }) ) const sdJwtVcs = (await agent.sdJwtVc.getAll()).map( (record): DcApiCredential => ({ id: record.id, display: { title: record.getTags().vct }, credential: { format: 'dc+sd-jwt', vct: record.getTags().vct, claims: sdJwtClaims(record.firstCredential.prettyClaims), }, }) ) // iOS only registers the mdocs whose document type is in the config plugin's `ios.documentTypes` await registerCredentials({ credentials: [...mdocs, ...sdJwtVcs] }) } // The Android picker shows these values and matches requests against them. // Values it can't compare, such as arrays and images, are registered as null. function claimValue(value: unknown): DcApiClaimValue { if (typeof value === 'string' || typeof value === 'number' || typeof value === 'boolean') return value if (value instanceof Date || value instanceof DateOnly) return value.toISOString() return null } function sdJwtClaims(claims: object): SdJwtClaims { return Object.fromEntries( Object.entries(claims).map(([name, value]) => [ name, typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && !Array.isArray(value) ? sdJwtClaims(value) : claimValue(value), ]) ) } dc-api-wallet-response.ts // What Credo does in the wallet's request UI (dc-api-wallet-request.tsx): resolve the request for // the origin the operating system passed, and create the response to hand back to it. import type { IsoMdocProtocolRequest, IsoMdocResponseOptions, Openid4vpProtocolRequest, Openid4vpResponseOptions, } from '@animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api/request-handler' import type { WalletAgent } from './dc-api-wallet-agent.js' export async function createOpenId4VpResponse( agent: WalletAgent, { protocol, data }: Openid4vpProtocolRequest, origin: string ): Promise<Openid4vpResponseOptions> { // The request arrives as a JSON string const resolved = await agent.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest(JSON.parse(data), { origin }) if (!resolved.dcql?.queryResult.can_be_satisfied) throw new Error('No matching credentials') const { authorizationResponse } = await agent.openid4vc.holder.acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest({ authorizationRequestPayload: resolved.authorizationRequestPayload, dcql: { credentials: agent.openid4vc.holder.selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest(resolved.dcql.queryResult) }, origin, }) // Answer with the protocol of the request return { protocol, data: authorizationResponse } } export async function createIsoMdocResponse( agent: WalletAgent, { data }: IsoMdocProtocolRequest, origin: string ): Promise<IsoMdocResponseOptions> { const resolved = await agent.mdoc.resolveDcApiRequest({ request: data, origin }) if (!resolved.success || resolved.docRequestsAsAlternatives) throw new Error('No matching mdoc') const { response } = await agent.mdoc.createDcApiResponse({ resolvedRequest: resolved, credentials: resolved.docRequests.map(({ docRequestIndex, validCredentials }) => ({ docRequestIndex, record: validCredentials[0].record, })), }) return { protocol: 'org-iso-mdoc', data: { response } } } dc-api-wallet-request.tsx // The request UI of the wallet: the `entry` file of the config plugin. The operating system shows it // when the user picks a credential of this wallet for a website. It's bundled separately from the app, // and on iOS runs in its own process, so it opens the wallet itself. import { type DcApiRequest, registerDcApiScreen } from '@animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api/request-handler' import { useState } from 'react' import { Button, Text, View } from 'react-native' import { initializeWalletAgent } from './dc-api-wallet-agent.js' import { createIsoMdocResponse, createOpenId4VpResponse } from './dc-api-wallet-response.js' function DcApiScreen({ request }: { request: DcApiRequest }) { const [error, setError] = useState<string>() async function share() { // Always use the origin from the operating system. On Android it's undefined when an app asks // for itself instead of a website. const { origin } = request if (!origin) return request.decline('No website origin') const agent = await initializeWalletAgent() try { if (request.platform === 'ios') { // iOS only hands over the request once the user approved, and only as org-iso-mdoc const [isoMdocRequest] = await request.approve() if (!isoMdocRequest) return request.decline('No org-iso-mdoc request') return await request.respond(await createIsoMdocResponse(agent, isoMdocRequest, origin)) } // On Android, the request that the credentials picked in the system picker were matched against const { requests, selection } = request const protocolRequest = requests[selection?.requestIndex ?? selection?.candidateRequestIndexes[0] ?? 0] if (!protocolRequest) return request.decline('No supported protocol') await request.respond( protocolRequest.protocol === 'org-iso-mdoc' ? await createIsoMdocResponse(agent, protocolRequest, origin) : await createOpenId4VpResponse(agent, protocolRequest, origin) ) } catch (shareError) { // The request stays open, so the user can try again or decline setError(shareError instanceof Error ? shareError.message : String(shareError)) } finally { await agent.shutdown() } } return ( <View style={{ flex: 1, gap: 16, padding: 24, backgroundColor: 'white' }}> <Text>{request.origin ?? 'An app'} asks for:</Text> {/* On Android the system picker already showed the credential. iOS has no picker, so show what the operating system parsed from the request. */} {request.platform === 'ios' && request.presentmentRequests .flatMap(({ documentRequestSets }) => documentRequestSets.flatMap((set) => set.documentRequests)) .map(({ doctype, namespaces }) => ( <Text key={doctype}> {doctype}: {Object.values(namespaces).flatMap(Object.keys).join(', ')} </Text> ))} {error && <Text style={{ color: 'red' }}>{error}</Text>} <Button title="Share" onPress={share} /> <Button title="Decline" onPress={() => request.decline()} /> </View> ) } // The entry file registers the screen export default registerDcApiScreen(DcApiScreen)

Building a verifier: the other side of the flow. Presenting credentials: resolve OpenID4VP requests and select credentials. Trusted issuers: decide which issuers, verifiers and readers your wallet trusts. Proximity (ISO 18013-5): present mdocs in person.

DIDComm is a messaging protocol for agents that keep a long-lived, encrypted connection with each other. Once two agents are connected, either side can start a protocol over that connection: issue a credential, request a proof, or send a message. Credo implements DIDComm v1 and the Aries RFCs built on it in @credo-ts/didcomm. This page explains when to use DIDComm and how to set up the module.

Use DIDComm when the parties have an ongoing relationship, because the connection stays usable after the first exchange. It is also the only protocol Credo supports for AnonCreds credentials, and the one other Aries-based agents use. For one-off issuance or verification, and for wallets built for the EU Digital Identity Wallet ecosystem, use OpenID4VC instead. An agent can register both modules. DIDComm OpenID4VC Relationship A connection that either side can use at any time One exchange per offer or request Credential formats AnonCreds, W3C VCs SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C VCs Mobile wallet Needs a mediator to receive messages Calls the issuer and verifier over HTTPS DIDs and DIDComm explains the concepts.

Protocol Aries RFC API Out-of-band 1.1 0434 agent.didcomm.oob DID Exchange 1.1 0023 agent.didcomm.connections Connections 1.0 (deprecated) 0160 agent.didcomm.connections DID Rotate 1.0 0794 agent.didcomm.connections Trust Ping 1.0 0048 agent.didcomm.connections Issue Credential 2.0 0453 agent.didcomm.credentials Issue Credential 1.0 (deprecated) 0036 agent.didcomm.credentials, with DidCommCredentialV1Protocol from @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm Revocation Notification 1.0 and 2.0 0183, 0721 agent.didcomm.credentials Present Proof 2.0 0454 agent.didcomm.proofs Present Proof 1.0 (deprecated) 0037 agent.didcomm.proofs, with DidCommProofV1Protocol from @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm Coordinate Mediation 1.0 0211 agent.didcomm.mediator, agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient Pickup 1.0 and 2.0 0212, 0685 agent.didcomm.messagePickup Discover Features 1.0 and 2.0 0031, 0557 agent.didcomm.discovery Basic Message 1.0 0095 agent.didcomm.basicMessages Action Menu 1.0 0509 @credo-ts/action-menu Question Answer 1.0 0113 @credo-ts/question-answer DIDComm RPC 1.0 0804 @credo-ts/drpc Use DID Exchange and the 2.0 protocols. The deprecated protocols are removed in Credo 0.8, so only use them for agents that support nothing else. Credo doesn't implement DIDComm v2.

npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 On Node.js the inbound transports come from @credo-ts/node, which you install when you set up the agent.

Register a DidCommModule under the key didcomm. Credo only exposes the API as agent.didcomm under that key. Under any other key it is available as agent.modules.<key>. Node.js React Native A server agent listens for incoming messages and advertises the URLs where other agents reach it. agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommConnectionEventTypes, type DidCommConnectionStateChangedEvent, DidCommDidExchangeState, DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommModule, DidCommWsOutboundTransport, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage' import { didcommBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/didcomm' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport, DidCommWsInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs' import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { // Drizzle stores the records. Run its migrations before you start the agent. storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database: drizzle('file:agent.db'), bundles: [didcommBundle] }), // Askar stores the keys: DIDComm needs its XSalsa20-Poly1305 support askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, enableStorage: false, store: { id: 'acme-agent-keys', key: 'acme-agent-store-key' }, }), didcomm: new DidCommModule({ // The public URLs other agents use to reach this agent, in order of preference endpoints: ['http://localhost:4040', 'ws://localhost:4041'], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port: 4040 }), new DidCommWsInboundTransport({ port: 4041 })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport(), new DidCommWsOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() A mobile agent has no public address, so it only sends messages and receives them through a mediator. agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy, DidCommModule, DidCommWsOutboundTransport, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' // The invitation URL your mediator hands out const mediatorInvitationUrl = 'https://mediator.example.com/invite?oob=eyJ...' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: 'wallet-key' }, }), didcomm: new DidCommModule({ // No endpoints and no inbound transports: messages reach the wallet through the mediator transports: { outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, mediationRecipient: { mediatorInvitationUrl, mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode, }, // A wallet doesn't act as a mediator mediator: false, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() The Node.js example stores records with Drizzle, which also explains the packages and migrations it needs, and keys with Askar. DIDComm needs Askar, or another key management backend with XSalsa20-Poly1305, for its keys. See Storage for the options.

endpoints lists the public URLs that go into your invitations and DID documents, in order of preference. Behind a reverse proxy, use the public URL (for example https://agent.example.com/didcomm), not the local port. An agent without endpoints can only receive messages through a mediator, or over a WebSocket it opened itself. Transport Package Platforms DidCommHttpOutboundTransport @credo-ts/didcomm Node.js, React Native DidCommWsOutboundTransport @credo-ts/didcomm Node.js, React Native DidCommHttpInboundTransport @credo-ts/node Node.js DidCommWsInboundTransport @credo-ts/node Node.js DidCommHttpInboundTransport takes a port and an optional path. Pass app instead of port to mount it on an Express app you start yourself. DidCommWsInboundTransport takes a port, or a server (a WebSocketServer from ws). To serve HTTP and WebSocket on one port, give the WebSocket server noServer: true and forward the HTTP server's upgrade events to it, as the sample mediator does.

The connection, out-of-band and discover features protocols are always on. The other protocols are on by default. Pass false to turn one off, which also removes its API from agent.didcomm, or pass an object to configure it. Option Configures Details connections Connections and DID Exchange Connections credentials Issue Credential 2.0 Issuing credentials proofs Present Proof 2.0 Requesting proofs mediator Acting as a mediator Mediation mediationRecipient Using a mediator Mediation messagePickup Pickup 1.0 and 2.0 Mediation basicMessages Basic messages Messaging warning By default, credentials and proofs register the 2.0 protocols without any credential formats, so the agent can't issue or verify anything. Configure the formats you need as described in Issuing credentials and Requesting proofs.

Option Default Description processDidCommMessagesConcurrently false Process incoming messages in parallel instead of one at a time. queueTransportRepository in memory Where messages for agents without an endpoint wait until they are picked up. Mediators need a persistent queue. didCommMimeType DidCommMimeType.V1 Content type for sent messages. DidCommMimeType.V0 (application/ssi-agent-wire) is for older agents. useDidKeyInProtocols true Encode keys as did:key in protocol messages (RFC 0360). useDidSovPrefixWhereAllowed false Use the legacy did:sov:BzCbsNYhMrjHiqZDTUASHg;spec message type prefix for older agents.

Credo emits an event for every state change, such as a connection being completed or a message arriving. Listen with agent.events.on(), and remove the listener with agent.events.off(). agent.events.observable() returns the same events as an RxJS observable. agent.ts agent.events.on<DidCommConnectionStateChangedEvent>( DidCommConnectionEventTypes.DidCommConnectionStateChanged, ({ payload }) => { const { connectionRecord, previousState } = payload console.log(`Connection ${connectionRecord.id}: ${previousState} -> ${connectionRecord.state}`) if (connectionRecord.state === DidCommDidExchangeState.Completed) { console.log(`Connected with ${connectionRecord.theirLabel}`) } } ) The event type enums and payload types are exported from @credo-ts/didcomm. Event type Payload DidCommConnectionEventTypes.DidCommConnectionStateChanged connectionRecord, previousState DidCommOutOfBandEventTypes.OutOfBandStateChanged outOfBandRecord, previousState DidCommCredentialEventTypes.DidCommCredentialStateChanged credentialExchangeRecord, previousState DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged proofRecord, previousState DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes.DidCommBasicMessageStateChanged basicMessageRecord, message DidCommRoutingEventTypes.MediationStateChanged mediationRecord, previousState Each event also has metadata.contextCorrelationId, which tells you which tenant it belongs to when you use multi-tenancy. Connections Create and accept out-of-band invitations, connect agents with DID Exchange, reuse connections and track connection state in Credo. Issuing credentials Issue credentials over DIDComm with the Issue Credential v2 protocol, register credential formats and handle offers, requests and auto-accept. Requesting proofs Request and verify presentations over DIDComm with the Present Proof v2 protocol, using AnonCreds or DIF Presentation Exchange. Mediation Run a DIDComm mediator with Credo and connect mobile agents to it, with message pickup, live delivery and keylist updates. Messaging and other protocols Send basic messages over a DIDComm connection, and add the action menu, question answer and DIDComm RPC protocols to a Credo agent. AnonCreds with DIDComm Issue AnonCreds credentials and request proofs with predicates over DIDComm, and handle revocation. W3C VCs with DIDComm Issue W3C Verifiable Credentials over DIDComm as JSON-LD, Data Integrity or VCDM 2.0 SD-JWT credentials, and present them with DIF Presentation Exchange.
