Issue Credential v2 (Aries RFC 0453) exchanges a credential between two connected DIDComm agents. Format services plug the credential formats into the protocol. This page covers the protocol, with a W3C JSON-LD credential as the example. You need an agent with the DIDComm module and a connection to the other party, see DIDComm and Connections.

DidCommModule enables the credentials module by default, but its Issue Credential v2 protocol has no formats registered, so it can't issue or receive anything. Pass a DidCommCredentialV2Protocol with the format services you need. Both agents must register a format to exchange credentials in it. agent.ts import { Agent, type KeyDidCreateOptions, w3cDate } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommAutoAcceptCredential, DidCommCredentialEventTypes, DidCommCredentialState, type DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent, DidCommCredentialV2Protocol, DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService, DidCommModule, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup didcomm: new DidCommModule({ endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, credentials: { autoAcceptCredentials: DidCommAutoAcceptCredential.ContentApproved, credentialProtocols: [ new DidCommCredentialV2Protocol({ credentialFormats: [new DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService()], }), ], }, }), }, }) } Format Format service Import from Key AnonCreds AnonCredsDidCommCredentialFormatService @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm anoncreds AnonCreds with Hyperledger Indy attachments LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm indy W3C VCDM 1.1 JSON-LD (RFC 0593) DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService @credo-ts/didcomm jsonld W3C VCDM 1.1 and 2.0 Data Integrity (RFC 0809) DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService @credo-ts/didcomm dataIntegrity W3C VCDM 2.0 secured with SD-JWT, vc+sd-jwt (RFC 0881) DidCommW3cV2SdJwtCredentialFormatService @credo-ts/didcomm w3cV2SdJwt The key is the property name you use under credentialFormats in the API calls. The format-specific options are on AnonCreds with DIDComm and W3C VCs with DIDComm. Which format to use depends on the credentials your ecosystem uses and how holders present them: anoncreds for AnonCreds credentials, for example when verifiers need predicates such as "older than 18". Add indy only for agents that don't support anoncreds yet. jsonld for W3C credentials that holders present over DIDComm. w3cV2SdJwt and dataIntegrity with a VCDM 2.0 credential can't be presented over DIDComm. Use them only when holders present elsewhere, see W3C VCs with DIDComm. There is no DIDComm format for SD-JWT VC, mdoc or W3C VCDM 1.1 JWT credentials. Issue those with OpenID4VC.

Usually the issuer starts with an offer. The holder can also start with a proposal, and either side can answer with a counter-proposal or counter-offer (negotiateOffer, negotiateProposal). Each agent tracks the exchange in a DidCommCredentialExchangeRecord, and emits an event whenever its state changes.

Issuer issuer.ts await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({ connectionId, protocolVersion: 'v2', credentialFormats: { jsonld: { credential: { '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json'], type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'OpenBadgeCredential'], issuer: issuerDid, issuanceDate: w3cDate(), credentialSubject: { id: holderDid, type: ['AchievementSubject'], achievement: { id: 'https://example.com/achievements/credo-docs', type: ['Achievement'], name: 'Read the Credo docs', }, }, }, options: { proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod' }, }, }, }) protocolVersion: 'v2' selects Issue Credential v2, and credentialFormats holds the format data. Here the issuer is a did:key created in the issuer's agent, and credentialSubject.id is the holder's DID. W3C VCs with DIDComm explains the JSON-LD options. To offer a credential without an existing connection, create the offer with createOffer and attach the returned message to an out-of-band invitation with agent.didcomm.oob.createInvitation({ messages: [message] }). The holder then connects first and receives the offer over the new connection. Add handshake: false to run the exchange connectionless.

The holder listens for state changes. When an offer arrives, show it to the user, then accept it to send a credential request. Holder holder.ts async function onCredentialStateChanged({ payload: { credentialExchangeRecord } }: DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent) { if (credentialExchangeRecord.state === DidCommCredentialState.OfferReceived) { // Show the offer to the user before accepting it const { offer } = await holder.didcomm.credentials.getFormatData(credentialExchangeRecord.id) console.log('Received offer', JSON.stringify(offer?.jsonld?.credential)) await holder.didcomm.credentials.acceptOffer({ credentialExchangeRecordId: credentialExchangeRecord.id }) } if (credentialExchangeRecord.state === DidCommCredentialState.Done) { const [{ credentialRecordId }] = credentialExchangeRecord.credentials const w3cCredentialRecord = await holder.w3cCredentials.getById(credentialRecordId) console.log('Stored credential', w3cCredentialRecord.firstCredential.type) } } holder.events.on(DidCommCredentialEventTypes.DidCommCredentialStateChanged, onCredentialStateChanged) getFormatData returns the offer per format. declineOffer rejects it, and with sendProblemReport: true it tells the issuer. When the credential arrives, the format service verifies and stores it before the exchange completes. credentialExchangeRecord.credentials lists the stored records: credentialRecordType is w3c for W3C VCDM 1.1 and AnonCreds credentials, and w3c-v2 for VCDM 2.0 SD-JWT credentials. W3C VCs with DIDComm covers the exception for Data Integrity VCDM 2.0 credentials. Deleting the exchange record with agent.didcomm.credentials.deleteById also deletes the stored credential, unless you pass deleteAssociatedCredentials: false.

The holder proposes the credential it wants, in the same shape as an offer: Holder holder.ts await holder.didcomm.credentials.proposeCredential({ connectionId: connectionRecord.id, protocolVersion: 'v2', credentialFormats: { jsonld: { credential: { '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json'], type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'OpenBadgeCredential'], issuer: issuerDid, issuanceDate: w3cDate(), credentialSubject: { id: holderDid, type: ['AchievementSubject'], achievement: { id: 'https://example.com/achievements/credo-docs', type: ['Achievement'], name: 'Read the Credo docs', }, }, }, options: { proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod' }, }, }, }) The issuer accepts the proposal, which sends an offer with the proposed content. To offer something else, call negotiateProposal instead. Issuer issuer.ts if (credentialExchangeRecord.state === DidCommCredentialState.ProposalReceived) { await issuer.didcomm.credentials.acceptProposal({ credentialExchangeRecordId: credentialExchangeRecord.id }) } With ContentApproved auto-accept on both sides, the rest of this exchange runs by itself: the offer matches the proposal, the request matches the offer, and the credential matches the request.

Set autoAcceptCredentials on the credentials module, or autoAcceptCredential on a single API call (it then applies to that exchange). DidCommAutoAcceptCredential Behaviour Never (default) Every step needs an API call: acceptOffer, acceptRequest, acceptCredential, and so on. ContentApproved After one manual approval, Credo continues as long as each message matches the previous one. An offer that doesn't answer your own proposal always needs acceptOffer. Always Credo answers every message, including offers from any connection. For an issuer, ContentApproved is a good default: creating the offer is the approval, and Credo issues when the request matches it. Proposals still wait for acceptProposal. For a wallet, ContentApproved keeps the user in control: offers wait for acceptOffer, and Credo sends the ack when the credential arrives. Don't use Always on either side: an issuer would issue whatever a holder proposes, and a wallet would accept every offer.

Listen to DidCommCredentialEventTypes.DidCommCredentialStateChanged. The payload has the credentialExchangeRecord and its previousState. DidCommCredentialState Agent Next step ProposalSent holder wait for the offer ProposalReceived issuer acceptProposal or negotiateProposal OfferSent issuer wait for the request OfferReceived holder acceptOffer, declineOffer or negotiateOffer RequestSent holder wait for the credential RequestReceived issuer acceptRequest issues the credential CredentialIssued issuer wait for the ack CredentialReceived holder the credential is stored, acceptCredential sends the ack Done both Declined holder Abandoned both the exchange failed, errorMessage says why Query exchanges with agent.didcomm.credentials.findAllByQuery({ state, connectionId }).

Deprecated Issue Credential v1 (Aries RFC 0036) is deprecated and removed in Credo 0.8. Use v2 unless the other agent only supports v1. Issue Credential v1 only carries AnonCreds credentials in the indy format. Register it next to v2, and pass protocolVersion: 'v1' in the API calls: import { DidCommCredentialV1Protocol, LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm' const credentialProtocol = new DidCommCredentialV1Protocol({ indyCredentialFormat: new LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService(), })

A mediator is an agent that receives messages on behalf of agents that can't be reached directly, and holds them until they are picked up. This page covers running a mediator, connecting an agent to it as a recipient, choosing a pickup strategy, and how routing keys stay in sync.

An agent needs a mediator when other agents can't reach it. A mobile wallet always needs one when it uses DIDComm: a phone has no public address, and the app is often closed. A server agent with public endpoints doesn't need one. A wallet with a mediator puts the mediator's endpoint and routing key in its invitations and DID documents. Senders wrap their messages in a forward message to the mediator, and the mediator delivers them to the wallet over a WebSocket, or queues them until the wallet picks them up. Credo implements Coordinate Mediation 1.0 and message pickup (Pickup 1.0 and 2.0) for both roles. Messages from a wallet to other agents don't go through its mediator.

A mediator is a Node.js agent with the mediator protocol turned on. It needs an HTTP endpoint for senders and a WebSocket endpoint so wallets can receive messages live. mediator.ts import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes, DidCommBasicMessageRole, type DidCommBasicMessageStateChangedEvent, DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, type DidCommKeylistUpdatedEvent, DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy, DidCommModule, DidCommRoutingEventTypes, DidCommWsOutboundTransport, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport, DidCommWsInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' const mediator = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...mediatorStorage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup didcomm: new DidCommModule({ endpoints: ['http://localhost:4040', 'ws://localhost:4041'], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port: 4040 }), new DidCommWsInboundTransport({ port: 4041 })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport(), new DidCommWsOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, mediator: { autoAcceptMediationRequests: true }, // A mediator only routes messages, so it doesn't need the other protocols mediationRecipient: false, credentials: false, proofs: false, basicMessages: false, }), }, }) await mediator.initialize() const mediatorOutOfBandRecord = await mediator.didcomm.oob.createInvitation({ label: 'Mediator', multiUseInvitation: true, }) const mediatorInvitationUrl = mediatorOutOfBandRecord.outOfBandInvitation.toUrl({ domain: 'http://localhost:4040/invite', }) The mediator shares one multi-use invitation with all wallets. Without autoAcceptMediationRequests, listen for DidCommRoutingEventTypes.MediationStateChanged and grant requests in the requested state with agent.didcomm.mediator.grantRequestedMediation(mediationRecordId). Option Default Description mediator.autoAcceptMediationRequests false Grant every mediation request. mediator.messageForwardingStrategy DirectDelivery DirectDelivery sends a forwarded message right away over an open session with the recipient, and queues it if that isn't possible. QueueOnly always queues. QueueAndLiveModeDelivery queues, then delivers the queue to recipients in live mode. messagePickup.maximumBatchSize 10 Maximum number of messages per pickup batch. queueTransportRepository in memory Where queued messages are stored. Pass a persistent implementation in production, or messages are lost on restart. For production, look at DIDComm Mediator Credo, a mediator built on Credo with a persistent message queue and a Docker image.

On the recipient, set mediatorInvitationUrl in the mediationRecipient options: Node.js React Native wallet.ts const alice = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...aliceStorage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup didcomm: new DidCommModule({ transports: { outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, mediationRecipient: { mediatorInvitationUrl, mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode, }, mediator: false, }), }, }) // Connects to the mediator, requests mediation and starts message pickup await alice.initialize() agent.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy, DidCommModule, DidCommWsOutboundTransport, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' // The invitation URL your mediator hands out const mediatorInvitationUrl = 'https://mediator.example.com/invite?oob=eyJ...' const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: 'wallet-key' }, }), didcomm: new DidCommModule({ // No endpoints and no inbound transports: messages reach the wallet through the mediator transports: { outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, mediationRecipient: { mediatorInvitationUrl, mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode, }, // A wallet doesn't act as a mediator mediator: false, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy is exported from @credo-ts/didcomm. Pickup strategies explains the options. During initialize(), Credo connects to the mediator if it isn't connected yet, requests mediation, waits for the grant and sets the mediator as the default. Then it starts picking up messages. Startup therefore depends on the mediator being reachable. To keep startup independent, leave out mediatorInvitationUrl and connect later with the API: Method on agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient Description provision(connection) Request mediation over a connection, wait for the grant, and set the mediator as default. initiateMessagePickup(mediator?, strategy?) Start picking up messages, from the default mediator unless you pass a mediation record. stopMessagePickup() Stop all message pickup. findDefaultMediator() Get the mediation record of the default mediator. setDefaultMediator(mediationRecord) Change the default mediator. Once a default mediator is set, new invitations and connections route through it without extra code: wallet.ts // The invitation points to the mediator's endpoint and routing keys const outOfBandRecord = await alice.didcomm.oob.createInvitation({ label: 'Alice' }) const invitationUrl = outOfBandRecord.outOfBandInvitation.toUrl({ domain: 'https://alice.example.com' }) To use another mediator for one connection, create routing with agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient.getRouting({ mediatorId }) and pass it as routing to createInvitation() or receiveInvitation().

mediatorPickupStrategy decides how the recipient gets its messages: Strategy How it works PickUpV2LiveMode Opens a WebSocket, picks up queued messages, then asks the mediator to push new messages as they arrive (Pickup 2.0 live mode). PickUpV2 Polls with Pickup 2.0 every mediatorPollingInterval milliseconds. PickUpV1 Polls with Pickup 1.0 every mediatorPollingInterval milliseconds. Implicit Opens a WebSocket and keeps it open, so the mediator can send messages over it. None Doesn't pick up messages automatically. For a mobile wallet, use PickUpV2LiveMode: messages arrive as soon as the mediator receives them, and Credo reopens the WebSocket when it drops. It needs a WebSocket endpoint on the mediator and DidCommWsOutboundTransport on the wallet. Use PickUpV2 if the mediator has no WebSocket endpoint, and Implicit for mediators that don't support a pickup protocol. Without a strategy, Credo asks the mediator which pickup protocols it supports and uses PickUpV2, PickUpV1 or Implicit, in that order. It never chooses live mode on its own. Credo stores the choice on the mediation record, and the stored choice wins over mediatorPickupStrategy from then on, so set the strategy before the agent first connects to the mediator. Option Default Description mediatorPollingInterval 5000 Milliseconds between polls for PickUpV1 and PickUpV2. maximumMessagePickup 10 Messages per batch when polling. baseMediatorReconnectionIntervalMs 100 First delay before reconnecting a closed WebSocket. It doubles after each attempt. maximumMediatorReconnectionIntervalMs no limit Longest delay between reconnection attempts.

A mobile app usually stops pickup when it goes to the background and starts it again when it returns: wallet.ts // For example when the app goes to the background await alice.didcomm.mediationRecipient.stopMessagePickup() // Back in the foreground: picks up queued messages, then resumes live delivery await alice.didcomm.mediationRecipient.initiateMessagePickup() If you'd rather decide when pickup runs, set mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.None and pass the strategy when you start it: initiateMessagePickup(undefined, DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode). To fetch queued messages once, for example in a background task, use the message pickup API and wait until the messages are processed: wallet.ts const mediatorConnection = await alice.didcomm.mediationRecipient.findDefaultMediatorConnection() if (mediatorConnection) { await alice.didcomm.messagePickup.pickupMessages({ connectionId: mediatorConnection.id, protocolVersion: 'v2', awaitCompletion: true, }) }

The mediator only forwards messages for keys in the recipient's keylist. Credo keeps the keylist up to date: every time it creates routing through a mediator, for a new invitation, connection or DID rotation, it adds the new key and waits for the mediator to confirm. Deleting a connection with connections.deleteById(), or with connections.hangup({ connectionId, deleteAfterHangup: true }), removes its keys again. After a DID rotation, connections.removePreviousDids({ connectionId }) removes the old keys. Each confirmed update emits an event: wallet.ts alice.events.on<DidCommKeylistUpdatedEvent>(DidCommRoutingEventTypes.RecipientKeylistUpdated, ({ payload }) => { for (const update of payload.keylist) { console.log(`Mediator keylist update: ${update.action} ${update.recipientKey}`) } }) For keys created outside of Credo's routing, send the update yourself with agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient.notifyKeylistUpdate(connection, verkey, action).

Besides credentials and proofs, two connected agents can exchange plain text messages, menus, questions and remote procedure calls. Basic messages are built into @credo-ts/didcomm. The other three protocols come in separate packages. All examples on this page assume an Acme and a Bob agent with a connection between them.

Basic Message sends a text message over a connection, like a chat. The protocol is on by default. acme.ts await acme.didcomm.basicMessages.sendMessage(acmeToBob.id, 'Your order has shipped') The receiving agent stores the message and emits an event: bob.ts bob.events.on<DidCommBasicMessageStateChangedEvent>( DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes.DidCommBasicMessageStateChanged, ({ payload: { basicMessageRecord } }) => { // The event fires for sent and received messages if (basicMessageRecord.role !== DidCommBasicMessageRole.Receiver) return console.log(`Bob received: ${basicMessageRecord.content}`) } ) Every message, sent or received, is stored as a DidCommBasicMessageRecord with content, sentTime, role and connectionId. To load the history of a connection: bob.ts const history = await bob.didcomm.basicMessages.findAllByQuery({ connectionId: bobToAcme.id }) sendMessage() takes a thread id as third argument, to link the message to another thread with ~thread.pthid. To turn the protocol off, pass basicMessages: false to the DidCommModule.

Package Protocol Use it for @credo-ts/question-answer Question Answer 1.0 Asking a question with a fixed set of answers. @credo-ts/action-menu Action Menu 1.0 Offering a menu of actions that the other agent can choose from. @credo-ts/drpc DIDComm RPC 1.0 Sending JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and responses. Install the packages you need: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ @credo-ts/question-answer@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/action-menu@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drpc@^0.7.2 pnpm add \ @credo-ts/question-answer@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/action-menu@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drpc@^0.7.2 yarn add \ @credo-ts/question-answer@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/action-menu@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drpc@^0.7.2 bun add \ @credo-ts/question-answer@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/action-menu@^0.7.2 \ @credo-ts/drpc@^0.7.2 Register each one as an agent module next to the DidCommModule. Both agents in a conversation need the module. Its API is available under the key you register it with, for example agent.modules.questionAnswer. agent.ts import { ActionMenu, ActionMenuEventTypes, ActionMenuModule, ActionMenuRole, ActionMenuState, type ActionMenuStateChangedEvent, } from '@credo-ts/action-menu' import type { BaseEvent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes, DidCommBasicMessageRole, type DidCommBasicMessageStateChangedEvent, DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommModule, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { DrpcModule } from '@credo-ts/drpc' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' import { QuestionAnswerEventTypes, QuestionAnswerModule, QuestionAnswerState, type QuestionAnswerStateChangedEvent, } from '@credo-ts/question-answer' function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup didcomm: new DidCommModule({ endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, }), // Each package adds its API under the key you choose: agent.modules.actionMenu, ... actionMenu: new ActionMenuModule(), questionAnswer: new QuestionAnswerModule(), drpc: new DrpcModule(), }, }) }

The questioner sends a question with the answers it accepts. The responder picks one of them. acme.ts await acme.modules.questionAnswer.sendQuestion(acmeToBob.id, { question: 'Do you want to receive your membership credential?', detail: 'We will issue it right after you answer.', validResponses: [{ text: 'Yes' }, { text: 'No' }], }) The responder answers when the question arrives, and the questioner reads the answer from the record: bob.ts and acme.ts bob.events.on<QuestionAnswerStateChangedEvent>( QuestionAnswerEventTypes.QuestionAnswerStateChanged, async ({ payload: { questionAnswerRecord } }) => { if (questionAnswerRecord.state !== QuestionAnswerState.QuestionReceived) return console.log(`Acme asks: ${questionAnswerRecord.questionText}`) await bob.modules.questionAnswer.sendAnswer(questionAnswerRecord.id, 'Yes') } ) acme.events.on<QuestionAnswerStateChangedEvent>( QuestionAnswerEventTypes.QuestionAnswerStateChanged, ({ payload: { questionAnswerRecord } }) => { if (questionAnswerRecord.state !== QuestionAnswerState.AnswerReceived) return console.log(`Bob answered: ${questionAnswerRecord.response}`) } ) sendAnswer() throws if the response isn't one of the validResponses.

The responder sends a menu, the requester chooses an option, and the responder acts on the choice, for example by offering a credential. The requester can also ask for the menu with requestMenu({ connectionId }). acme.ts await acme.modules.actionMenu.sendMenu({ connectionId: acmeToBob.id, menu: new ActionMenu({ title: 'Acme services', description: 'What would you like to do?', options: [ { name: 'get-membership', title: 'Get a membership credential', description: 'Issue a new credential' }, { name: 'contact', title: 'Contact support', description: 'Start a chat with Acme' }, ], }), }) The requester shows the menu and performs the chosen action. The responder receives the selection in performedAction: bob.ts and acme.ts bob.events.on<ActionMenuStateChangedEvent>( ActionMenuEventTypes.ActionMenuStateChanged, async ({ payload: { actionMenuRecord } }) => { if (actionMenuRecord.state !== ActionMenuState.PreparingSelection || !actionMenuRecord.menu) return // A wallet would show the menu and let the user pick an option const [firstOption] = actionMenuRecord.menu.options await bob.modules.actionMenu.performAction({ connectionId: actionMenuRecord.connectionId, performedAction: { name: firstOption.name }, }) } ) acme.events.on<ActionMenuStateChangedEvent>( ActionMenuEventTypes.ActionMenuStateChanged, ({ payload: { actionMenuRecord } }) => { if (actionMenuRecord.role !== ActionMenuRole.Responder || actionMenuRecord.state !== ActionMenuState.Done) return console.log(`Bob selected: ${actionMenuRecord.performedAction?.name}`) } ) An option can include a form with parameters. The requester then sends the values as params in the selection. findActiveMenu({ connectionId, role }) returns the current menu of a connection, and clearActiveMenu({ connectionId, role }) removes it. By default the module checks the state of the menu before each step. Pass new ActionMenuModule({ strictStateChecking: false }) to skip that check.

DIDComm RPC carries JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and responses over a connection. The server waits for a request and answers it: acme.ts async function handleNextRequest() { const incoming = await acme.modules.drpc.recvRequest() // Batch requests arrive as an array if (!incoming || Array.isArray(incoming.request)) return const { request, sendResponse } = incoming if (request.method === 'getOrderStatus') { await sendResponse({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: request.id, result: { status: 'shipped' } }) } else { await sendResponse({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: request.id, error: { code: -32601, message: 'Method not found' } }) } } // Start listening before the request can arrive const handledRequest = handleNextRequest() The client sends a request and gets a function that waits for the response: bob.ts const waitForResponse = await bob.modules.drpc.sendRequest(bobToAcme.id, { jsonrpc: '2.0', method: 'getOrderStatus', params: { orderId: '1234' }, id: 1, }) // Resolves to undefined if no response arrives within 5000 ms const response = await waitForResponse(5000) recvRequest() only returns the next request that arrives after you call it, from any connection. Call it again for every request you want to handle. Both recvRequest() and the function returned by sendRequest() take an optional timeout in milliseconds and resolve to undefined when it expires.

Present Proof v2 (Aries RFC 0454) lets a verifier request a presentation from a connected holder and verify it. Like issuance, the protocol relies on format services for the request and presentation. This page shows the protocol with DIF Presentation Exchange and a W3C JSON-LD credential. You need an agent with the DIDComm module and a connection, see DIDComm and Connections.

The proofs module that DidCommModule enables by default runs Present Proof v2 without formats. Pass a DidCommProofV2Protocol with the format services you need, on both the verifier and the holder. agent.ts import { Agent, type KeyDidCreateOptions, w3cDate } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommAutoAcceptCredential, DidCommCredentialEventTypes, DidCommCredentialState, type DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent, DidCommCredentialV2Protocol, DidCommDifPresentationExchangeProofFormatService, DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService, DidCommModule, DidCommProofEventTypes, DidCommProofState, type DidCommProofStateChangedEvent, DidCommProofV2Protocol, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup didcomm: new DidCommModule({ endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, credentials: { credentialProtocols: [ new DidCommCredentialV2Protocol({ credentialFormats: [new DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService()] }), ], }, proofs: { proofProtocols: [ new DidCommProofV2Protocol({ proofFormats: [new DidCommDifPresentationExchangeProofFormatService()], }), ], }, }), }, }) } Format Format service Import from Key Presents AnonCreds AnonCredsDidCommProofFormatService @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm anoncreds AnonCreds credentials AnonCreds with Hyperledger Indy attachments LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService @credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm indy AnonCreds credentials DIF Presentation Exchange (RFC 0510) DidCommDifPresentationExchangeProofFormatService @credo-ts/didcomm presentationExchange W3C VCDM 1.1 credentials as JSON-LD (ldp_vp) or JWT (jwt_vp) presentations, and AnonCreds credentials issued in W3C format Use anoncreds for AnonCreds credentials and presentationExchange for W3C credentials. Present Proof doesn't support SD-JWT VC, mdoc or W3C VCDM 2.0 credentials, including the VCDM 2.0 credentials you can receive over DIDComm. Present SD-JWT VC, mdoc and VCDM 2.0 SD-JWT credentials with OpenID4VC instead. The Presentation Exchange format uses version 1 presentation definitions, which need a schema on each input descriptor.

The verifier usually starts with a request. The holder can also propose what it wants to share with proposeProof, and the verifier answers with acceptProposal. Both sides track the exchange in a DidCommProofExchangeRecord.

Verifier verifier.ts await verifier.didcomm.proofs.requestProof({ connectionId, protocolVersion: 'v2', proofFormats: { presentationExchange: { presentationDefinition: { id: 'credo-docs-badge', input_descriptors: [ { id: 'open-badge', schema: [{ uri: 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json' }], constraints: { fields: [ { path: ['$.credentialSubject.achievement.name'], filter: { type: 'string', const: 'Read the Credo docs' }, }, ], }, }, ], }, }, }, }) Credo looks up candidate credentials by the schema URI, which matches a JSON-LD context or an expanded type of the credential. The constraints then filter on the credential's content with JSONPath and JSON Schema. Credo adds a random challenge to the request, which the holder signs, unless you set options.challenge yourself. To request a proof without a connection, create it with createRequest and attach the returned message to an out-of-band invitation, with handshake: false to skip creating a connection.

Holder holder.ts holder.events.on<DidCommProofStateChangedEvent>( DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged, async ({ payload: { proofRecord } }) => { if (proofRecord.state !== DidCommProofState.RequestReceived) return // Picks the first matching credential for every requested item const { proofFormats } = await holder.didcomm.proofs.selectCredentialsForRequest({ proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id, }) await holder.didcomm.proofs.acceptRequest({ proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id, proofFormats }) } ) selectCredentialsForRequest picks the first matching credential for each requested item and throws if something can't be satisfied. To let the user choose, call getCredentialsForRequest, which lists all candidates per item, and pass the chosen credentials in proofFormats to acceptRequest. declineRequest rejects the request. The holder signs a JSON-LD or JWT presentation with an authentication key of the DID in credentialSubject.id, so that DID must be one the holder created in its agent.

The verifier verifies the presentation as soon as it arrives. A valid presentation moves the exchange to PresentationReceived with isVerified: true. An invalid one moves it to Abandoned, sets errorMessage and sends a problem report to the holder. Verifier verifier.ts verifier.events.on<DidCommProofStateChangedEvent>( DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged, async ({ payload: { proofRecord } }) => { if (proofRecord.state === DidCommProofState.PresentationReceived) { // Only valid presentations reach this state, so `proofRecord.isVerified` is true const { presentation } = await verifier.didcomm.proofs.getFormatData(proofRecord.id) console.log('Verified presentation', JSON.stringify(presentation?.presentationExchange)) // Sends the ack and completes the exchange await verifier.didcomm.proofs.acceptPresentation({ proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id }) } if (proofRecord.state === DidCommProofState.Abandoned) { console.log('Verification failed', proofRecord.errorMessage) } } ) Verification covers the signatures, the challenge, holder binding and whether the presentation satisfies the request. Which issuers you trust is up to you: restrict them in the request (for AnonCreds with restrictions), configure trusted issuers for W3C credentials, or check the issuer in the format data. acceptPresentation sends the ack and completes the exchange. With ContentApproved auto-accept, Credo sends the ack for you, so leave that call out.

Set autoAcceptProofs on the proofs module, or autoAcceptProof on a single API call. DidCommAutoAcceptProof Behaviour Never (default) Every step needs an API call: acceptRequest, acceptPresentation, and so on. ContentApproved The holder answers a request automatically only when it matches the holder's own proposal. The verifier acknowledges valid presentations automatically. Always The holder answers every request with automatically selected credentials, without asking the user. The verifier only acknowledges automatically when the request had willConfirm set, which is the default. For a verifier, ContentApproved saves the acceptPresentation call. For a wallet, use ContentApproved or Never, so the user approves each request. Always shares credentials without asking the user.

Listen to DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged. The payload has the proofRecord and its previousState. DidCommProofState Agent Next step ProposalSent holder wait for the request ProposalReceived verifier acceptProposal or negotiateProposal RequestSent verifier wait for the presentation RequestReceived holder acceptRequest, declineRequest or negotiateRequest PresentationSent holder wait for the ack PresentationReceived verifier the presentation is valid, acceptPresentation sends the ack Done both Declined holder Abandoned both the exchange failed, errorMessage says why agent.didcomm.proofs.getFormatData(proofRecordId) returns the proposal, request and presentation per format.

Deprecated Present Proof v1 (Aries RFC 0037) is deprecated and removed in Credo 0.8. Use v2 unless the other agent only supports v1. Present Proof v1 only carries AnonCreds proofs in the indy format. Register it next to v2, and pass protocolVersion: 'v1' in the API calls: import { DidCommProofV1Protocol, LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm' const proofProtocol = new DidCommProofV1Protocol({ indyProofFormat: new LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService(), })

Credo issues W3C Verifiable Credentials over DIDComm with three credential formats, and presents VCDM 1.1 credentials with DIF Presentation Exchange. This page covers the options and limits of each format. The protocol flow itself is on Issuing credentials and Requesting proofs, and the credential model on W3C Verifiable Credentials.

Format key Spec Credential Holder binding Stored as Present over DIDComm jsonld RFC 0593 VCDM 1.1 with an Ed25519 Linked Data signature DID in credentialSubject.id W3cCredentialRecord yes, as ldp_vp dataIntegrity RFC 0809 VCDM 1.1 with a Linked Data signature, or VCDM 2.0 with a Data Integrity proof signed nonce, AnonCreds link secret, or DID in credentialSubject.id VCDM 1.1: W3cCredentialRecord, VCDM 2.0: W3cV2CredentialRecord VCDM 1.1 only w3cV2SdJwt RFC 0881 VCDM 2.0 secured with SD-JWT (vc+sd-jwt) signed nonce, as cnf W3cV2CredentialRecord no vc+sd-jwt here is a W3C VCDM 2.0 credential secured with SD-JWT, not an IETF SD-JWT VC (dc+sd-jwt). There is no DIDComm format for SD-JWT VC, mdoc or VCDM 1.1 JWT credentials. Use jsonld when holders present the credential over DIDComm. Use w3cV2SdJwt for VCDM 2.0 credentials with selective disclosure, which holders present with OpenID4VP. Use dataIntegrity for AnonCreds credentials in W3C format, or for agents that only support RFC 0809.

Register the formats you need on both agents: agent.ts import { Agent, DidKey, type KeyDidCreateOptions, w3cDate } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DidCommAutoAcceptCredential, DidCommCredentialEventTypes, DidCommCredentialState, type DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent, DidCommCredentialV2Protocol, DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService, DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService, DidCommModule, DidCommW3cV2SdJwtCredentialFormatService, } from '@credo-ts/didcomm' import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node' function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) { return new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup didcomm: new DidCommModule({ endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`], transports: { inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })], outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()], }, connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true }, credentials: { autoAcceptCredentials: DidCommAutoAcceptCredential.ContentApproved, credentialProtocols: [ new DidCommCredentialV2Protocol({ credentialFormats: [ new DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService(), new DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService(), new DidCommW3cV2SdJwtCredentialFormatService(), ], }), ], }, }), }, }) } The issuer signs with a key of a DID it created in its own agent, for example a did:key: Issuer issuer.ts const { didState } = await issuer.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({ method: 'key', options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } }, }) if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the issuer DID failed') const issuerDid = didState.did

Issuer issuer.ts await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({ connectionId, protocolVersion: 'v2', credentialFormats: { jsonld: { credential: { '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json'], type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'OpenBadgeCredential'], issuer: issuerDid, issuanceDate: w3cDate(), credentialSubject: { id: holderDid, type: ['AchievementSubject'], achievement: { id: 'https://example.com/achievements/credo-docs', type: ['Achievement'], name: 'Read the Credo docs', }, }, }, // did:key Ed25519 keys are Ed25519VerificationKey2018 verification methods options: { proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod' }, }, }, }) The holder accepts the offer without format options, and stores the credential as a W3cCredentialRecord. Credo signs with Ed25519Signature2018 or Ed25519Signature2020, so the issuer needs an Ed25519 key. Each suite only accepts its own verification method type: a did:key has Ed25519VerificationKey2018 methods, so use Ed25519Signature2018, with proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod'. Credo signs with the first verification method of the issuer DID that fits the proof type. Pass jsonld: { verificationMethod } to acceptRequest to choose another. Every @context must resolve. Credo bundles common contexts, such as the VC data model, the security suites, Open Badges 3.0 and schema.org, and fetches others over the network. W3C Verifiable Credentials shows how to add your own. Don't add credentialStatus. Credo can't check W3C credential status, so the holder fails to verify such a credential. The holder proves control of the DID in credentialSubject.id when it presents the credential. To learn the holder's DID, let the holder start with a proposal that contains it.

Present JSON-LD credentials, and VCDM 1.1 Data Integrity credentials, with the DIF Presentation Exchange format, as shown on Requesting proofs. The holder signs an ldp_vp presentation with an authentication key of the DID in credentialSubject.id. VCDM 1.1 JWT credentials you received another way, such as with OpenID4VC, can be presented as jwt_vp.

The RFC 0881 format issues a VCDM 2.0 credential secured with SD-JWT, with selectively disclosable claims. It needs @credo-ts/didcomm 0.7.2 or later. Issuer issuer.ts await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({ connectionId, protocolVersion: 'v2', credentialFormats: { w3cV2SdJwt: { credential: { '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/ns/credentials/v2'], type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'EmployeeCredential'], issuer: issuerDid, validFrom: w3cDate(), credentialSubject: { name: 'Jane Doe', role: 'Developer' }, }, disclosureFrame: { credentialSubject: { _sd: ['name', 'role'] } }, // The holder proves control of a DID, which becomes the credential subject and `cnf` bindingRequired: true, didCommSignedAttachmentBinding: {}, }, }, }) credential is a VCDM 2.0 credential without proof. You can leave out issuer and pass it to acceptRequest instead. disclosureFrame lists the claims the holder can disclose selectively. @context, type, credentialStatus, credentialSchema and relatedResource can't be selectively disclosable at the top level. With bindingRequired and didCommSignedAttachmentBinding, the holder must sign a nonce with a key of one of its DIDs. Restrict the accepted keys with didMethodsSupported and algsSupported. Without binding, anyone who has the credential can present it, so require binding unless you want a bearer credential. Auto-accept can't answer an offer that requires binding. The holder calls acceptOffer and picks the key: Holder holder.ts await holder.didcomm.credentials.acceptOffer({ credentialExchangeRecordId: credentialExchangeRecord.id, credentialFormats: { // Signs the issuer's nonce with this key, the issuer binds the credential to it w3cV2SdJwt: { didCommSignedAttachment: { kid: holderKid } }, }, }) The issuer sets the holder's DID as credentialSubject.id and the key as cnf, signs the credential and sends it. With ContentApproved this happens automatically. Otherwise call acceptRequest, where you can also set alg, issuerVerificationMethod, disclosureFrame or credentialSubjectId. The holder verifies the credential, checks that it matches the offer and stores it as a W3cV2CredentialRecord. The exchange always starts with an offer: proposals and holder-initiated requests aren't supported. Holders can't present these credentials over DIDComm. They present them with OpenID4VP.

The RFC 0809 format issues VCDM 1.1 and 2.0 credentials. The first @context entry decides the data model. Issuer issuer.ts await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({ connectionId, protocolVersion: 'v2', credentialFormats: { dataIntegrity: { credential: { '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/ns/credentials/v2'], type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'EmployeeCredential'], issuer: issuerDid, validFrom: w3cDate(), credentialSubject: { id: holderDid, name: 'Jane Doe', role: 'Developer' }, }, bindingRequired: false, }, }, }) A VCDM 1.1 credential gets a Linked Data signature, as with the JSON-LD format. A VCDM 2.0 credential gets a Data Integrity proof with eddsa-jcs-2022, the only cryptosuite Credo registers, so the issuer needs an Ed25519 key. The exchange always starts with an offer. Binding with didCommSignedAttachmentBinding works as in the RFC 0881 format, but the issuer doesn't derive credentialSubject.id from it. Put the holder's DID in the offer, or pass credentialSubjectId to acceptRequest; without a subject id, auto-accept doesn't issue the credential. The anonCredsLinkSecretBinding option issues AnonCreds credentials in W3C format, see AnonCreds with DIDComm. @credo-ts/anoncreds also exports this service as DataIntegrityDidCommCredentialFormatService. That alias is deprecated and removed in 0.8: import DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService from @credo-ts/didcomm. For VCDM 2.0 credentials: Credo doesn't check the holder's binding proof. Put the holder's DID in credentialSubject.id instead. The holder stores the credential as a W3cV2CredentialRecord, but the exchange record lists it with credentialRecordType: 'w3c'. Look it up with agent.w3cV2Credentials.getById. The credential can't be presented over DIDComm or OpenID4VC.

ISO/IEC 18013-5 defines the mdoc, the credential format of the mobile driving licence (mDL), together with a protocol to present it in person. ISO/IEC TS 18013-7 adds presentation over the internet, and its Annex C defines org-iso-mdoc for the W3C Digital Credentials API. These protocols carry only mdocs. This page explains how an mdoc presentation works, how it differs from OpenID4VP, and what Credo does for each. For the format, see mdoc. To issue mdocs, or to present them over OpenID4VP, see mdoc with OpenID4VC.

The wallet holds the mdoc, and the verifier is called the mdoc reader. A presentation has these parts: Part What it is Device engagement Only in proximity. The wallet shows a QR code, or answers an NFC tap, with an ephemeral key and the transports it supports. The reader answers with its own ephemeral key, and both derive session keys that encrypt the rest of the exchange. Device request Per document type, the data elements the reader wants and whether it keeps them (intent to retain). The reader can sign each document request with its certificate (reader authentication), so the wallet can show who is asking. Device response The disclosed data elements as the issuer signed them, and a signature over the session transcript made with the device key the mdoc is bound to. Session transcript Never sent. Both sides derive it from the session: from the engagement in proximity, from the website's origin and the encryption parameters with the Digital Credentials API. The device signature covers it, so a response is only valid in the session it was made for.

Credo supports two ways to present an mdoc with these protocols: Proximity Digital Credentials API Standard ISO/IEC 18013-5 ISO/IEC TS 18013-7 Annex C Use In person, for example at a counter or a gate A website, through the browser and the operating system Started by The reader scanning a QR code, or an NFC tap The page calling navigator.credentials.get() with protocol org-iso-mdoc Transport BLE, NFC or Wi-Fi Aware The browser and the operating system Encryption Session keys from the engagement The response is encrypted to the verifier with HPKE The Digital Credentials API also carries OpenID4VP requests. Digital Credentials API covers both protocols, with a guide for the verifier and one for the wallet. Which to use depends on where the presentation happens. In person, use proximity. On a website, use the Digital Credentials API, and pass an OpenID4VP and an org-iso-mdoc request in one call, as iOS only accepts org-iso-mdoc. Where the browser doesn't support the API, fall back to OpenID4VP with a QR code or a link, see mdoc with OpenID4VC.
documents.s: Proximity and the Digital Credentials API

documents.t: OpenID4VP can present the same mdoc, and the device response inside it has the same structure. ISO/IEC TS 18013-7 also describes mdoc presentation over OpenID4VP. Everything around the device response differs: ISO 18013-5 and 18013-7 Annex C OpenID4VP Encoding CBOR JSON and JWT Request A device request with document types and data element identifiers An authorization request with a DCQL query Credential formats mdoc SD-JWT VC, mdoc and W3C VCs Alternatives Can't be expressed. Several document requests can mean all of them or any one. DCQL credential sets and claim sets Verifier identity Reader certificate, optional Client identifier, usually with a signed request Credo API agent.mdoc and MdocDeviceResponse in @credo-ts/core agent.openid4vc in @credo-ts/openid4vc

Step Proximity Digital Credentials API Engagement and transport A native module, such as expo-mdoc-data-transfer in a React Native wallet The browser and the operating system. In the wallet, a native module such as @animo-id/expo-digital-credentials-api Encryption The native module Credo Create the device request Not supported agent.mdoc.createDcApiVerificationSession Read the request in the wallet Decode it with @owf/mdoc agent.mdoc.resolveDcApiRequest, which also finds matching mdocs Reader authentication Not checked Created and verified Create the device response MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse agent.mdoc.createDcApiResponse Verify the device response MdocDeviceResponse.verify agent.mdoc.verifyDcApiResponse, which also checks the response against the request Credo signs device responses with the device key (device signature). It doesn't support device MAC authentication, so it can't verify a response authenticated with a MAC either. Neither standard covers issuance. Wallets usually receive mdocs over OpenID4VCI, see mdoc with OpenID4VC. Proximity (ISO 18013-5) Present mdocs in person over BLE after a QR code or NFC engagement from a React Native wallet with expo-mdoc-data-transfer and Credo, and verify the device response in a reader.
Present mdocs in person over BLE after a QR code or NFC engagement from a React Native wallet with expo-mdoc-data-transfer and Credo, and verify the device response in a reader.

In a proximity presentation the wallet and the verifier's reader are in the same place, for example at a counter, and exchange the request and response over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) after the reader scans a QR code or taps the phone. A native module handles the engagement, the transport and the session encryption. Credo creates the device response in the wallet and verifies it in the reader. This page builds a screen for a React Native wallet that uses expo-mdoc-data-transfer, then shows how a reader verifies the response. ISO mdoc explains the messages. Paradym Wallet, an open source wallet built on Credo, presents mdocs in person this way. See its proximity code.

The module derives the session keys and the session transcript from the engagement, decrypts the request, and encrypts the response. Your app only handles the decrypted device request and the device response. Credo doesn't decode device requests, so the wallet decodes them with @owf/mdoc, the mdoc library Credo builds on. Credo also doesn't check reader authentication on a proximity request, and only supports device signatures, not device MAC authentication.

npm pnpm yarn bun npm install \ expo-mdoc-data-transfer \ expo-build-properties \ @owf/mdoc@^0.8.2 \ react-native-qrcode-svg \ react-native-svg pnpm add \ expo-mdoc-data-transfer \ expo-build-properties \ @owf/mdoc@^0.8.2 \ react-native-qrcode-svg \ react-native-svg yarn add \ expo-mdoc-data-transfer \ expo-build-properties \ @owf/mdoc@^0.8.2 \ react-native-qrcode-svg \ react-native-svg bun add \ expo-mdoc-data-transfer \ expo-build-properties \ @owf/mdoc@^0.8.2 \ react-native-qrcode-svg \ react-native-svg Add the config plugins to app.json and run npx expo prebuild: app.json { "expo": { "plugins": [ "expo-mdoc-data-transfer", ["expo-build-properties", { "android": { "minSdkVersion": 26 }, "ios": { "useFrameworks": "dynamic" } }] ] } } Use the @owf/mdoc version that @credo-ts/core depends on, so the app has one copy. The config plugin adds the Bluetooth and NFC permissions and the NFC engagement service to the Android manifest. See the module README. Dynamic frameworks on iOS change how every pod links. Paradym Wallet keeps some pods static, askar and anoncreds among them, with the plugin option ios.buildStatic. Bluetooth and NFC don't work in emulators, so test on physical devices. Android also asks the user for the Bluetooth permissions at runtime: Holder mdoc-proximity-wallet.tsx // Android 12 and later need the Bluetooth permissions, earlier versions the location permissions async function requestBluetoothPermissions() { if (Platform.OS !== 'android') return const { PERMISSIONS } = PermissionsAndroid await PermissionsAndroid.requestMultiple( Platform.Version >= 31 ? [PERMISSIONS.BLUETOOTH_ADVERTISE, PERMISSIONS.BLUETOOTH_CONNECT, PERMISSIONS.BLUETOOTH_SCAN] : [PERMISSIONS.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, PERMISSIONS.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION] ) } The wallet itself is an agent with storage and the stored mdocs, see Your first agent. The screen below gets it as a prop.

When the user taps the button, the screen starts the engagement, shows the QR code and waits for the reader's request: Holder mdoc-proximity-wallet.tsx async function start() { await requestBluetoothPermissions() const transfer = mdocDataTransfer.instance() setQrCode(await transfer.startQrEngagement()) // Also lets the reader engage with an NFC tap. Android only. transfer.enableNfc() // Resolves when a reader has scanned the QR code, connected over BLE and sent its request. // The module decrypts the request and derives the session transcript. const { deviceRequest, sessionTranscript } = await transfer.waitForDeviceRequest() setReaderRequest({ documentRequests: decodeDeviceRequest(deviceRequest), sessionTranscript }) } startQrEngagement() returns the device engagement to show as a QR code. On iOS, the reader always engages by scanning it. waitForDeviceRequest() resolves when a reader has connected and sent its request, and rejects when the transfer fails. decodeDeviceRequest reads the requested data elements from the request: Holder mdoc-proximity.ts import { type Agent, CredentialMultiInstanceUseMode, isNonEmptyArray, type Mdoc, MdocDeviceResponse, type MdocDocumentRequest, TypedArrayEncoder, useInstanceFromCredentialRecord, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DeviceRequest } from '@owf/mdoc' // The requested data elements per document type, with the reader's intent to retain each one export function decodeDeviceRequest(deviceRequest: Uint8Array): MdocDocumentRequest[] { return DeviceRequest.decode(deviceRequest).docRequests.map(({ itemsRequest }) => ({ docType: itemsRequest.docType, nameSpaces: Object.fromEntries( Array.from(itemsRequest.namespaces, ([nameSpace, elements]) => [nameSpace, Object.fromEntries(elements)]) ), })) } documentRequests lists, per document type, the requested data elements and the reader's intent to retain each one. The screen shows them to the user before it shares anything.

When the user agrees, the screen creates the device response and hands it to the module. shutdown() ends the session, and useMdocDataTransferShutdownOnUnmount() in the full example also does that when the user leaves the screen: Holder mdoc-proximity-wallet.tsx async function share(request: ReaderRequest) { const transfer = mdocDataTransfer.instance() // The module encrypts the response with the session keys and sends it await transfer.sendDeviceResponse(await createDeviceResponse(agent, request)) stop() } function stop() { mdocDataTransfer.instance().shutdown() setQrCode(undefined) setReaderRequest(undefined) } The device response itself is plain Credo: Holder mdoc-proximity.ts export async function createDeviceResponse( agent: Agent, options: { documentRequests: MdocDocumentRequest[]; sessionTranscript: Uint8Array } ) { const mdocs: Mdoc[] = [] const documentRequests: MdocDocumentRequest[] = [] for (const { docType, nameSpaces } of options.documentRequests) { const [record] = await agent.mdoc.findAllByQuery({ docType }) if (!record) continue // A new instance for every presentation, if the mdoc was issued in a batch const { credentialInstance: mdoc } = await useInstanceFromCredentialRecord({ agentContext: agent.context, credentialRecord: record, useMode: CredentialMultiInstanceUseMode.NewOrFirst, }) // Disclose the requested elements the mdoc has. Requesting an element it doesn't have fails. const issuerSigned = mdoc.issuerSignedNamespaces const disclosed = Object.fromEntries( Object.entries(nameSpaces).map(([nameSpace, elements]) => [ nameSpace, Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(elements).filter(([element]) => element in (issuerSigned[nameSpace] ?? {}))), ]) ) mdocs.push(mdoc) documentRequests.push({ docType, nameSpaces: disclosed }) } if (!isNonEmptyArray(mdocs)) throw new Error('No mdoc of the requested document types') const deviceResponse = await MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse(agent.context, { mdocs, documentRequests, sessionTranscriptOptions: { type: 'sessionTranscriptBytes', sessionTranscriptBytes: options.sessionTranscript }, }) // The encoded DeviceResponse, for the transport to encrypt and send return deviceResponse.deviceResponse.encode() } createDeviceResponse throws when a requested element isn't in the mdoc, so the function only passes the elements the mdoc has. The reader sees the others as missing. useInstanceFromCredentialRecord takes a new instance of an mdoc issued in a batch, so readers can't link presentations. When no new instance is left, it reuses the first one. The session transcript from the module goes in as sessionTranscriptBytes, and the device key of the mdoc signs over it. The module encrypts the returned DeviceResponse with the session keys.
documents.s: Create and send the device response

documents.t: Credo doesn't implement the reader side of the transport, and expo-mdoc-data-transfer only covers the wallet. When your reader app has the device response and the session transcript from its own transport, Credo verifies the response: Verifier mdoc-proximity.ts export async function verifyDeviceResponse( agent: Agent, options: { deviceResponse: Uint8Array; sessionTranscript: Uint8Array; trustedCertificates: string[] } ) { const deviceResponse = MdocDeviceResponse.fromBase64Url(TypedArrayEncoder.toBase64Url(options.deviceResponse)) // Throws when the response is invalid. Doesn't use the agent's trust configuration. await deviceResponse.verify(agent.context, { trustedCertificates: options.trustedCertificates, sessionTranscriptOptions: { type: 'sessionTranscriptBytes', sessionTranscriptBytes: options.sessionTranscript }, }) return deviceResponse.issuerClaims } verify doesn't use the agent's trust configuration. Pass the certificates of the issuers you trust, usually the IACA root certificates, as trustedCertificates, or every response fails. verify throws when the response is invalid. It checks the issuer signature and certificate chain, the element digests, the device signature over the session transcript, the validity period and the status. It doesn't check that the response contains what you asked for, so check issuerClaims (per document type and namespace) yourself.

The wallet screen, and the Credo functions it and the reader use. Render PresentInPersonScreen with the wallet's agent. mdoc-proximity-wallet.tsx mdoc-proximity.ts mdoc-proximity-wallet.tsx // A screen of a React Native wallet that presents mdocs to a reader in person. expo-mdoc-data-transfer // handles the engagement and the transport, Credo the device response (mdoc-proximity.ts). import type { Agent, MdocDocumentRequest } from '@credo-ts/core' import { mdocDataTransfer, useMdocDataTransferShutdownOnUnmount } from 'expo-mdoc-data-transfer' import { useState } from 'react' import { Button, PermissionsAndroid, Platform, Text, View } from 'react-native' import QRCode from 'react-native-qrcode-svg' import { createDeviceResponse, decodeDeviceRequest } from './mdoc-proximity.js' interface ReaderRequest { documentRequests: MdocDocumentRequest[] sessionTranscript: Uint8Array } export function PresentInPersonScreen({ agent }: { agent: Agent }) { const [qrCode, setQrCode] = useState<string>() const [readerRequest, setReaderRequest] = useState<ReaderRequest>() // Ends the session when the user leaves the screen useMdocDataTransferShutdownOnUnmount() async function start() { await requestBluetoothPermissions() const transfer = mdocDataTransfer.instance() setQrCode(await transfer.startQrEngagement()) // Also lets the reader engage with an NFC tap. Android only. transfer.enableNfc() // Resolves when a reader has scanned the QR code, connected over BLE and sent its request. // The module decrypts the request and derives the session transcript. const { deviceRequest, sessionTranscript } = await transfer.waitForDeviceRequest() setReaderRequest({ documentRequests: decodeDeviceRequest(deviceRequest), sessionTranscript }) } async function share(request: ReaderRequest) { const transfer = mdocDataTransfer.instance() // The module encrypts the response with the session keys and sends it await transfer.sendDeviceResponse(await createDeviceResponse(agent, request)) stop() } function stop() { mdocDataTransfer.instance().shutdown() setQrCode(undefined) setReaderRequest(undefined) } if (readerRequest) { return ( <View style={{ gap: 16, padding: 24 }}> <Text>The reader asks for:</Text> {readerRequest.documentRequests.map(({ docType, nameSpaces }) => ( <Text key={docType}> {docType}: {Object.values(nameSpaces).flatMap(Object.keys).join(', ')} </Text> ))} <Button title="Share" onPress={() => share(readerRequest)} /> <Button title="Decline" onPress={stop} /> </View> ) } return ( <View style={{ alignItems: 'center', gap: 16, padding: 24 }}> {qrCode ? <QRCode value={qrCode} size={250} /> : <Button title="Show QR code" onPress={start} />} </View> ) } // Android 12 and later need the Bluetooth permissions, earlier versions the location permissions async function requestBluetoothPermissions() { if (Platform.OS !== 'android') return const { PERMISSIONS } = PermissionsAndroid await PermissionsAndroid.requestMultiple( Platform.Version >= 31 ? [PERMISSIONS.BLUETOOTH_ADVERTISE, PERMISSIONS.BLUETOOTH_CONNECT, PERMISSIONS.BLUETOOTH_SCAN] : [PERMISSIONS.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, PERMISSIONS.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION] ) } mdoc-proximity.ts import { type Agent, CredentialMultiInstanceUseMode, isNonEmptyArray, type Mdoc, MdocDeviceResponse, type MdocDocumentRequest, TypedArrayEncoder, useInstanceFromCredentialRecord, } from '@credo-ts/core' import { DeviceRequest } from '@owf/mdoc' // The requested data elements per document type, with the reader's intent to retain each one export function decodeDeviceRequest(deviceRequest: Uint8Array): MdocDocumentRequest[] { return DeviceRequest.decode(deviceRequest).docRequests.map(({ itemsRequest }) => ({ docType: itemsRequest.docType, nameSpaces: Object.fromEntries( Array.from(itemsRequest.namespaces, ([nameSpace, elements]) => [nameSpace, Object.fromEntries(elements)]) ), })) } export async function createDeviceResponse( agent: Agent, options: { documentRequests: MdocDocumentRequest[]; sessionTranscript: Uint8Array } ) { const mdocs: Mdoc[] = [] const documentRequests: MdocDocumentRequest[] = [] for (const { docType, nameSpaces } of options.documentRequests) { const [record] = await agent.mdoc.findAllByQuery({ docType }) if (!record) continue // A new instance for every presentation, if the mdoc was issued in a batch const { credentialInstance: mdoc } = await useInstanceFromCredentialRecord({ agentContext: agent.context, credentialRecord: record, useMode: CredentialMultiInstanceUseMode.NewOrFirst, }) // Disclose the requested elements the mdoc has. Requesting an element it doesn't have fails. const issuerSigned = mdoc.issuerSignedNamespaces const disclosed = Object.fromEntries( Object.entries(nameSpaces).map(([nameSpace, elements]) => [ nameSpace, Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(elements).filter(([element]) => element in (issuerSigned[nameSpace] ?? {}))), ]) ) mdocs.push(mdoc) documentRequests.push({ docType, nameSpaces: disclosed }) } if (!isNonEmptyArray(mdocs)) throw new Error('No mdoc of the requested document types') const deviceResponse = await MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse(agent.context, { mdocs, documentRequests, sessionTranscriptOptions: { type: 'sessionTranscriptBytes', sessionTranscriptBytes: options.sessionTranscript }, }) // The encoded DeviceResponse, for the transport to encrypt and send return deviceResponse.deviceResponse.encode() } export async function verifyDeviceResponse( agent: Agent, options: { deviceResponse: Uint8Array; sessionTranscript: Uint8Array; trustedCertificates: string[] } ) { const deviceResponse = MdocDeviceResponse.fromBase64Url(TypedArrayEncoder.toBase64Url(options.deviceResponse)) // Throws when the response is invalid. Doesn't use the agent's trust configuration. await deviceResponse.verify(agent.context, { trustedCertificates: options.trustedCertificates, sessionTranscriptOptions: { type: 'sessionTranscriptBytes', sessionTranscriptBytes: options.sessionTranscript }, }) return deviceResponse.issuerClaims }
Digital Credentials API: request mdocs from a website. mdoc: signing, storing and verifying mdocs. Trusted issuers: decide which issuers you trust.

OpenID for Verifiable Credentials (OpenID4VC) is a family of protocols, built on OAuth 2.0, for issuing and presenting credentials over HTTPS. This page explains the protocols and roles, and how to set up the @credo-ts/openid4vc module. The pages below it cover each role.

Specification What it covers OpenID4VCI Issuance. A holder gets credentials from an issuer. The issuer authorizes it with a pre-authorized code in the offer, or with the OAuth authorization code flow. OpenID4VP Presentation. A verifier sends an authorization request with a DCQL query, and the holder responds with presentations of matching credentials. HAIP The High Assurance Interoperability Profile of both protocols, used by ecosystems such as the EU Digital Identity Wallet. It requires SD-JWT VC or mdoc. For issuance: the authorization code flow with PKCE, DPoP, and wallet authentication, usually with wallet attestations. For presentation: DCQL, requests signed with an X.509 certificate (x509_hash) and encrypted responses. Authorization and wallet security explains the issuance part, Verifying credentials the presentation part. There is no connection between the parties. Each exchange is a separate session, started by a credential offer or an authorization request that the holder receives as a QR code or link. Supported standards lists the versions and drafts Credo supports, and which credential formats work with each protocol.

Role API Platform Guide Issuer agent.openid4vc.issuer Node.js Issuing credentials Holder agent.openid4vc.holder Node.js and React Native Receiving and presenting credentials Verifier agent.openid4vc.verifier Node.js Verifying credentials Issuers and verifiers serve HTTP endpoints with Express, so they run on Node.js. On React Native only the holder is available.

npm pnpm yarn bun npm install @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 pnpm add @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 yarn add @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 bun add @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 For an issuer or verifier, also install Express 5: npm pnpm yarn bun npm install express@^5 pnpm add express@^5 yarn add express@^5 bun add express@^5 npm pnpm yarn bun npm install --save-dev @types/express@^5 pnpm add -D @types/express@^5 yarn add -D @types/express@^5 bun add -d @types/express@^5

An agent that issues and verifies credentials: agent.ts import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import express from 'express' const app = express() const agent = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // The key must be `openid4vc` for the module to be available as agent.openid4vc openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, issuer: { baseUrl: 'https://example.com/oid4vci', credentialRequestToCredentialMapper, }, verifier: { baseUrl: 'https://example.com/oid4vp', }, }), }, }) await agent.initialize() // Credo adds its routes to the app, you start the server. Make https://example.com // reach this server, for example through a reverse proxy. const server = app.listen(4022) Register the module under the key openid4vc, so it's available as agent.openid4vc. issuer and verifier are optional and turn on that role. The holder is always available, so a wallet registers the module without options: openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), The module stores issuers, verifiers and sessions as records. With Drizzle storage, add openid4vcBundle from @credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc to the bundles. baseUrl is the public URL of the endpoints, and Credo serves them under its path (/oid4vci and /oid4vp here). OpenID4VCI also requires the issuer metadata at the root of the host (/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer/oid4vci/<issuerId>), so your server must pass requests for the whole host to the Express app. app is your Express app. Without it, Credo creates one, available as agent.openid4vc.config.app. Either way, you start the server. Credo adds its routes during agent.initialize(), so register your own middleware and routes after that. The issuer and verifier support multi-tenancy: Credo finds the tenant from the issuer or verifier id in the URL. For local development over http://localhost, set allowInsecureHttpUrls: true in the agent config of all parties. Never enable it in production.

The pages for each role build one example: an issuer that issues an employee badge as an SD-JWT VC with the pre-authorized code flow, a holder that receives and presents it, and a verifier that requests two of its claims. This runs them in one process: flow.ts import { holder, presentCredential, receiveCredential } from './openid4vc-holder.js' import { createEmployeeBadgeOffer, issuer, issuerServer } from './openid4vc-issuer.js' import { createEmployeeBadgeRequest, getEmployeeBadgeClaims, verifier, verifierServer } from './openid4vc-verifier.js' // Issuer: create an offer for a known user const { credentialOffer, txCode } = await createEmployeeBadgeOffer('employee-123') // Holder: resolve the offer, enter the code, store the credential await receiveCredential(credentialOffer, txCode) // Verifier: request given_name and department const { authorizationRequest, verificationSessionId } = await createEmployeeBadgeRequest() // Holder: resolve the request and share the credential await presentCredential(authorizationRequest) // Verifier: read the verified claims console.log(await getEmployeeBadgeClaims(verificationSessionId)) Issuance (OpenID4VCI) 3 items Presentation (OpenID4VP) 2 items Formats 3 items
