This page is about issuance (OpenID4VCI): how an issuer decides who gets a credential beyond the pre-authorized code, and the protections that profiles such as HAIP ask for when a wallet requests credentials: PKCE, DPoP, wallet attestations and key attestations. Each section has an issuer part and a holder part. For the verifier side of security, such as signed requests and encrypted responses, see Verifying credentials. Issuing credentials and Receiving credentials explain the basics.

Flow Who authenticates the user Use when Configure with Pre-authorized code Your application, before it creates the offer You already know the user, for example after a login on your website. preAuthorizedCodeFlowConfig, see Issuing credentials Presentation during issuance Credo, which asks the holder to present a credential with OpenID4VP The user proves who they are with a credential they already have, such as a PID. requirePresentationDuringIssuance and getVerificationSession Chained authorization server Your identity provider, with Credo's authorization server in between Users log in with your existing OpenID Connect provider. authorizationServerConfigs with type: 'chained' External authorization server Your OAuth 2.0 authorization server, which holders use directly You run an authorization server that already supports OpenID4VCI. authorizationServerConfigs with type: 'direct' Start with the pre-authorized code. HAIP requires the authorization code flow, which the other three use. When users have to log in, prefer a chained authorization server over an external one: Credo's authorization server then still handles PAR, PKCE, DPoP and wallet attestations, which an external server has to implement itself. Every credential configuration you offer with the authorization code flow needs a scope. Credo's built-in authorization server handles the first three flows, and requires pushed authorization requests (PAR).

Feature Protects against HAIP Credo issuer default PKCE Another app redeeming an intercepted authorization code Required, with S256 Off DPoP Someone else using a stolen access token. DPoP binds the token to a key of the holder. Required Off Wallet attestation Wallet apps you don't trust getting credentials. The wallet authenticates with an attestation from its wallet provider. Issuers must authenticate wallets, usually with wallet attestations Off Key attestation Credentials bound to keys without the protection you need, for example outside a secure element Wallets must support them Off, set per credential configuration For an issuer: turn on PKCE and DPoP. Require wallet and key attestations only when the wallets you issue to get them from their wallet provider, as in the EU Digital Identity Wallet ecosystem. Wallets without them can't get your credentials. For a wallet: the Credo holder uses PKCE and DPoP automatically when the issuer supports them. Wallet and key attestations need a backend from your wallet provider, see Wallet and key attestations.

Each requirement has a module option that applies to all issuance sessions, and an option per session: in authorization when you create an offer, or in the result of getDynamicIssuanceSession for wallet-initiated issuance. Module option Per session Default pkceRequired requirePkce false dpopRequired requireDpop false walletAttestationsRequired requireWalletAttestation false If you leave the per-session option out, the module option applies. requirePkce: false turns PKCE off for that session, even when the module option requires it. requireDpop: false and requireWalletAttestation: false fall back to the module option, so you can't turn a requirement of the module off for one session. These options apply to Credo's authorization server. An external authorization server enforces its own rules. Credo only checks at the credential endpoint that the access token is bound with DPoP when the offer sets requireDpop: true.

The issuer asks the holder to present a credential, for example a PID, before it issues a new one. Credo creates the presentation request, verifies the response and only then gives the holder an authorization code:

The issuer agent also needs the verifier part of the module, and a getVerificationSession callback: Issuer issuer.ts const issuer = new Agent({ config: { allowInsecureHttpUrls: true }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...issuerStorage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, issuer: { baseUrl: `${issuerUrl}/oid4vci`, credentialRequestToCredentialMapper, // Creates the OpenID4VP request for presentation during issuance getVerificationSession, // Require DPoP and PKCE for all issuance sessions. PKCE is off by default. dpopRequired: true, pkceRequired: true, }, // Presentation during issuance uses the verifier of the same agent verifier: { baseUrl: `${issuerUrl}/oid4vp` }, }), }, }) The callback creates the OpenID4VP request when a holder starts the authorization. scopes are the requested scopes that match the offered credentials. Return the request together with the scopes it grants. The request needs a verifier record, here one with the same id as the issuer: Issuer issuer.ts const getVerificationSession: OpenId4VciGetVerificationSession = async ({ agentContext, issuanceSession, scopes }) => { if (!scopes.includes('diploma')) throw new Error(`Unsupported scopes ${scopes.join(', ')}`) // Resolve the verifier from the agent context, so this also works for tenants const verifier = agentContext.resolve(OpenId4VcVerifierApi) const authorizationRequest = await verifier.createAuthorizationRequest({ // A verifier with the same id as the issuer (created next to the issuer) verifierId: issuanceSession.issuerId, requestSigner: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] }, dcql: { query: { credentials: [ { id: 'pid', format: 'dc+sd-jwt', meta: { vct_values: ['urn:example:pid:1'] }, claims: [{ path: ['given_name'] }, { path: ['family_name'] }], }, ], }, }, }) // The scopes that are granted once the presentation is verified return { ...authorizationRequest, scopes: ['diploma'] } } Create the issuer with a scope per credential configuration, and an offer that requires the presentation. Leave authorizationServerUrl out (or set it to the issuer itself), as only Credo's authorization server handles this flow: Issuer issuer.ts const issuerRecord = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createIssuer({ issuerId: 'example-issuer', // Advertise DPoP support in the authorization server metadata dpopSigningAlgValuesSupported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256], credentialConfigurationsSupported: { diploma: { format: OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc, vct: 'urn:example:diploma:1', // Required for the authorization code flow scope: 'diploma', cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['jwk'], proof_types_supported: { jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256] }, }, }, }, }) await issuer.openid4vc.verifier.createVerifier({ verifierId: issuerRecord.issuerId }) const { credentialOffer } = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createCredentialOffer({ issuerId: issuerRecord.issuerId, credentialConfigurationIds: ['diploma'], authorizationCodeFlowConfig: { requirePresentationDuringIssuance: true }, }) The mapper receives the verified presentation in verification: Issuer issuer.ts const credentialRequestToCredentialMapper: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper = async ({ credentialConfiguration, holderBinding, verification, }) => { if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc) { throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format ${credentialConfiguration.format}`) } if (holderBinding.bindingMethod !== 'jwk') throw new Error('Expected jwk holder binding') // The verified presentation from the authorization step const [pid] = verification?.dcql?.presentations.pid ?? [] if (pid?.claimFormat !== ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc) throw new Error('Expected a verified PID presentation') return { type: 'credentials', format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc, credentials: holderBinding.keys.map((holder) => ({ holder, issuer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate], issuer: issuerUrl }, payload: { vct: credentialConfiguration.vct, name: `${pid.prettyClaims.given_name} ${pid.prettyClaims.family_name}`, degree: 'Bachelor of Science', }, disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['name', 'degree'] }, })), } satisfies OpenId4VciSignSdJwtCredentials }

Holder holder.ts const clientId = 'example-wallet' const redirectUri = 'https://wallet.example.com/redirect' const resolvedOffer = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveCredentialOffer(credentialOffer) const authorization = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VciAuthorizationRequest(resolvedOffer, { clientId, redirectUri, scope: getScopesFromCredentialConfigurationsSupported(resolvedOffer.offeredCredentialConfigurations), }) if (authorization.authorizationFlow !== OpenId4VciAuthorizationFlow.PresentationDuringIssuance) { throw new Error('Expected presentation during issuance') } // Present the PID with OpenID4VP const presentationRequest = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest( authorization.openid4vpRequestUrl ) if (!presentationRequest.dcql?.queryResult.can_be_satisfied) throw new Error('No matching credentials') const presentation = await holder.openid4vc.holder.acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest({ authorizationRequestPayload: presentationRequest.authorizationRequestPayload, dcql: { credentials: holder.openid4vc.holder.selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest(presentationRequest.dcql.queryResult) }, }) if (!presentation.ok) throw new Error('Presentation was rejected') // Exchange the presentation for an authorization code const { authorizationCode, dpop } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.retrieveAuthorizationCodeUsingPresentation({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, authSession: authorization.authSession, presentationDuringIssuanceSession: presentation.presentationDuringIssuanceSession, dpop: authorization.dpop, }) const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, code: authorizationCode, clientId, redirectUri, // PKCE: proves this is the client that started the authorization codeVerifier: authorization.codeVerifier, // Keep using the same DPoP key dpop, }) const { credentials } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, ...token, clientId, credentialBindingResolver: async () => { const key = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) return { method: 'jwk', keys: [PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(key.publicJwk)] } }, }) resolveOpenId4VciAuthorizationRequest starts the authorization. authorizationFlow tells you whether the issuer wants a presentation or a browser redirect (below). Present the credential like any other OpenID4VP request: the result has presentationDuringIssuanceSession, which proves the presentation to the issuer. Pass codeVerifier (PKCE) and the dpop from the previous call to the token request.

With a chained authorization server, holders talk to Credo's authorization server, which sends the user to your identity provider to log in. PAR, PKCE, DPoP and wallet attestations work as with Credo alone: Issuer issuer.ts // Wallets use Credo's authorization server, which sends the user to your identity provider const chainedIssuer = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createIssuer({ issuerId: 'employee-chained', credentialConfigurationsSupported, authorizationServerConfigs: [ { type: 'chained', issuer: 'https://idp.example.com', // Credo's client at the identity provider. Register // https://issuer.example.com/oid4vci/employee-chained/redirect as its redirect URI. clientAuthentication: { type: 'clientSecret', clientId: 'credo-issuer', clientSecret: 'secret' }, // Credential scope -> scopes to request from the identity provider scopesMapping: { employee: ['openid', 'profile'] }, }, ], }) await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createCredentialOffer({ issuerId: chainedIssuer.issuerId, credentialConfigurationIds: ['employee'], // Selects the chained authorization server authorizationCodeFlowConfig: { authorizationServerUrl: 'https://idp.example.com' }, }) Credo exchanges the code at your identity provider with clientAuthentication. Register <baseUrl>/<issuerId>/redirect as the redirect URI of that client. scopesMapping maps each credential scope to the scopes Credo requests from your identity provider. To decide per session instead, use the getChainedAuthorizationRequestParameters callback in the issuer module config. Set redirectUris to the redirect URIs of the wallets you accept. Without it, Credo accepts any redirect URI. In the mapper, the token response of your identity provider, including an id_token, is in issuanceSession.chainedIdentity.externalAccessTokenResponse. A chained flow can't be combined with presentation during issuance.

With a direct authorization server, Credo lists it in the issuer metadata, and holders use it directly: Issuer issuer.ts // Wallets use your authorization server directly const directIssuer = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createIssuer({ issuerId: 'employee-direct', credentialConfigurationsSupported, authorizationServerConfigs: [ { type: 'direct', issuer: 'https://auth.example.com', // Only needed if Credo has to introspect the access tokens clientAuthentication: { clientId: 'credo-issuer', clientSecret: 'secret' }, }, ], }) await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createCredentialOffer({ issuerId: directIssuer.issuerId, credentialConfigurationIds: ['employee'], authorizationCodeFlowConfig: { authorizationServerUrl: 'https://auth.example.com' }, }) Your authorization server must link the authorization to the offer through issuer_state, and handle PAR, PKCE, DPoP and wallet attestations itself if you need them. Credo verifies its access tokens at the credential endpoint, and only needs clientAuthentication for token introspection. For issuance without an offer, where the access token isn't linked to an issuance session, use getDynamicIssuanceSession.

With both kinds, the holder opens the authorization URL in a browser and receives the code on its redirect URI: Holder holder.ts /** * `openAuthorizationUrl` opens the URL in a browser and resolves with the URL the * authorization server redirected to, for example using an in-app browser session. */ export async function receiveWithRedirect( credentialOffer: string, openAuthorizationUrl: (authorizationRequestUrl: string) => Promise<string> ) { const clientId = 'example-wallet' const redirectUri = 'https://wallet.example.com/redirect' const resolvedOffer = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveCredentialOffer(credentialOffer) const authorization = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VciAuthorizationRequest(resolvedOffer, { clientId, redirectUri, scope: getScopesFromCredentialConfigurationsSupported(resolvedOffer.offeredCredentialConfigurations), }) if (authorization.authorizationFlow !== OpenId4VciAuthorizationFlow.Oauth2Redirect) { throw new Error('Expected a redirect to the authorization server') } const authorizationResponseRedirectUrl = await openAuthorizationUrl(authorization.authorizationRequestUrl) const { authorizationCode } = holder.openid4vc.holder.parseAuthorizationCodeFromAuthorizationResponse({ authorizationResponseRedirectUrl, resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, }) const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, code: authorizationCode, clientId, redirectUri, codeVerifier: authorization.codeVerifier, // Bound to the DPoP key used for the pushed authorization request, if any dpop: authorization.dpop, }) return holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, ...token, clientId, credentialBindingResolver: async () => { const key = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) return { method: 'jwk', keys: [PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(key.publicJwk)] } }, }) } The authorization request goes through PAR when the authorization server supports it. When the server supports PKCE, Credo adds it and returns the codeVerifier for the token request.

PKCE ties the authorization code to the holder that started the authorization. Credo's authorization server doesn't require it by default. Turn it on with pkceRequired: true, as in the full example. Credo only supports the S256 method. When a holder sends a code challenge, Credo always checks the code verifier, also for sessions that don't require PKCE. DPoP binds the access token to a key of the holder. Enable it on the issuer record with dpopSigningAlgValuesSupported, as in the presentation during issuance example: Credo only advertises DPoP when it's set. Require it with dpopRequired or requireDpop. When a holder uses DPoP in its first request, Credo requires it for the rest of that session.

Credo creates the PKCE code challenge when the authorization server supports PKCE, and returns codeVerifier. Pass it to requestToken. Credo uses DPoP when the authorization server supports it. Each call returns the dpop options for the next call, as in the examples above. Spreading the token response into requestCredentials passes them on.

A wallet attestation is a JWT from the wallet provider (the organization behind the wallet app) that says the wallet is a genuine instance of its app. The wallet uses it to authenticate to the authorization server (OAuth 2.0 Attestation-Based Client Authentication). A key attestation lists keys of the wallet and how they're protected, such as in a secure element, with levels from ISO/IEC 18045 (iso_18045_high, iso_18045_moderate, iso_18045_enhanced-basic, iso_18045_basic). The issuer can require it before it binds credentials to those keys. Both come from the wallet provider's backend. Credo doesn't create them.

Trust the wallet provider, for example with getTrustedIssuersForVerification in the agent config: Issuer issuer.ts // Trust the wallet provider for wallet attestations and key attestations const getTrustedIssuersForVerification: GetTrustedIssuersForVerification< VerificationSigner, OpenId4VcVerificationTypes > = async (_agentContext, { verification }) => { if (verification.type === 'oauth2ClientAttestation' || verification.type === 'openId4VciKeyAttestation') { return { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: [walletProviderCertificate.toString('pem')] }] } } // Use the other trust configuration for everything else return undefined } Credo checks attestations signed with an X.509 certificate against your trust configuration, and accepts DID-signed attestations unless you return a list of trusted DIDs. See Trusted issuers. warning Your trust configuration only applies to attestations signed with an x5c certificate chain or a DID. Credo accepts an attestation signed with a bare JWK (a jwk header) from anyone whose signature verifies, so it proves nothing about the wallet provider. Then require wallet attestations, advertise attestation-based client authentication (clientAttestationSigningAlgValuesSupported and clientAttestationPopSigningAlgValuesSupported), and set the key attestation requirements: Issuer issuer.ts config: { allowInsecureHttpUrls: true, getTrustedIssuersForVerification }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...issuerStorage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, issuer: { baseUrl: `${issuerUrl}/oid4vci`, credentialRequestToCredentialMapper, // Every issuance session requires a wallet attestation walletAttestationsRequired: true, }, }), }, issuer.ts const issuerRecord = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createIssuer({ issuerId: 'example-issuer', // Advertise attestation based client authentication clientAttestationSigningAlgValuesSupported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256], clientAttestationPopSigningAlgValuesSupported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256], batchCredentialIssuance: { batchSize: 2 }, credentialConfigurationsSupported: { membership: { format: OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.MsoMdoc, doctype: 'org.example.membership.1', cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['cose_key'], proof_types_supported: { jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256], // The holder keys must be attested at this level key_attestations_required: { key_storage: [OpenId4VciKeyAttestationLevel.High], user_authentication: [OpenId4VciKeyAttestationLevel.High], }, }, }, }, }, }) key_attestations_required on a proof type requires a key attestation with at least these levels. A higher level satisfies a lower one. Add an attestation proof type as well if wallets may send the key attestation as the proof itself. By default Credo verifies a wallet attestation whenever a wallet sends one, and then requires it for the rest of the session. ignoreWalletAttestationsWhenNotRequired ignores attestations for sessions that don't require them. clientAttestationPopChallengeRequired makes wallets fetch a challenge for the proof of possession first. The mapper gets the attested keys in holderBinding.keys, and the verified key attestation in holderBinding.keyAttestation: Issuer issuer.ts const credentialRequestToCredentialMapper: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper = async ({ credentialConfiguration, holderBinding, }) => { if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.MsoMdoc) { throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format ${credentialConfiguration.format}`) } if (holderBinding.bindingMethod !== 'jwk') throw new Error('Expected jwk holder binding') // Credo verified the key attestation, its trust and the required levels console.log('Attested key storage', holderBinding.keyAttestation?.payload.key_storage) return { type: 'credentials', format: ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc, // One credential per attested key credentials: holderBinding.keys.map(({ jwk }) => ({ docType: credentialConfiguration.doctype, holderKey: jwk, issuerCertificate, validityInfo: { validUntil: new Date(Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) }, namespaces: { 'org.example.membership.1': { member_id: 'M-1234', issuing_country: 'NL' } }, })), } satisfies OpenId4VciSignMdocCredentials }

Holder holder.ts const resolvedOffer = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveCredentialOffer(credentialOffer) // Credo signs the attestation proof of possession with the key in the attestation's `cnf` const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, walletAttestationJwt, }) const { credentials } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, ...token, clientId, credentialBindingResolver: ({ proofTypes }) => { if (!proofTypes.jwt?.keyAttestationsRequired) throw new Error('Expected key attestations to be required') // Without a nonce, Credo sends a jwt proof signed with the first attested key return { method: 'attestation', keyAttestationJwt } }, }) Pass walletAttestationJwt to every call to the authorization server: resolveOpenId4VciAuthorizationRequest, retrieveAuthorizationCodeUsingPresentation, requestToken and refreshToken. Credo signs the proof of possession with the key in the attestation's cnf, so that key must be in the wallet's KMS. When the issuer requires key attestations, proofTypes.jwt.keyAttestationsRequired (or proofTypes.attestation) says so, and the binding resolver must return { method: 'attestation', keyAttestationJwt }. Binding to a DID isn't possible then. The attested keys must be in the wallet's KMS, with their KMS key id as kid, and you get one credential instance per attested key. Without a nonce in the key attestation, Credo sends a jwt proof signed with the first attested key. With the issuer's cNonce (passed to the resolver) as nonce, it sends the key attestation as an attestation proof.

Presentation during issuance with PKCE and DPoP, in one process: openid4vc-auth.ts openid4vc-auth.ts import { Agent, ClaimFormat, SdJwtVcRecord, type X509Certificate } from '@credo-ts/core' import { verification?.dcql?.presentations.pid ?? PKCE is off by default. dpopRequired: true, pkceRequired: true, }, // Presentation during issuance uses the verifier of the same agent verifier: { baseUrl: `${issuerUrl}/oid4vp` }, }), }, }) const holder = new Agent({ config: { allowInsecureHttpUrls: true }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...holderStorage, openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) await issuer.initialize() await holder.initialize() const server = app.listen(4030) // Self-signed certificate for the example. The SAN must match the host of `issuerUrl`. issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk((await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })).publicJwk), issuer: { commonName: 'Credo example issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, extensions: { subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'localhost' }] } }, }) 'family_name'] }, }) await holder.sdJwtVc.store({ record: new SdJwtVcRecord({ credentialInstances: [{ compactSdJwtVc: pid.compact, kmsKeyId: pidKey.keyId }] }), }) const issuerRecord = await cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['jwk'], proof_types_supported: { jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256] }, }, }, }, }) await issuer.openid4vc.verifier.createVerifier({ verifierId: issuerRecord.issuerId }) const { credentialOffer } = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createCredentialOffer({ issuerId: issuerRecord.issuerId, credentialConfigurationIds: ['diploma'], authorizationCodeFlowConfig: { requirePresentationDuringIssuance: true }, }) const clientId = 'example-wallet' const redirectUri = an authorization code const { authorizationCode, dpop } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.retrieveAuthorizationCodeUsingPresentation({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, authSession: authorization.authSession, presentationDuringIssuanceSession: presentation.presentationDuringIssuanceSession, dpop: authorization.dpop, }) const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, code: authorizationCode, clientId, redirectUri, // PKCE: proves this is the client that started the authorization codeVerifier: authorization.codeVerifier, // Keep using the same DPoP key dpop, }) const { credentials } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, ...token, clientId, credentialBindingResolver: async () => { const key = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) return { method: 'jwk', keys: [PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(key.publicJwk)] } }, }) for (const { record } of credentials) { if (!(record instanceof SdJwtVcRecord)) throw new Error('Expected an SD-JWT VC') await holder.sdJwtVc.store({ record }) console.log('Received diploma', record.firstCredential.prettyClaims.name, 'with DPoP', token.dpop !== undefined) } server.close() await issuer.shutdown() await holder.shutdown() Wallet and key attestations, with a stand-in for the This page covers issuing credentials with OpenID4VCI from a Node.js agent: the issuer metadata, the callback that creates each credential, and credential offers with the pre-authorized code flow. The examples issue an SD-JWT VC.
Your application decides who gets which credential and creates the offer. Credo hosts the OpenID4VCI endpoints, checks the holder's requests and signs the credentials your callback returns.

Format Use when SD-JWT VC By default. JSON claims with selective disclosure, required by HAIP and used for the EU PID. mdoc The credential follows an ISO document type, such as the mobile driving licence, or holders must also present it in person over BLE or NFC. W3C VC Your ecosystem requires the W3C data model. Use jwt_vc_json or VCDM 2.0 with SD-JWT. You can offer the same credential in several formats, each as its own credential configuration. The format pages cover the configuration and signing for each.

Register OpenId4VcModule with an issuer configuration. OpenID4VC explains the module options. issuer.ts import { Agent, ClaimFormat, Kms, type SdJwtVcSignOptions } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionState, type OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionStateChangedEvent, OpenId4VcIssuerEvents, OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile, type OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapperOptions, type OpenId4VciSignSdJwtCredentials, OpenId4VcModule, } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import express from 'express' const issuerPort = 4020 const app = express() export const issuer = new Agent({ config: { // Allows the http://localhost URLs of this example. Never enable this in production. allowInsecureHttpUrls: true, }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({ app, issuer: { baseUrl: `http://localhost:${issuerPort}/oid4vci`, credentialRequestToCredentialMapper, }, }), }, }) await issuer.initialize() export const issuerServer = app.listen(issuerPort) baseUrl is the public URL of the issuer endpoints. Each issuer you create gets the credential issuer identifier <baseUrl>/<issuerId>. credentialRequestToCredentialMapper creates the credentials when a holder requests them, see Create the credentials.

The issuer signs credentials with a key from the agent's KMS. For SD-JWT VC and mdoc it includes an X.509 certificate for that key, so holders and verifiers can check who signed. issuer.ts const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } }) // Self-signed for this example. In production, a CA issues the certificate for your key. export const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: Kms.PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk), issuer: { commonName: 'Example Corp', countryName: 'NL' }, }) The example uses a self-signed certificate. In production a certificate authority issues it, and holders and verifiers trust that CA. See X.509 certificates. If you load a certificate instead of creating it, set certificate.keyId to the KMS key id of its key so Credo can sign with it. To sign with a DID instead, use issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl } in the callback.
documents.s: Create a signing key and certificate

documents.t: An issuer record holds the metadata that holders fetch from /.well-known/openid-credential-issuer: the issuer's display name and the credentials it offers. One agent can host several issuers. issuer.ts const issuerRecord = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createIssuer({ display: [{ name: 'Example Corp', locale: 'en' }], credentialConfigurationsSupported: { 'employee-badge': { format: OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc, vct: 'urn:example:employee-badge:1', cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['jwk'], credential_signing_alg_values_supported: [Kms.KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256], proof_types_supported: { jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [Kms.KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256] }, }, credential_metadata: { display: [{ name: 'Employee badge', locale: 'en', background_color: '#12107c', text_color: '#ffffff' }], claims: [ { path: ['given_name'], display: [{ name: 'Given name', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: ['family_name'], display: [{ name: 'Family name', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: ['department'], display: [{ name: 'Department', locale: 'en' }] }, ], }, }, }, }) Each key of credentialConfigurationsSupported is a credential configuration id. You use these ids when you create offers. For each configuration: Set proof_types_supported. Credo only issues credentials bound to a holder key, so it always asks for a proof of possession, and a Credo holder rejects configurations without this field. Put display information under credential_metadata, as OpenID4VCI 1.0 defines. Wallets that implement draft 15 read display and claims at the top level of the configuration, so add them there as well if you need to support those wallets. Create the issuer once, for example when you deploy, and keep its issuerId. Credo generates a UUID unless you pass one. Change the metadata later with updateIssuerMetadata. For batch issuance, set batchCredentialIssuance: { batchSize } on the issuer. A holder can then request up to that many instances of a credential in one request, each bound to a different key, so verifiers can't link its presentations to each other.

Credo checks each credential request (the access token and the holder's proof of possession of its keys) and then calls your credentialRequestToCredentialMapper with, among others: issuanceSession: the session created with the offer, including the issuanceMetadata you passed. credentialConfigurationId and credentialConfiguration: the configuration the holder requests. holderBinding: the verified keys or DIDs to bind the credentials to. issuer.ts // Stands in for your own user database const employees = new Map([['employee-123', { given_name: 'Jane', family_name: 'Doe', department: 'Engineering' }]]) async function credentialRequestToCredentialMapper({ credentialConfiguration, holderBinding, issuanceSession, }: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapperOptions): Promise<OpenId4VciSignSdJwtCredentials> { if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc) { throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format '${credentialConfiguration.format}'`) } // Set as issuanceMetadata when creating the offer const employeeId = issuanceSession.issuanceMetadata?.employeeId const employee = typeof employeeId === 'string' ? employees.get(employeeId) : undefined if (!employee) throw new Error('Unknown employee') return { type: 'credentials', format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc, // One credential per key the wallet wants the credential bound to credentials: holderBinding.keys.map( (holder): SdJwtVcSignOptions => ({ payload: { vct: credentialConfiguration.vct, ...employee }, holder, issuer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] }, disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name', 'family_name', 'department'] }, }) ), } } Return exactly one credential for each entry in holderBinding.keys. With batch issuance there are several entries, and Credo rejects the result if the counts differ. The format you return decides how Credo signs: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc for SD-JWT VC, ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc for mdoc, or one of the W3C formats. To issue the credential later, return a deferral instead (see Deferred issuance).

An offer tells the holder which credentials it can get and how to get authorization. Pick the flow: Pre-authorized code (this page): your application has already identified the user, for example after a login on your website, and the offer itself carries the authorization. Use it by default. Authorization code: the holder sends the user to an authorization server to log in, or presents a credential such as a PID first. Use it when the user isn't known yet, or when your ecosystem follows HAIP. See Authorization and wallet security. issuer.ts export async function createEmployeeBadgeOffer(employeeId: string) { const { credentialOffer, issuanceSession } = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createCredentialOffer({ issuerId: issuerRecord.issuerId, credentialConfigurationIds: ['employee-badge'], preAuthorizedCodeFlowConfig: { txCode: { input_mode: 'numeric', length: 6, description: 'Enter the code from the email we sent you' }, }, issuanceMetadata: { employeeId }, }) // Show credentialOffer as a QR code or link. Send the code (userPin) to the user over another channel. return { credentialOffer, txCode: issuanceSession.userPin } } credentialOffer is a URI such as openid-credential-offer://?credential_offer_uri=.... Show it as a QR code when the wallet runs on another device, or as a link on the same device. baseUri changes the openid-credential-offer:// prefix, for example to a custom scheme or an HTTPS link. txCode makes the wallet ask the user for a transaction code. Credo generates the code and stores it as issuanceSession.userPin (4 digits unless you set length). Send it over a different channel than the offer, such as email or SMS, so that someone who intercepts the offer can't redeem it. The holder must finish the whole issuance before the offer expires: 3 minutes by default. Change it per offer with expirationInSeconds, or for all offers with statefulCredentialOfferExpirationInSeconds in the issuer configuration.

Each offer creates an issuance session. Listen for state changes to update your application: issuer.ts issuer.events.on<OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionStateChangedEvent>( OpenId4VcIssuerEvents.IssuanceSessionStateChanged, ({ payload: { issuanceSession } }) => { if (issuanceSession.state === OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionState.Completed) { console.log(`Issuance session ${issuanceSession.id} completed`) } else if (issuanceSession.state === OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionState.Error) { console.error(`Issuance session ${issuanceSession.id} failed: ${issuanceSession.errorMessage}`) } } ) In the pre-authorized code flow a session goes through OfferCreated, OfferUriRetrieved, AccessTokenRequested, AccessTokenCreated, CredentialRequestReceived and Completed. Other states: State When AuthorizationInitiated, AuthorizationGranted Authorization code flow with Credo as the authorization server. CredentialsPartiallyIssued The offer has several credential configurations and the holder hasn't requested all of them yet. Error The session failed or expired. errorMessage says why. To read a session at any time, call agent.openid4vc.issuer.getIssuanceSessionById(id).

If a credential isn't ready when the holder asks for it, for example because it needs manual approval, return { type: 'deferral', transactionId, interval } from the mapper. The holder retries at the deferred credential endpoint after interval seconds. Credo then calls deferredCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper from the issuer configuration, which returns the credentials or another deferral. The session stays valid for interval plus deferralIntervalGracePeriodInSeconds (7 days by default).

Receiving credentials: the holder side of this flow. SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC: claims, selective disclosure and type metadata. Authorization and wallet security: the authorization code flow, PKCE, DPoP and wallet attestations.

This page covers what is specific to mdoc (ISO/IEC 18013-5, mso_mdoc) in OpenID4VC, in the order of the flow. Issuance covers the issuer's credential configuration, certificate and signing, and the holder's trust and storage. Presentation covers the verifier's DCQL query and the result. Issuing credentials, Receiving credentials, Presenting credentials and Verifying credentials explain the flow itself, and mdoc explains the format. Use mdoc for credentials that follow an ISO document type, such as the mobile driving licence, or that holders also present in person (ISO mdoc). To request mdocs from a website, see Digital Credentials API.

Add an mso_mdoc entry to the credentialConfigurationsSupported of the issuer: Issuer issuer.ts const mdlNamespace = 'org.iso.18013.5.1' const credentialConfigurationsSupported = { 'mdl-mdoc': { format: OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.MsoMdoc, doctype: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL', scope: 'mdl', cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['cose_key'], proof_types_supported: { jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256] }, }, credential_metadata: { display: [{ name: 'Mobile driving licence', locale: 'en' }], claims: [ { path: [mdlNamespace, 'given_name'], display: [{ name: 'Given name', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: [mdlNamespace, 'family_name'], display: [{ name: 'Family name', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: [mdlNamespace, 'birth_date'], display: [{ name: 'Date of birth', locale: 'en' }] }, ], }, }, } satisfies Record<string, OpenId4VciCredentialConfigurationSupportedWithFormats> doctype is the document type, such as org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL for a mobile driving licence. Credo checks that every mdoc the mapper returns has this doctype. An mdoc is always bound to a key of the holder, never to a DID. cose_key (or jwk) in cryptographic_binding_methods_supported tells the wallet so. In credential_metadata.claims, the path of a data element is its namespace and element identifier. Add a scope if you offer the credential through the authorization code flow.

mdocs are signed with an X.509 certificate, the document signer certificate: Issuer issuer.ts // Self-signed for the example. In production this is a document signer certificate issued by your IACA. issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({ authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk((await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })).publicJwk), // mdoc verification requires a country (C) in the issuer certificate issuer: { commonName: 'Credo example mDL issuer', countryName: 'NL' }, }) The subject must have a country (countryName): verification fails without it, and checks that issuing_country in the mdoc matches it (and issuing_jurisdiction the state, if present). In production, your issuing authority CA (IACA) issues the document signer certificate, and verifiers trust the IACA certificate. Pass the chain as an array, leaf first, to include it in the mdoc. X.509 certificates explains creating certificates and chains.

The mapper returns the mdoc sign options, one entry for each holder key: Issuer issuer.ts const credentialRequestToCredentialMapper: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper = async ({ credentialConfiguration, holderBinding, }) => { if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.MsoMdoc) { throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format ${credentialConfiguration.format}`) } // An mdoc is always bound to a key, never to a DID if (holderBinding.bindingMethod !== 'jwk') throw new Error('Expected jwk holder binding') const oneYearFromNow = new Date(Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) return { type: 'credentials', format: ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc, credentials: holderBinding.keys.map(({ jwk }) => ({ docType: credentialConfiguration.doctype, holderKey: jwk, issuerCertificate, // `signed` and `validFrom` default to now validityInfo: { validUntil: oneYearFromNow }, namespaces: { [mdlNamespace]: { given_name: 'Erika', family_name: 'Mustermann', birth_date: new DateOnly('1984-01-26'), issue_date: new DateOnly(), expiry_date: new DateOnly(oneYearFromNow.toISOString().slice(0, 10)), // Must match the country (C) of the issuer certificate issuing_country: 'NL', document_number: 'NL-123456', }, }, })), } satisfies OpenId4VciSignMdocCredentials } docType must be the doctype of the configuration, and holderKey is the key from holderBinding. validityInfo needs validUntil. Leave signed and validFrom out so they default to now: Credo rejects a validFrom that is even a few milliseconds before signed, which happens if you pass new Date(). namespaces maps each namespace to its data elements. Use DateOnly for elements of type full-date, such as birth_date. Every data element can be disclosed on its own. For revocation, add statusInfo with a status list. keyAuthorizations lists data elements the wallet may sign itself (device signed).

The holder verifies the mdoc when it receives it, and the verifier verifies it again in the presentation. Both need the issuer certificate or its IACA root: trust.ts // The holder verifies the mdoc when receiving it, and the verifier when it is presented holder.x509.config.addTrustedCertificate(issuerCertificate) verifier.x509.config.addTrustedCertificate(issuerCertificate) Without a trusted certificate, verification fails. To decide per verification, for example from a list of IACAs, use getTrustedIssuersForVerification in the agent config. See Trusted issuers.

The binding resolver must return keys (method: 'jwk'): Holder holder.ts const resolvedOffer = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveCredentialOffer(credentialOffer) const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer }) const { credentials } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, ...token, // mdoc only supports binding to a key (jwk) credentialBindingResolver: async ({ proofTypes }) => { const algorithm = proofTypes.jwt?.supportedSignatureAlgorithms[0] if (!algorithm) throw new Error('No supported proof of possession algorithm') const key = await holder.kms.createKeyForSignatureAlgorithm({ algorithm }) return { method: 'jwk', keys: [PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(key.publicJwk)] } }, }) for (const { record } of credentials) { if (!(record instanceof MdocRecord)) throw new Error('Expected an mdoc') await holder.mdoc.store({ record }) console.log(record.firstCredential.docType, record.firstCredential.issuerSignedNamespaces) } requestCredentials doesn't store anything. The MdocRecord has one instance per mdoc the issuer returned. record.firstCredential.issuerSignedNamespaces has the data elements per namespace.
The verifier needs the same trust configuration as the holder, see Trust the issuer.

The verifier asks for an mdoc by doctype and lists the data elements it needs: Verifier verifier.ts const { authorizationRequest, verificationSession } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.createAuthorizationRequest({ verifierId: verifierRecord.verifierId, requestSigner: { method: 'none' }, // Encrypted response (the default) responseMode: 'direct_post.jwt', dcql: { query: { credentials: [ { id: 'mdl', format: 'mso_mdoc', meta: { doctype_value: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL' }, claims: [ { path: ['org.iso.18013.5.1', 'given_name'], intent_to_retain: false }, { path: ['org.iso.18013.5.1', 'birth_date'], intent_to_retain: false }, ], }, ], }, }, }) format is mso_mdoc and meta.doctype_value the doctype. Each claim path is a namespace and a data element identifier, and intent_to_retain tells the wallet whether you store the element. The wallet discloses only the requested data elements. Keep the default response mode direct_post.jwt: with OpenID4VP drafts 21 and 24, mdoc requests require it.

Presenting works as for other formats. Credo creates an ISO 18013-5 device response, signed with the key the mdoc is bound to: Holder holder.ts const resolvedRequest = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest(authorizationRequest) if (!resolvedRequest.dcql?.queryResult.can_be_satisfied) throw new Error('No matching mdoc') const result = await holder.openid4vc.holder.acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest({ authorizationRequestPayload: resolvedRequest.authorizationRequestPayload, dcql: { credentials: holder.openid4vc.holder.selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest(resolvedRequest.dcql.queryResult) }, }) if (!result.ok) throw new Error(`Verifier rejected the presentation: ${result.serverResponse.status}`)

After the session reaches ResponseVerified, the presentation is an MdocDeviceResponse: Verifier verifier.ts const { dcql } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.getVerifiedAuthorizationResponse(verificationSession.id) const [deviceResponse] = dcql?.presentations.mdl ?? [] if (deviceResponse?.claimFormat !== ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc) throw new Error('Expected an mdoc presentation') // { 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL': { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { given_name: 'Erika', birth_date: DateOnly } } } console.log(deviceResponse.issuerClaims) issuerClaims has the issuer-signed data elements per doctype and namespace. deviceClaims has the data elements the wallet signed itself, if any.

mdoc: signing, presenting and verifying outside OpenID4VC. Digital Credentials API: request mdocs from a website, with OpenID4VP or ISO 18013-7 Annex C. ISO mdoc: present mdocs in person. Authorization and wallet security: DPoP, wallet attestations and key attestations.

This page covers the holder side of OpenID4VP: resolving a verifier's authorization request, showing the user what it asks for, and sending the response. It uses the holder agent from Receiving credentials, which also trusts the verifier's certificate, and the SD-JWT VC it received there. The verifier side is in Verifying credentials.

A verifier sends an authorization request as a QR code or link (openid4vp://...). resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest fetches the request, verifies its signature and finds the stored credentials that match its DCQL query: holder.ts const resolvedRequest = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest(authorizationRequest) // Who is asking, e.g. prefix 'x509_san_dns' and client id 'x509_san_dns:localhost' const { clientIdPrefix, effectiveClientId } = resolvedRequest.verifier const queryResult = resolvedRequest.dcql?.queryResult if (!queryResult?.can_be_satisfied) throw new Error('Your stored credentials do not match the request') // For each credential query: the matching credentials and the claims they would disclose for (const [queryId, match] of Object.entries(queryResult.credential_matches)) { if (!match.success) continue for (const { record, claims } of match.valid_credentials) { console.log(queryId, record.type, claims.valid_claim_sets[0].output) } } resolvedRequest.verifier tells you who is asking. With x509_san_dns or x509_hash the request was signed with a certificate that the holder trusts, and resolving throws if it doesn't. With decentralized_identifier it was signed with a DID. With redirect_uri the request isn't signed, so anyone could have created it: show the user that the verifier is unverified, or reject such requests. queryResult.can_be_satisfied is false when the holder doesn't have the credentials the verifier asks for. Otherwise credential_matches lists, for each credential query, the matching credentials and the claims each would disclose. Use it to show the user what they're about to share.

After the user agrees, select the credentials and send the response: holder.ts // Picks the first matching credential for each query. Ask the user for consent before you submit. const credentials = holder.openid4vc.holder.selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest(queryResult) const result = await holder.openid4vc.holder.acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest({ authorizationRequestPayload: resolvedRequest.authorizationRequestPayload, dcql: { credentials }, }) if (!result.ok) throw new Error(`The verifier rejected the response: ${JSON.stringify(result.serverResponse.body)}`) selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest picks the first matching credential for each query and discloses only the requested claims. For credentials received in a batch it uses an unused instance while there is one (useMode, default NewOrFirst). Credo posts the response to the verifier's response endpoint. If the verifier rejects it, the call doesn't throw: result.ok is false and result.serverResponse holds the verifier's answer. result.redirectUri is set when the verifier wants the user to continue on its website or app. Open it in the browser. Verifiers that use an OpenID4VP draft may send a DIF Presentation Exchange definition instead of a DCQL query. Then resolvedRequest.presentationExchange is set instead of dcql: select with selectCredentialsForPresentationExchangeRequest and pass presentationExchange: { credentials } when accepting. For requests that include transaction data, see SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC. For requests from a website through the browser, see Digital Credentials API.

SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC and mdoc with OpenID4VC: format details, such as transaction data. Digital Credentials API: answer requests that a website sends through the browser. Trusted issuers: decide which verifiers your wallet accepts.

This page covers the holder side of OpenID4VCI: resolving a credential offer, getting an access token, requesting the credentials and storing them. The holder API is the same on Node.js and React Native. The examples continue the SD-JWT VC flow from Issuing credentials. To present the credentials afterwards, see Presenting credentials.

Register OpenId4VcModule without options. The holder part is always available as agent.openid4vc.holder. Node.js React Native holder.ts import { Agent, Kms, MdocRecord, SdJwtVcRecord, W3cCredentialRecord, X509Module } from '@credo-ts/core' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node' import { type OpenId4VciCredentialBindingResolver, OpenId4VcModule, preAuthorizedCodeGrantIdentifier, } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { issuerCertificate } from './openid4vc-issuer.js' import { verifierCertificate } from './openid4vc-verifier.js' export const holder = new Agent({ config: { // Allows the http://localhost URLs of this example. Never enable this in production. allowInsecureHttpUrls: true, }, dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup // Certificates (or root CAs) of the issuers and verifiers you trust x509: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate, verifierCertificate] }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) await holder.initialize() holder.ts import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar' import { Agent, X509Module } from '@credo-ts/core' import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc' import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native' import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native' // PEM certificates (or root CAs) of the issuers and verifiers the wallet trusts, bundled with the app const trustedCertificates = ['-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n...\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----'] export const holder = new Agent({ dependencies: agentDependencies, modules: { askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, // In a real wallet, derive the key from a secret in the device's secure storage store: { id: 'holder', key: 'holder-key' }, }), x509: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates }), openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(), }, }) await holder.initialize() The holder verifies the credentials it receives, and later the requests of verifiers. To verify X.509 signatures, it needs the certificates, or root CAs, of the issuers and verifiers you trust. The Node.js example trusts the certificates from the issuer and verifier examples. See Trusted issuers. For storage and keys, see Storage and Key management. The React Native example uses Askar, the default for mobile wallets.

The wallet gets a credential offer URI from a QR code or a link. resolveCredentialOffer fetches the offer and the issuer metadata: holder.ts const resolvedCredentialOffer = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveCredentialOffer(credentialOffer) // What to show the user: the issuer, the offered credentials and whether a code is needed const issuerName = resolvedCredentialOffer.metadata.credentialIssuer.display?.[0]?.name const offeredCredentials = Object.keys(resolvedCredentialOffer.offeredCredentialConfigurations) const txCodeRequest = resolvedCredentialOffer.credentialOfferPayload.grants?.[preAuthorizedCodeGrantIdentifier]?.tx_code Use the issuer metadata and offeredCredentialConfigurations to show the user who offers what. Display names, colors and claim labels are under credential_metadata of each configuration, or at its top level for issuers that implement draft 15. If txCodeRequest is defined, the issuer sent the user a code (by email, for example), and description, length and input_mode tell you what to ask for.

In the pre-authorized code flow, exchange the code from the offer for an access token, with the transaction code the user entered: holder.ts // txCode is the code the user received from the issuer, if txCodeRequest is defined const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer, txCode }) If the issuer supports DPoP, Credo creates the DPoP proof and returns its options in token.dpop. Pass them to the next calls. PKCE and DPoP need nothing else from you. Issuers that follow HAIP also ask for wallet attestations and key attestations, which your wallet gets from its wallet provider's backend. Authorization and wallet security covers those and offers that use the authorization code flow.

The issuer binds each credential to a key the holder controls. Credo calls your credentialBindingResolver once for each offered credential configuration, with what the issuer supports, and you return the keys to bind to: holder.ts const credentialBindingResolver: OpenId4VciCredentialBindingResolver = async ({ supportsJwk, proofTypes }) => { // The algorithms the issuer accepts for this credential that the wallet's KMS supports const algorithm = proofTypes.jwt?.supportedSignatureAlgorithms[0] if (!supportsJwk || !algorithm) throw new Error('The issuer does not support jwk binding with a jwt proof') const key = await holder.kms.createKeyForSignatureAlgorithm({ algorithm }) return { method: 'jwk', keys: [Kms.PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(key.publicJwk)] } } The resolver returns one of: Binding Use for { method: 'jwk', keys } SD-JWT VC and mdoc. Keys from the agent's KMS. This is the default choice, and what HAIP requires. { method: 'did', didUrls } W3C formats, which can't bind to a bare key. Verification methods of DIDs the agent created, when the issuer lists the DID method in supportedDidMethods or accepts all (supportsAllDidMethods). Not allowed for mdoc. { method: 'attestation', keyAttestationJwt } Issuers that require key attestations. See Authorization and wallet security. To receive a batch, return up to issuerMaxBatchSize keys of the same key type, and you get one credential instance per key. Then request the credentials: holder.ts const { credentials, deferredCredentials } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer, accessToken: token.accessToken, cNonce: token.cNonce, dpop: token.dpop, credentialBindingResolver, }) By default this requests every credential in the offer. Pass credentialConfigurationIds to request only some of them.

requestCredentials verifies each credential, including the issuer's signature and trust, but it doesn't store anything. Each result has a record that you store with the API for its format: holder.ts // requestCredentials verifies the credentials, but doesn't store them for (const { record } of credentials) { if (record instanceof SdJwtVcRecord) await holder.sdJwtVc.store({ record }) else if (record instanceof MdocRecord) await holder.mdoc.store({ record }) else if (record instanceof W3cCredentialRecord) await holder.w3cCredentials.store({ record }) else await holder.w3cV2Credentials.store({ record }) } A batch arrives as one record with several instances in record.credentialInstances. If the issuer defers issuance, the credential is in deferredCredentials instead: call requestDeferredCredentials with its transactionId after interval seconds. If a credential has a notificationId, tell the issuer whether you stored it with sendNotification (credential_accepted, credential_deleted or credential_failure).

Presenting credentials: present the stored credentials to a verifier. Authorization and wallet security: offers with the authorization code flow, and wallet and key attestations. SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC and mdoc with OpenID4VC: format details for wallets. Trusted issuers: decide which issuers your wallet accepts.

This page covers what is specific to SD-JWT VC in OpenID4VC, in the order of the flow. Issuance covers the issuer's credential configuration and signing, and what the holder stores. Presentation covers the verifier's DCQL query, transaction data and the result. Issuing credentials, Receiving credentials, Presenting credentials and Verifying credentials explain the flow itself, and SD-JWT VC explains the format. Use SD-JWT VC by default. HAIP requires SD-JWT VC or mdoc, and the EU PID uses SD-JWT VC.

Add a dc+sd-jwt entry to the credentialConfigurationsSupported of the issuer: Issuer issuer.ts const credentialConfigurationsSupported = { 'identity-sd-jwt': { format: OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc, vct: 'urn:example:identity:1', scope: 'identity', cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['jwk'], credential_signing_alg_values_supported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256], proof_types_supported: { jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256] }, }, credential_metadata: { display: [{ name: 'Identity card', locale: 'en', background_color: '#1d3557', text_color: '#ffffff' }], claims: [ { path: ['given_name'], display: [{ name: 'Given name', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: ['family_name'], display: [{ name: 'Family name', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: ['birthdate'], display: [{ name: 'Date of birth', locale: 'en' }] }, { path: ['address', 'country'], display: [{ name: 'Country', locale: 'en' }] }, ], }, }, } satisfies Record<string, OpenId4VciCredentialConfigurationSupportedWithFormats> vct is the credential type. Verifiers request credentials by it, and Credo checks that every credential the mapper returns has this vct. If it's an HTTPS URL, a Credo holder fetches the type metadata from it when it receives the credential and keeps it on the record (record.typeMetadata). cryptographic_binding_methods_supported decides what the holder binds the credential to: jwk for a key (the default choice, and what HAIP requires), or DID methods such as did:key. credential_metadata holds what wallets show: the card in display and a label per claim in claims, where path points into the credential. Add a scope if you offer the credential through the authorization code flow. Wallets that implement older drafts use the format vc+sd-jwt. Credo accepts it as SD-JWT VC when the configuration has a vct, and signs the credential with vc+sd-jwt as typ. Without a vct, vc+sd-jwt means a W3C VCDM 2.0 credential, see W3C VCs with OpenID4VC.

The mapper returns the SD-JWT VC sign options, one entry for each holder key: Issuer issuer.ts const credentialRequestToCredentialMapper: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper = async ({ credentialConfiguration, holderBinding, issuanceSession, }) => { if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc) { throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format ${credentialConfiguration.format}`) } if (holderBinding.bindingMethod !== 'jwk') throw new Error('Only jwk holder binding is supported') // Look up the data for this user, e.g. based on the issuance metadata of the offer const { userId } = issuanceSession.issuanceMetadata ?? {} if (userId !== 'user-123') throw new Error('Unknown user') return { type: 'credentials', format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc, // One credential per holder key (more than one with batch issuance) credentials: holderBinding.keys.map((holder) => ({ holder, issuer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate], issuer: issuerUrl }, payload: { vct: credentialConfiguration.vct, given_name: 'Erika', family_name: 'Mustermann', birthdate: '1984-01-26', address: { street_address: 'Heidestraße 17', locality: 'Köln', country: 'DE' }, }, disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name', 'family_name', 'birthdate'], address: { _sd: ['street_address', 'locality', 'country'] }, }, })), } satisfies OpenId4VciSignSdJwtCredentials } payload.vct must be the vct of the configuration. Credo adds iat, and sets iss and cnf from issuer and holder. issuer signs with an X.509 certificate chain (x5c, leaf first) or a DID ({ method: 'did', didUrl }, for a DID created in this agent). The optional issuer URL becomes the iss claim and must match a DNS or URI subject alternative name of the leaf certificate. disclosureFrame lists in _sd the claims the holder can disclose one by one. Claims that aren't listed are always visible. SD-JWT VC explains nested frames and decoys. For revocation, add a status claim to the payload. See Status lists.

The holder verifies each credential when it receives it, and the verifier verifies it again in the presentation. For an X.509-signed credential, both need the issuer certificate or its root CA: trust.ts // Both the holder and the verifier only accept credentials from issuers they trust holder.x509.config.addTrustedCertificate(issuerCertificate) verifier.x509.config.addTrustedCertificate(issuerCertificate) DID-signed credentials are accepted from any DID unless you configure trusted issuers. Trusted issuers covers both, and how to decide per verification.

The holder side is the same as for other formats. Only the record type differs: Holder holder.ts const resolvedOffer = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveCredentialOffer(credentialOffer) const token = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestToken({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer }) const { credentials } = await holder.openid4vc.holder.requestCredentials({ resolvedCredentialOffer: resolvedOffer, ...token, credentialBindingResolver: async ({ proofTypes }) => { const algorithm = proofTypes.jwt?.supportedSignatureAlgorithms[0] if (!algorithm) throw new Error('No supported proof of possession algorithm') const key = await holder.kms.createKeyForSignatureAlgorithm({ algorithm }) return { method: 'jwk', keys: [PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(key.publicJwk)] } }, }) for (const { record } of credentials) { if (!(record instanceof SdJwtVcRecord)) throw new Error('Expected an SD-JWT VC') await holder.sdJwtVc.store({ record }) console.log('Stored SD-JWT VC with claims', record.firstCredential.prettyClaims) } requestCredentials doesn't store anything. The SdJwtVcRecord has one instance per credential the issuer returned, so a batch ends up in one record. record.firstCredential.prettyClaims has all claims, decoded.
The verifier needs the same trust configuration as the holder, see Trust the issuer.

The verifier asks for SD-JWT VCs by vct and lists the claims it needs: Verifier verifier.ts const { authorizationRequest, verificationSession } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.createAuthorizationRequest({ verifierId: verifierRecord.verifierId, requestSigner: { method: 'none' }, dcql: { query: { credentials: [ { id: 'identity', format: 'dc+sd-jwt', meta: { vct_values: ['urn:example:identity:1'] }, // Only these claims are disclosed, the others stay hidden claims: [{ path: ['given_name'] }, { path: ['address', 'country'] }], }, ], }, }, transactionData: [ { type: 'urn:example:transaction:age-check', credential_ids: ['identity'], transaction_data_hashes_alg: ['sha-256'], }, ], }) format is dc+sd-jwt. meta.vct_values also matches credentials whose type metadata extends one of the values. Each entry in claims has a path into the credential. null in a path selects all items of an array, and a number selects one item. Add values to only accept certain values, and claim_sets to accept alternative combinations of claims. The wallet discloses only the requested claims. Claims the issuer didn't make selectively disclosable are always in the presentation.

A verifier can ask the holder to sign over extra data, such as the details of a payment, as part of the presentation. The request above has one transactionData entry. type is defined by your application, and credential_ids lists the DCQL credential query ids that may sign it. transaction_data_hashes_alg defaults to sha-256. Credo supports transaction data for SD-JWT VC only, and not with OpenID4VP draft 21.

resolvedRequest.transactionData lists each entry with the credentials that can sign it. Show the user what they're signing, and pass one credential id per entry when you accept: Holder holder.ts const resolvedRequest = await holder.openid4vc.holder.resolveOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest(authorizationRequest) if (!resolvedRequest.dcql?.queryResult.can_be_satisfied) throw new Error('No matching credentials') const result = await holder.openid4vc.holder.acceptOpenId4VpAuthorizationRequest({ authorizationRequestPayload: resolvedRequest.authorizationRequestPayload, dcql: { credentials: holder.openid4vc.holder.selectCredentialsForDcqlRequest(resolvedRequest.dcql.queryResult) }, // Sign each transaction data entry with one of the credentials it lists transactionData: resolvedRequest.transactionData?.map(({ matchedCredentialIds }) => ({ credentialId: matchedCredentialIds[0], })), }) if (!result.ok) throw new Error(`Verifier rejected the presentation: ${result.serverResponse.status}`) The holder includes a hash of each entry in the key binding JWT.

After the session reaches ResponseVerified, the presentation is an SdJwtVc: Verifier verifier.ts const { dcql, transactionData } = await verifier.openid4vc.verifier.getVerifiedAuthorizationResponse( verificationSession.id ) const [presentation] = dcql?.presentations.identity ?? [] if (presentation?.claimFormat !== ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc) throw new Error('Expected an SD-JWT VC presentation') // Only the disclosed claims (plus the always visible ones, like vct and iss) console.log('Disclosed claims', presentation.prettyClaims) console.log( 'Signed transaction data', transactionData?.map(({ decoded }) => decoded.type) ) prettyClaims has the disclosed claims and the claims that are always visible, such as vct, iss and cnf. payload has the raw JWT payload. transactionData has an entry per transaction data entry, with the decoded entry, the credential query id that signed it, and the hashes Credo checked.
